Within less than a day of launch, $REBATE had distributed 231m bonus tokens to buyers, worth approximately $78,549 at the prices at the time. Holder distributions and REBATE buybacks and burns had also begun.

0xb7ff57631b97000d950236ef63bd463da5beba7e 

What I find particularly interesting about this project, however, is that it directly incorporates holding duration into the distribution mechanism: the longer you hold, the greater your distribution weight, reaching up to twice the base weight.

This gives Rebate Pad an opportunity to change the typical behavior of capital in new-token launchpads. Buyers no longer have to wait for the price to rise before selling; holding can also generate distributions paid in USDG. What remains to be proven is whether this mechanism can retain users and turn short-term trading activity into sustained platform revenue and genuine demand for REBATE.

The project has already attracted considerable attention during its initial launch phase. Approximately 90 minutes after launch, the team reported six community-launched tokens, around 1,300 trades, 68 million bonus tokens distributed to buyers, and three rounds of holder distributions completed. About 14 hours after launch, the reported market cap had reached a high of 1.551 million USDG, with 902 token holders, approximately 455,000 USDG in trading volume, 14 rounds of hourly distributions, 97 million bonus tokens distributed, and around 1.5 million REBATE burned. By the time of the approximately 17-hour update, buyers had received a cumulative 231 million bonus tokens, valued at around $78,549 at the prevailing prices, across 2,907 buy transactions.

A subsequent update on the official website showed that the bonus tokens distributed were worth approximately $78,877.66 at the prices at the time. Holders had received approximately $3,476.55 in cumulative distributions across 30 payout rounds, with 7,583 individual payout records. Approximately 1.91 million REBATE had been burned, representing 0.191% of the initial supply, with a stated value of approximately $3,403 at the price displayed on the website. Over the same period, the number of community launches had increased from the initial six to eight. These figures confirm that buy bonuses, holder distributions, and buybacks and burns have all begun operating in practice rather than remaining theoretical mechanisms in a whitepaper.

What really draws my attention is the treatment of holding duration. Many dividend tokens distribute earnings based on the amount held, but Rebate Pad introduces an additional holding-time multiplier: holdings from day 0 to day 3 receive a 1x multiplier, holdings from day 3 to day 7 receive 1.5x, and holdings held for seven days or longer receive 2x. Distribution weight is determined jointly by the amount held and the holding-time tier. Additional purchases do not reset the holding clock for tokens already held, while selling resets the clock only for the portion of tokens sold.

This detail matters because it changes the incentives facing holders. The usual launchpad strategy is to buy early, wait for a price increase, and look for an exit. Holding tokens itself generally provides no additional return. Rebate Pad attempts to make holding economically meaningful: as long as trading activity continues, holders have the opportunity to receive distributions in the paired asset, with longer holding periods carrying greater weight. For REBATE, that distribution asset is USDG.

This could reduce some users' incentive to trade frequently and help the platform build a relatively stable holder base. In particular, once a holding period exceeds seven days and the multiplier reaches 2x, early participants have a reason to continue monitoring the platform rather than focusing exclusively on short-term price movements. However, one point must be made clear: the time multiplier increases distribution weight; it does not guarantee that actual returns will grow at a fixed rate over time. The amount each holder ultimately receives still depends on trading volume and the actual distributions generated. The official rules also explicitly state that distributions may be very small or even zero.

Buy bonuses, meanwhile, are designed to lower the psychological barrier for new users entering the market. Some traditional launchpads impose taxes when users buy tokens, meaning buyers can incur an immediate cost upon execution. Rebate Pad takes the opposite approach by adding bonus tokens directly to the purchase transaction. For REBATE, the bonus rate on each buy is 3%, and the sell fee is also 3%. For other tokens launched on the platform, the bonus rate, sell fee, and holder distribution ratio are set at launch, with the current rules allowing different projects to choose different parameters. Bonus tokens come from the project's locked treasury rather than being created through unlimited inflation.

However, bonus tokens are not cash refunds, and receiving them does not mean a purchase will be profitable. If the token price falls, receiving an additional 3% in tokens may not offset the price decline. Sellers must also pay the corresponding fees. Therefore, the real test of this mechanism is not how large the bonus looks on paper, but whether users remain willing to trade beyond the initial incentive.

For REBATE itself, the value-capture mechanism adds another layer. Its rules follow a structure similar to those of other tokens on the platform: a 3% buy bonus, a 3% sell fee, and a 0.5% holder distribution paid in USDG. In addition, the platform collects fees from trading in other launched tokens and uses the funds to buy and burn REBATE. According to the official rules, the protocol fee on ordinary platform tokens is 0.7%, while the protocol fee on REBATE's own trades is 0.2%. Once collected, the funds are converted into USDG, with 40% used to buy and burn REBATE at market prices and the remaining 60% used to place automatic buy orders below the current price. Tokens purchased through those orders are also burned.

There are two distinct return mechanisms here, and they should not be conflated. The first is the USDG distribution received by REBATE holders, which is linked to trading activity involving REBATE itself. The second is the use of fees generated by trading across all tokens launched on the platform to buy and burn REBATE. The latter creates an opportunity for the token to benefit from the broader launchpad's business growth.

This is also why the market may assign the project a higher valuation. If the community continues launching tokens on Rebate Pad, those tokens generate trading activity, trading produces platform fees, and those fees are used to buy and burn REBATE, then the native token has the potential to establish a more direct connection to the activity of the entire ecosystem. More importantly, the platform would not need to rely on a single popular token: in theory, trading across multiple projects could contribute to its fee revenue.

However, this model is still in its early validation stage. The initial trading volume of 455,000 USDG, thousands of buy transactions, and bonus tokens valued in the tens of thousands of dollars demonstrate that users are willing to try the mechanism, but they do not prove that the activity will persist. Trading during the first day is often driven by novelty and short-term expectations. Furthermore, the market value of bonus tokens fluctuates with token prices and does not mean the platform has paid out an equivalent amount of cash. What really matters is whether trading volume and holder distributions can remain stable after the initial excitement fades, whether the community continues launching new projects, and whether buybacks and burns can expand alongside the platform's business.

In my view, the most promising catalyst for REBATE is the point at which the holding-time mechanism begins to influence user behavior. As early holdings gradually enter the 1.5x and 2x tiers, users may reassess whether to keep holding or sell. If distributions remain meaningful as trading activity continues, the platform could establish a more stable holder base. However, this requires evidence from actual holding-retention and distribution data. Demand should not be assumed to increase simply because the time multiplier rises.

The second catalyst is the launch of more community tokens and the development of sustained trading activity around them. The platform already has multiple trading markets. The next question is whether these tokens can continue attracting buyers after launch rather than generating a burst of activity before quickly losing attention. If trading activity comes from multiple projects, the platform's sources of fees could become more resilient, strengthening the sustainability of the buyback-and-burn mechanism.

Third, the scale of buybacks and burns needs to become more meaningful relative to the token's market capitalization. The existing record of approximately 1.91 million tokens burned demonstrates that the mechanism is operating. However, based on the price displayed on the website, the burn value of approximately $3,403 remains modest compared with the early market-cap high of around $1.55 million USDG. If platform revenue grows, buyback amounts rise accordingly, and the process can be continuously verified through on-chain records, the market will have a stronger basis for assessing its impact. Conversely, if the rate of burning remains low, even a well-designed mechanism may struggle to support the token's long-term valuation through deflationary expectations alone.

The main risks fall into three areas. First, the distribution mechanism depends on genuine trading activity. If volume declines, the actual distributions received by holders may also shrink; a holding-time multiplier cannot create revenue that does not exist. Second, bonuses and distributions may attract participants who are interested only in short-term returns. If trading activity falls once incentives become less attractive, those users may not stay. Finally, allowing community members to launch tokens does not guarantee project quality. New tokens may lack liquidity or even involve deceptive projects, and the platform remains exposed to smart-contract, network, and external-service risks. The official terms explicitly state that bonus tokens and holder distributions do not prevent price losses, and some tokens may be impossible to sell at a reasonable price.

Overall, what makes REBATE worth watching is not simply the strength of its initial trading activity, but the combination of buy bonuses, holding duration, and platform-level buybacks. The time-based distribution multiplier is an important feature that distinguishes it from ordinary launchpads, while the buyback-and-burn mechanism offers a potential path for connecting the native token's value capture to trading activity across the ecosystem.

What will ultimately determine how far it can go is not the cumulative number of bonus tokens distributed, but whether early users remain, community tokens continue generating trades, and those trades translate into sustainable holder distributions and verifiable REBATE buybacks. If Rebate Pad can persuade traders to participate over the long term because of ongoing distributions, rather than simply chase price movements on launch day, it could change more than the reward structure of a launchpad. It could change how users participate in the broader new-token market.

text:
I've always believed that intelligence should come from simple, general building blocks that learn their own abstractions directly from raw data; in other words, the bitter lesson. I think we're finally seeing a real step towards AI that can learn from all data.

Language modeling on raw bytes is a microcosm of this ideal, and to me it's a central problem in AI: if we can't build LLMs that learn end-to-end from bytes, how will we handle the rest of the world's data that we understand even less?

Last year we introduced hierarchical networks (H-Nets) as a first step. Our new version finds up to 3-5x efficiency gains in controlled scaling law experiments, and at larger scale matches an open-source model trained on 11T tokens with ~10x less data and compute. The posts below walk through what we found and why we think it works.

我个人觉得，kntq 的价格行为本身是 sm 喊单+预期的产物。预期兑现期就是一部分钱获利止盈点时间段。

之前的公链生态和生态应用的一致性在于，应用为公链创造活动，公链赚取 gas 费用或者排序器收入。不过问题在于，大部分 layer2 的排序器收入都收归团队，并不会反馈给 layer2 代币持有者。而公链都在向高性能低费用转型，大量的活动无法为其产出足够的收入。这时候就会出现一个很大的缺口，即生态应用无法为代币持有者创造经济层面的价值，最多只是带来部分的注意力。而 elysium 不一样的一点在于其生态应用 @AscendLaunch 不发行代币，并选择使用费用回购 kntq，达成了与 elysium 真正意义上的一致性，这是一个我非常 bullish 的点。

所以我觉得 kinetiq:native 真正的大机会其实是在主网后，如果 ascend 能够占据50%+的 launchpad 份额，那就会有源源不断的费用回购 kntq，为其创造机械性买盘。因此，这是一个非常值得去关注的一个数据。

text:
In the 8 minutes before XPL dropped 18% today, 11 Hyperliquid accounts pulled $1.62M of margin out of their XPL longs.

Then they let the $12M position get liquidated into HLP at mark price.

HLP ate ~$0.6M.

Fresh accounts funded via CCTP. Test withdrawals 20-50 min before. 7 rejected withdrawals while scraping the margin to the limit. $0 left after.

Looks planned. Whether the same operator was short on Binance, I can't see.

Timeline (Nov 1, UTC) 👇

Oct 29-31
9 of the 10 largest accounts are created, each funded once via CCTP with $145k-$243k. On Hyperliquid the sender only shows as Circle's deposit wallet.

03:45-04:15
10 of the 11 make test withdrawals of $500-$1.6k.

04:24-04:32
10 accounts withdraw $98k-$232k each, $1.62M total.
7 more attempts get rejected: "Insufficient balance for withdrawal".
Every dollar the margin check allows comes out. The longs stay open.

04:32
XPL -18% in 1 minute, 0.086 to 0.0705.
$11.2M (144M XPL) trades on Binance perps in that minute.
Hyperliquid itself barely trades.

04:32:50-04:32:59
All 11 get liquidated into the HLP backstop vault, plus 19 small accounts.
160M XPL / $12.2M taken over at avg 0.0759, in a minute that printed a 0.0705 low.

After
All 11 accounts: $0.
Backstop vault: $1.00M to $0.44M while unwinding.
HLP daily PnL: +$21k to -$655k (~0.4% of the vault).

Why it works
Dumping $12M of XPL into the HL book would wreck your own exit.
Drain the margin first, and a small move is enough to trigger liquidation.
Liquidation hands the whole position to HLP at mark with zero slippage. HLP eats the drop after.

Same playbook as the Mar 2025 ETH whale that cost HLP $4M.
If they were also short on Binance, the crash itself was the profit.

Addresses + fills in the reply.

这几天二级市场天天担心AI泡沫破裂、巨头现金流承压，但我翻了一下一级市场的最新动向，发现完全是另一幅冰火两重天的景象。

刚看到彭博社的一个消息，做AI推理部署的初创公司Baseten正在谈新一轮融资，金额大概20亿美元，估值最高直接干到了300亿美元。要知道，就在今年6月份，它的估值才130亿美元。短短三四个月，估值直接翻了一倍多，而且这轮融资连英伟达都跑去参投了。

在这个大家天天喊AI融资断流的节点，这笔钱砸下来，我看了一下背后的逻辑，觉得挺有意思的。

首先，钱在往“推理层”跑。
以前大家搞AI，钱全砸在买卡训练大模型上。但现在模型越来越成熟，开始大规模落地干活了，推理需求直接爆炸。Baseten就是干这个的，帮企业把训练好的模型部署起来运行，据说每天处理超过10亿次推理请求，像Notion、Cursor这些公司都在用。

其次，这个赛道拼的核心是“便宜”。
现在模型跑起来太贵了，云厂商的算力租金居高不下。Baseten主打的卖点就是比OpenAI和Anthropic更便宜的替代方案。对于真正要把AI放进业务流程里的企业来说，谁能帮他们省下那点昂贵的算力费，谁就能拿到钱。

最后，英伟达的参投是个很微妙的信号。
老黄现在不仅是卖GPU铲子，他还在到处买“怎么把铲子用得更便宜、更好”的入口。一级市场的风投和产业资本都不傻，在二级市场因为资本开支过高和现金流而杀跌的时候，他们正拿着钱在押注离商业变现最近的一层。

我个人的看法是，不管二级市场的股价怎么被宏观利率和债务结构按在地上摩擦，AI的真实需求其实一直在一线疯狂运转。巨头们在砸几千亿建基建，而这些像Baseten一样的推理初创公司，就在帮企业以更低的成本消化这些算力。

只要企业还在往AI上砸钱，只要推理的需求还在指数级往上走，AI这波浪潮的底座就是稳的。二级市场的情绪总有退潮的时候，但一级市场真金白银抢着买单的地方，才是产业真实的温度。

text:
I support the ZCG compromise.

But since X is now the place of discussion let me be clear on my personal Zcash positions.

End ZCG and Dev fund. It's painful but it's right. I didn't like the delivery during Zcon, but I don't like state sponsored programs. Don't need to get into philosophy about it it's pretty straightforward. 

Coinholder voting IMO should not control money flows. GINI coeff is too high and it's a plutocracy. Coinholder voting on funds lets the rich vote money to their pet projects. Just kill the whole treasury into NSM.

We should also explore every avenue to recover unspent and unnecessary treasury funds from past grants back to NSM. If there are unspent funds they belong in NSM. Legal fund can be setup to get this money back.

If the community is moving away from a central purse we want to know that the decentralized purse is not a Sybil attack. 

Track incentives and donors for key Zcash programs. Anonymous donors are fine. The big risk is any hidden bonuses for any coordinated behaviors or price targets. 

This isn't necessary or compelled but should be a norm when people are discussing consensus. 

Maybe keep some emergency funding in a "break in case of fire" box that flows into NSM over time if not used. That's like a military and may be a job of the state. Maybe have an elected security council who's only job is to break that box open if needed. It's messy.

On the future: private teams, public goals. 

For example maybe a privately funded Zcash growth team to work w/ teams and pick a set of annual OKRs for the network. Work together to improve those. Metrics should be easy to calculate from any full node to maintain decentralization.

People who do the most to improve OKRs should be publicly identifiable and maybe get donations or further private funding. 

Community can self organize and raise money for projects towards other goals. All voluntary.

I am way more interested in seeing the decentralized efforts towards positive sum goals kick off.

But just to be clear on my politics: I want all the coins back in NSM aside from an emergency box and I want norms around decentralization.

text:
STH筹码结构：重定价，再分配，出现承接力

截止10月31日，STH总供应量（实体调整）为223.53w枚BTC；其中114.7w枚处于浮亏状态，占比51.30%；

STH的持仓成本明显呈现双峰结构：

$78K-$86K是最主要的高位筹码集中区，聚集了114.5w枚BTC，占STH总供应量的51.2%。

$60K-$65K是重要的低成本筹码集中区，有55.6w枚BTC，占比24.9%（图1）。

经过统计，我们发现今年9月是“低成本筹码”减少速度最快的阶段，日均净减少6,733枚；但到了10月的速度开始明显减缓（图2）。

然而，在Binance安全事件发生后，出现了一个非常值得关注的反转：

此前在$78K–$87K持续增加的高成本筹码开始减少，而 $75K–$78K区间在两天内净增加了9w枚BTC，其中4w枚来自高成本区（图3）。

这意味着，BTC的成本重新定价开始向更低的价格区间集中。从市场行为推断，我认为这是一种偏积极的现象。

因为当市场受到突发利空冲击时，仍然有大量筹码在较低价格形成新的持仓成本。这与完全缺乏承接的市场环境存在明显区别。

低成本筹码没有出现持续的，异常剧烈的减少；高成本区间的减少量相对于其庞大的存量仍然有限。

我个人对此的判断是：黑天鹅事件加速了筹码换手和重定价，同时在$75K–$78K区间出现了一批承接力量。

虽然我们还不能据此确认这种力量足够强大到能推动下一轮上涨。但至少可以对下跌形成阻力，平复恐慌情绪。

text:
10 Spicy Takes After Talking to 50 Friends at the Frontier of Robotics 🤖🔥

1/ Astra IS robotics' GPT-3 moment. Ironically, now that it's finally here, some in robotics seem reluctant to acknowledge it. Perhaps because it (sadly) didn't come from a robotics company?

2/ Robotics is becoming just another vertical for frontier labs. Not so different from coding in some respects. Why reinvent general intelligence for every industry?

3/ Robotics was too hard to underwrite until now. No convincing pretraining scaling law, no convergence on models, data, or hardware. No wonder some critics dismissed it as a fragmented industry playing an expensive "demo game". Astra may finally offer a credible path to scale.

4/ Robotics foundation-model startups have a case. But how strong is it? The argument: Astra handles System 2 (reasoning), while specialized models retain System 1 (skills) and System 0 (motor control). Fair. But isn't that already a narrower value proposition? And who says the boundary stops there?

5/ Follow the talent. Word is OpenAI reorganized its 30–40-person robotics team around the core Astra model. Hearing similar moves toward general models at @Tesla_Optimus. Org charts may tell us more than any demo.

6/ The robotics data gold rush is real. Million-hour procurement programs, some potentially reaching tens of millions of hours. Talk of budgets approaching $1B per frontier lab.

7/ Bullish on robotics hardware volumes. As intelligence becomes more accessible, the barriers to building useful robots could fall dramatically. The moat shifts toward reliability, dexterity, integration, and deployment.

8/ Robotics could fuel the next semiconductor and memory supercycle. A 100B-parameter model running on the edge requires ~50GB just for 4-bit weights. Now multiply that by millions of robots. Why do you think @JensenHuang is so obsessed with robotics? @elonmusk saw it coming: https://t.co/oKQi0XDhiL

9/ Is self-driving immune to the general-model threat? After coding and robotics, why assume self-driving remains the exclusive domain of proprietary, vertical models? Robotaxi increasingly feels like a solved problem to me. But if and when frontier labs move into self-driving, we could see an Apple vs. Android dynamic. Think about the implications for $TSLA, Waymo, and other OEMs.

10/ The next bottleneck may not be intelligence. It's deployment. Models are improving faster than our ability to deploy robots in the messy real world. Integration, hardware variance, failure recovery, and economics remain brutally hard. The real moat may be turning intelligence into reliable, profitable physical work.

--
I realize some of these takes may rub people the wrong way, especially those who have spent years doing the hard work of advancing robotics. That's not my intention. 

I'm sharing them to spark debate, not to declare winners and losers. Astra has only been out for a month or so, and it's far too early to draw definitive conclusions. More importantly, when the TAM is this enormous - potentially the largest in tech - there should be plenty of room for different approaches and many winners.

++

text:
I've been seeing a lot of negativity around $CC lately. The price, Featured App rewards, what Super Validators are receiving, the marketing and the delays.

I get it. Nobody enjoys watching something they hold lose value, especially when they see others earning significant amounts of CC. Most of my crypto holdings are in CC.

But I think some perspective is needed.

Starting with Featured Apps, yes, the rewards can be generous. But there are requirements attached, including locking 5 million CC for non issuers or 25 million CC for asset issuers.

Then there's the work of building and running the product. Developers, infrastructure, support and ongoing improvements. I don't know what every team has spent, but none of that is free.

The rewards aren't the same for every project either. Featured App status doesn't automatically mean collecting millions of CC. The product a team builds and the qualifying network activity it generates matter.

If someone builds something useful, attracts users and contributes meaningful activity to Canton, I have no issue with them being rewarded.

There are already over 100 apps participating in the Featured App rewards system, and I expect that number to grow significantly over the coming years.

As more apps gain Featured App status and attract activity, I expect competition for those rewards to increase, with more projects earning a share. That doesn't mean every app will earn an equal amount, but I don't expect today's distribution to stay the same as the ecosystem grows.

Some of the people who built early are benefiting from being early. That's true, and I don't see that as a bad thing. They put time and resources into building something before knowing how it would turn out.

Does that mean every reward is justified or nothing needs adjusting? Of course not. But earning substantial rewards doesn't automatically mean a project is doing something wrong either.

Super Validators also have responsibilities and commitments to meet. Some of their reward allocations depend on milestones and contributions to the network. Not everything they do is necessarily visible to the average CC holder, and some information is confidential.

I think that context matters when discussing what they're receiving.

And let's be honest about my own experience too.

I've been involved since the early days of CC, and there was a period when I earned quite a lot for doing very little. Quite literally. I benefited from that myself.

It was great while it lasted, but was that ever going to be sustainable forever? Of course not.

I think it's only fair to acknowledge that when talking about rewards going to other people.

Another thing I keep coming back to is how young Canton's retail ecosystem still is.

People keep comparing Canton to established blockchain ecosystems that have had years to attract developers, build communities, launch applications and work through problems.

How much are we realistically expecting in such a short period?

I don't expect Canton to have the same depth of applications, tools and communities as ecosystems that have spent years developing them. I want to see progress, but I also want to be realistic about how long this takes.

There are new applications, tools and infrastructure being built, and plenty more being worked on in the background.

When I see teams spending their time and money building on Canton, that means something to me.

Why are all these people choosing to build here?

Clearly, they see an opportunity. That doesn't guarantee they'll succeed, but people generally don't invest significant time and resources into something unless they believe there's potential.

Canton isn't perfect, and I don't need to pretend it is to remain bullish.

There are things that can improve, and some of the criticism is warranted. But I also think Yuval and the wider team deserve credit for the effort they're making.

The founders are active, regularly joining livestreams, interviews and discussions, and engaging with people on X. I genuinely think they're doing a good job of making themselves available to the community.

Could communication improve in some areas? Absolutely. But I also think it's important to recognise the effort already being made.

CIPs are another part of that ongoing improvement. They exist to propose changes, address problems and improve how the network operates.

I'd rather see things constantly being reviewed and improved than have anyone pretend everything is already perfect.

And I don't expect every timeline to be exact. Sometimes things take longer than planned. I'd rather something be delivered properly than rushed just to hit a date.

Yuval has also spoken about doing more for the community, which I think is great. I'm looking forward to seeing what comes of that.

Again, these things take time.

On the investment side, my approach hasn't really changed.

I bought Tesla, Amazon and Meta shares early. I wasn't on X complaining about every marketing decision, every mistake or every time the share price dropped.

I invested because I believed in those companies and their long term potential.

There were ups and downs, periods of uncertainty, bad decisions and times when things weren't looking particularly good.

But I had conviction in my investments and was prepared to ride through those periods.

Look at Nvidia as another example.

Do you think everyone who invested in Nvidia years ago was happy with every single decision the company made? Every mistake, every setback, every drop in the share price?

Of course not.

Every company makes mistakes. Every company has things it needs to improve. Some make terrible decisions along the way.

Why should Canton be any different?

Why is every decision, every delay and every price movement scrutinised as though it's the end of the world?

Some of that scrutiny is absolutely warranted, and I'm not suggesting otherwise.

But let's apply some perspective and hold Canton to reasonable standards, just as we would with any other investment.

And before anyone says it, yes, buying shares in an established company is very different from investing in a crypto token. The risks are different, and I'm not suggesting Canton will follow the same path as any of those companies.

I'm talking about the mindset behind investing.

I want to understand what I'm buying, why I believe in it and what would make me change my mind. I don't want my entire opinion of an investment to depend on whether the price is green or red that week.

And right now, the positives I see in Canton far outweigh the negatives. That's my current assessment, and that's why I'm comfortable staying invested. If those reasons no longer hold up, I'll reassess.

There's also the speculative side of crypto.

Let's be real, a lot of investment in this space is driven by speculation. Hype, narratives and expectations about what something could become, rather than what it has actually achieved.

And I don't think Canton has really attracted that same level of speculative interest from retail yet.

Will that change? I'd like to think so.

As more people discover Canton, more applications launch and the ecosystem continues to grow, hopefully that interest will follow.

I'm already seeing Canton mentioned more regularly across X, more people learning about the network and more projects getting involved.

Compare that to where things were not so long ago.

But I also understand why people are cautious.

Nearly everyone in crypto has been burned at some point. People have lost money, invested in projects that promised everything and delivered nothing, and watched entire ecosystems disappear.

It takes time to build trust, especially among retail investors who have been through all of that.

You can't expect everyone to suddenly discover Canton, trust the network, invest their money and become long term supporters overnight.

That trust needs to be earned.

And growing awareness doesn't automatically mean the price of CC will go up. Eventually, interest needs to translate into real adoption and sustainable network activity.

That's something I want to see develop over time.

Most of my crypto holdings are in CC, alongside a few other Canton ecosystem tokens. I'm holding, earning yield and watching how things develop.

Of course I want CC to go up. I'm hardly enjoying the dips. But I didn't buy expecting a straight line up, and I'm certainly not expecting a 10x within the next month.

I'm more interested in what Canton looks like in two, three or five years than what happens to the chart next week.

If you can't handle a price dip, or you're already fed up because your investment hasn't done a 10x, maybe CC isn't the right investment for you.

There's always a memecoin being hyped as the next 100x somewhere. 

I'm not here for a quick flip. I'm taking a longer view and I'm prepared to sit through difficult periods while my reasons for investing still hold up.

And this is probably the most important point.

If you can't handle losses, or losing money would seriously affect your daily life, be very careful about how much you invest. That applies to stocks and even more so to crypto.

As bullish as I am on Canton and CC, even I understand the risks involved. Nothing is guaranteed, and I could be wrong.

If you're investing for the long term, you need to be prepared for the ups and downs. If you're trading and looking for quick gains, that's a completely different approach, and CC might not be what you're looking for.

What I don't agree with is treating every setback as proof that the whole network has failed, any more than I agree with treating every announcement as proof that CC is about to take off.

I can be bullish on Canton and still disagree with decisions being made. I can question rewards, want better communication and still recognise the effort going into the network.

I don't think those positions contradict each other.

Look at the projects being built, the applications being launched, the institutions involved, the infrastructure being developed and the people spending their time and money trying to grow the ecosystem.

There's a lot happening, and much of it takes place without the average CC holder necessarily seeing it.

As cliche as it sounds, I genuinely believe we're still early in Canton's development.

Not early in the sense that everyone is guaranteed to make money by buying CC today, but early in terms of how much of the ecosystem still needs to be built and how much adoption still needs to happen.

There are challenges ahead, things that need improving and plenty that could go wrong.

But there's also a lot to be positive about.

And I think it's worth explaining why I spend so much time involved with Canton in the first place.

The goal with Canton Army and CantonNews has always been to educate people, promote the ecosystem and support the projects building within it.

That's what we're here to do.

We want to help people understand Canton, discover new projects, learn how things work and stay informed about what's happening across the network.

We'll share the information, highlight opportunities and showcase what teams are building. What you choose to do with that information is entirely up to you.

We're not here to give financial advice, convince anyone to buy CC or push people into buying other tokens or memecoins.

That's never been our goal.

We believe in Canton, which is why we dedicate so much time to covering the ecosystem and supporting the people building here.

And you won't see us crying on X every time the price drops.

Of course we'd prefer the price to be going up, but our long term conviction hasn't changed. We'll continue supporting Canton, helping projects get exposure and growing the community to the best of our ability, regardless of what the chart looks like on any given day.

For me, there's enough progress and potential to remain invested, keep building and give the ecosystem time to develop.

I don't expect everything to go perfectly, but the positives still heavily outweigh the negatives in my view.

And just to be clear, this isn't a post trying to convince anyone to buy CC, and it isn't a prediction that the price will go up.

It's simply my take on the current state of Canton and CC, why I remain invested and why I'm prepared to give it time.

Everyone has their own expectations, investment strategies and appetite for risk. You might disagree with some of what I've said, and that's absolutely fine.

I don't claim to have all the answers, and I'm certainly not saying Canton gets everything right.

I just think there's a much bigger picture here than the daily price movements.

That's my perspective, and it's why I'm still bullish on Canton for the long term.

quoted_text:
I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.

It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?

Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?

Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

text:
From an AI Model Aggregator to a Complete Creative Workflow: The Market Is Starting to Reprice the Relationship Between Darkwoods' Product and $DARK

0xdc45b71d7203c2e8baafc43a19bca0eb993bb54e 

I don't think the recent move in DARK can simply be attributed to speculation around the AI sector. What's more interesting is how Darkwoods' product is evolving. It initially focused on privacy-focused AI and multi-model aggregation, but is now gradually bringing chat, image generation, video, music, full-scale video production, and even coding into a single desktop workflow. At the same time, the connection between product revenue and DARK buybacks and staking distributions is becoming much clearer.

These two developments are the main reasons I remain bullish on the project. Compared with my previous analysis, I believe DARK's fundamentals have strengthened significantly at the product level, while its token value-capture mechanism has become more concrete. However, a stronger product doesn't automatically mean the business model has been proven, especially when on-chain data is still lagging behind recent product developments.

Let's start with the product. Previously, I was interested in Darkwoods mainly because it was trying to solve an overlooked problem in the AI industry: as more models emerge and their capabilities become increasingly similar, why would users continue using the same platform over the long term?

Simply aggregating more models is relatively easy for competitors to replicate. What can actually create a competitive advantage is whether users can consistently complete their work within one platform instead of switching between different tools every day.

Recent updates make me think the team is starting to find that direction.

Director Mode is one of the most interesting features. Users only need to enter an idea, and the system attempts to handle the entire production process, from scripting, character design, and storyboarding to shot generation and final video editing.

This is different from ordinary AI video generation tools. Those tools mainly help users generate individual pieces of content, while Director aims to solve the entire process of turning an idea into a complete video.

The real commercial value here isn't just how impressive the generated results are. It's whether creators can gradually build their characters, stories, and daily creative workflows within the same environment. Once usage frequency increases, the cost of switching to another platform could also rise.

The recently launched Darkwoods Studio takes this a step further by connecting image and video creation. Users can generate images from text prompts, choose different creative styles, and then bring those images into leading video models. The entire process, from the initial idea to the final video, takes place in one environment.

The previously demonstrated one-click character replacement feature is also interesting. Users can upload a video and a reference character, then replace the person in the video with a single prompt while preserving the original movements and scene as much as possible.

This has practical appeal for short-form video creators, derivative-content accounts, and content studios because it reduces the number of tools and steps previously required to complete the same workflow.

Another update is DarkCode. The team has started integrating an AI Coding Agent into its desktop application. Users can point it to a project and let the agent make changes on its own branch, review each modification, protect the main branch, and decide whether to merge the changes afterward.

This is no longer just an AI chat window. It's moving toward becoming a genuine development environment.

Looking at these updates together, Darkwoods is gradually evolving from a model aggregator into a platform combining creative and productivity tools. The number of models still matters, but what I care more about now is whether it can increase how frequently users work within the platform and whether they are willing to delegate more of their daily tasks to it.

According to the official website, the product currently covers chat, images, video, music, voice, APIs, and desktop applications, with a total of 136 models. It also includes custom models developed in-house for creators, such as DarkRoom Cinema 1.0.

I think this is more meaningful than simply adding a few more third-party models. Individual models can be replicated relatively quickly, but if users have already built their characters, creative workflows, project files, and daily working habits within the platform, Darkwoods has an opportunity to achieve stronger retention.

Privacy remains another important advantage for Darkwoods. It emphasizes wallet-signature login, not retaining prompts or generated content, and using Intel TDX, NVIDIA GPU-related trusted execution environments, and anonymous routing to handle different model requests.

It's important to make one distinction here: according to the team's disclosure, nine models currently run inside hardware-based trusted execution environments, while the remaining models mainly access third-party services through anonymous routing. This does not mean every model runs locally, nor does it mean every part of the system has exactly the same level of security.

Even so, reducing the exposure of personal information and content remains valuable for creators, developers, and people working with unpublished code and creative assets.

However, when it comes to DARK, I believe the most important development isn't simply the addition of more product features. It's that product revenue is beginning to establish a more concrete connection with the token.

Previously, the team disclosed that Darkwoods had generated more than $50,000 in Credit Revenue within less than a month after launch. At the very least, this shows that some users are willing to pay for the service rather than simply signing up to try it.

One thing to keep in mind is that Credit Revenue is revenue, not net profit. AI platforms have to bear inference costs, especially for image and video generation, where the cost structure is very different from that of ordinary chat products.

The team has also previously mentioned that some models were offered at heavily subsidized prices to lower the barrier for new users. What we really need to verify going forward is whether users will continue paying after these discounts end, and whether product revenue can cover model inference costs, development expenses, and operating costs.

The currently disclosed tokenomics are as follows: for each eligible AI Credit Purchase, 80% goes into the Treasury to cover inference and operational costs, 10% is allocated to DARK buybacks, and another 10% goes toward USDG rewards for stakers.

The important point here is that users don't need to hold DARK to use the product. They can purchase Credits with a bank card, stablecoins, or other supported cryptocurrencies, while their actual purchases can still be connected to the token through the buyback and staking mechanisms.

I think this design makes more sense than simply requiring users to buy tokens before they can use the product. It lowers the entry barrier for new users while giving product growth an opportunity to generate recurring demand for the token.

As users continue purchasing Credits, part of that spending flows into the buyback and staking distribution mechanisms. The more people use the product, the greater the potential for its token economy to be supported by actual business activity.

However, there's an important detail here: we shouldn't interpret this as every AI inference request directly triggering a DARK purchase and burn.

According to the official contract documentation, the allocation takes place when Credits are purchased. 80% goes into the inference treasury, 10% is used for buybacks, and 10% is allocated to staking rewards.

Payments processed through Request Network do not directly pass through the same on-chain purchase contract. Instead, they are settled periodically according to the allocation recorded in the order. The first payment made by referred users also receives special treatment and does not generate the normal staking and buyback allocations.

In addition, the purchase contract's administrator can adjust the allocation ratios and fund receiving addresses. These are details we shouldn't ignore when evaluating the token's value-capture mechanism.

The team also previously announced that the first $10,000 had been allocated from Creator Fees toward DARK buybacks.

This is positive, but allocating funds for buybacks does not mean the entire $10,000 has already been used to purchase and burn tokens on-chain. These are two separate things and shouldn't be counted twice as both revenue and completed buybacks.

Now let's look at the staking data on the official website.

During our previous analysis, the website showed a TVL of 23,918,967 DARK, 34 stakers, 274 USDG in rewards over the past seven days, 3,809 USDG over the past 30 days, 669 USDG claimed, and cumulative burns of 16,471,491 DARK.

In the latest data, TVL has increased to 28,762,586 DARK, the number of stakers has risen from 34 to 39, seven-day rewards have increased to 815 USDG, and claimed rewards have grown from 669 to 787 USDG.

There is an interesting change here: TVL has increased by approximately 20%, the number of stakers has grown by around 15%, and seven-day rewards have nearly tripled compared with the previous snapshot.

This suggests that recent staking distribution activity has increased and more addresses are willing to participate in staking.

However, the data isn't entirely positive. Rewards over the past 30 days have fallen from 3,809 USDG to 2,582 USDG, while cumulative burns remain unchanged at 16,471,491 DARK.

The increase in seven-day rewards suggests recent distribution activity has improved, but the decline in 30-day rewards is a reminder that we shouldn't conclude product revenue is growing consistently based on short-term data alone.

More importantly, there are currently only 39 stakers, which means the staking ecosystem and user coverage are still at a very early stage.

As for the previously announced buyback allocation, the latest website data doesn't show a corresponding increase in cumulative burns. I'd rather view this as evidence that a token value-capture mechanism has been established, while its actual execution scale still needs further verification.

So why has DARK been moving higher?

I lean toward the view that the move is being driven by a combination of product progress, expectations around token economics, and a technical rebound.

On the product side, Director, Studio, character replacement, and DarkCode have introduced new use cases one after another. The market is beginning to see that Darkwoods is no longer just putting third-party models into a single interface. It's attempting to provide a complete creative and development environment.

On the revenue side, the previously disclosed Credit Revenue and the 10% buyback and 10% staking allocation mechanisms have made the connection between product growth and the token much clearer.

For a small-cap token, this kind of improvement in fundamental expectations can easily become a reason for capital to pay attention again.

Now let's look at the chart.

The 4-hour chart showed a market cap of approximately $4.20M and 24-hour trading volume of around $115.9K at the time of the screenshot.

Price had moved back above the MA10 at approximately $3.93M and the MA20 at around $3.50M. RSI was at 58, suggesting that short-term momentum had recovered without entering an obviously overheated zone.

Price had also reclaimed the $3.71M level. The next area to watch on the upside is around $4.58M. If price can break above and hold that level, the next target to watch would be around $5.82M, followed by the previous high area near $7M.

On the downside, if price falls back below $3.71M, the MA20 area around $3.50M becomes the next level to monitor for support.

I don't think the current price action is enough to confirm a new major uptrend, but it at least shows signs of recovery following the previous correction.

Looking ahead, I believe there are three main catalysts that could drive DARK higher.

First, whether Director and Studio can generate sustained paid usage.

Launching new features can attract attention, but only when creators repeatedly use them and continue purchasing Credits can they generate more consistent product revenue and support future buybacks and staking distributions.

Second, whether DarkCode and the complete desktop workflow can expand the user base.

If Darkwoods can serve both creators and developers, its potential market will no longer be limited to AI video generation or model aggregation. The wider the range of use cases, the greater its opportunity to improve repeat purchases and user retention.

Finally, the tokenomics need to be further validated through actual execution.

Whether the previously allocated $10,000 buyback funds can be verified on-chain, how much DARK is actually purchased and burned each month, whether stakers continue receiving USDG, and whether the staking-exclusive AI Usage feature currently marked as Coming Soon on the website eventually launches will all influence how the market evaluates the token's value-capture capability.

Of course, there are risks that shouldn't be ignored.

First, competition in AI products is extremely intense. Features such as Director, character replacement, and Coding Agents are not impossible to replicate. Darkwoods needs to prove that its workflow integration, privacy capabilities, and overall user experience are good enough. Otherwise, adding more features could simply increase model inference costs without creating meaningful user retention.

Second, more than $50,000 in Credit Revenue does not mean the business is profitable. Model costs, subsidies, and operating expenses could all compress margins.

Third, holding DARK is not a requirement for using the product. Users can access Darkwoods without holding or staking the token. Therefore, token demand mainly relies on buyback and staking incentives rather than mandatory usage demand.

On top of that, some payment methods require off-chain settlement, the allocation parameters of the purchase contract can be adjusted, and different models follow different privacy execution paths. These are all areas where token value capture and security still need continuous verification.

But my view on DARK is now more positive than before.

Not because it has integrated a few more models, but because the product is evolving from individual AI features into a complete workflow, while the business model is beginning to connect actual user spending with token buybacks and staking rewards.

For an early-stage AI project, I think this is much more meaningful than simply riding the AI narrative.

What I really want to see next isn't another new feature announcement. It's whether Director and Studio can bring in more repeat paying users, whether Credit Revenue continues growing after subsidies are reduced, and whether the buyback funds already allocated can translate into verifiable on-chain purchases and burns.

To sum it up, the market is betting on an economic cycle that starts with AI usage, moves through product revenue, and eventually flows into DARK buybacks and staking rewards.

This cycle now has an initial structure, but it hasn't been fully proven yet.

What ultimately determines how far DARK can go isn't how many more models Darkwoods can integrate. It's how many users are willing to make it a tool they open every day and continue paying for.

In other words, DARK's product fundamentals are strengthening, but its token value capture still needs to be validated through three sets of data: revenue, buybacks, and user retention.

That's why I'm bullish on it at this stage, while still being unwilling to price in all the future expectations too early.

Instead, it can integrate different capabilities and become a unified entry point for users entering AI-powered creation. Of course, character replacement and generative content still involve compliance issues relating to likeness rights, copyright, and specific use cases, which will affect the markets the product can serve in the future.

Privacy remains another important differentiator for Darkwoods compared with ordinary AI tools. It emphasizes wallet-based login and not retaining prompts or generated content. It also offers DarkCode, a desktop application that allows users to perform code-related operations on local folders and run multiple agents in parallel. The product combines cloud-based models with local capabilities, and the team has also presented a privacy architecture built around Intel TDX, secure NVIDIA GPU environments, and anonymous routing.

This approach targets a clear group of users: creators, developers, and people working with sensitive material who may not want to hand over all their prompts, code, and generated assets to a traditional cloud service. If Darkwoods can strike a balance between usability and privacy, it could establish a more distinctive position than a simple model aggregator. However, I would not equate "private" with every operation being performed locally or data being absolutely secure in every circumstance. The data-processing boundaries and execution methods of different models still need further verification.

For DARK, the truly important change is happening in the connection between the product and the token.

The biggest question previously was whether improvements to Darkwoods' product would necessarily translate into value for DARK. The mechanisms disclosed by the project now provide at least one clear pathway. According to the official materials, when users purchase AI credits, approximately 80% is allocated to operations and model inference costs, 10% is used for DARK buybacks, and another 10% goes toward staking rewards paid in USDG. Users do not need to hold DARK before using the product, but product spending can still be connected to the token through the buyback and staking mechanisms.

It lowers the barrier to entry for new users while attempting to make product growth create demand for the token in return. If users continue purchasing credits, with part of the spending used to buy back DARK and another part supporting staking rewards, the token's economic thesis could gradually become grounded in actual usage rather than relying solely on market expectations for the AI sector.

Recently, Darkwoods also announced that it had allocated the first $10,000 from creator fees for DARK buybacks. Here, an important distinction must be made: the official announcement stated that the funds had been allocated for buybacks. It should not be interpreted as meaning that the entire $10,000 had already been used to execute on-chain purchases and burns. This funding source is also separate from the buyback allocation associated with credit purchases, so the two should not be counted twice as the same revenue.

In addition, the dashboard you provided shows approximately 16.47 million DARK burned, around 23.92 million DARK in staking TVL, 34 staking addresses, and approximately 3,809 USDG in rewards over the past 30 days. These figures show that the burn and staking mechanisms have left actual records of execution. However, the number of staking addresses remains limited, so I would treat this as early validation rather than evidence that a mature tokenomics flywheel has already been established.

Another signal worth monitoring is the approximately 274 USDG in rewards over the past seven days, compared with the cumulative 3,809 USDG over the past 30 days. If both figures use the same measurement methodology, the reward rate over the most recent week is below the average weekly rate over the preceding 30 days. This alone is not enough to conclude that product usage is declining, but it is a reminder that we cannot focus solely on cumulative revenue, cumulative burns, and cumulative rewards. We also need to monitor whether new paid usage continues and whether recent economic activity is slowing down.

Darkwoods previously disclosed that credit revenue had exceeded $50,000 less than a month after launch. This is a positive signal, showing that at least some users are willing to pay for the service. But revenue is not profit, especially for an AI platform that relies heavily on third-party models and must continually pay inference costs. The team has also acknowledged that some models are offered at heavily subsidized prices to lower the barrier for new users to try the product, with the broader chat, coding, image, and video workspace intended to improve retention.

This strategy can help the platform acquire users, but what ultimately determines whether the business model works is whether users remain willing to pay after subsidies end and whether revenue can cover model costs, development expenses, and operating costs. If users only try the product when model prices are heavily discounted and leave once those offers end, short-term revenue will be difficult to sustain long-term buybacks. Conversely, if Director Mode creates more frequent creative usage and users begin treating Darkwoods as a daily tool, product revenue has a better chance of becoming a more sustainable source of token demand.

Therefore, I believe DARK's fundamentals have strengthened significantly at the product level, and its value-capture mechanism has become more concrete, but the sustainability of its business model is still being tested. The most valuable recent development is not the addition of a few model integrations. It is that the product is beginning to connect a complete creative workflow, recurring paid usage, and token buybacks.

Going forward, I am most interested in whether Director Mode can generate sustained credit consumption and whether the announced $10,000 buyback can be confirmed through verifiable on-chain records. If product usage grows, buybacks are actually executed, and staking rewards remain at a reasonable level, the market will have a stronger basis for reassessing the relationship between DARK and Darkwoods' business growth. If new features continue to be released without sustained paid usage and buybacks, however, product development and token performance may still remain disconnected.

For me, what makes DARK worth being bullish on is its attempt to establish an economic cycle that starts with product usage: users pay for AI creation, the platform uses that revenue to maintain the service and develop the product, and part of the funds then flow back to token holders through buybacks and staking rewards. This cycle has not been fully established yet, but it is no longer just an abstract token narrative. What will ultimately determine how far DARK can go is not how many more models Darkwoods integrates, but how many users continue using it and whether that usage can translate into stable, verifiable demand for the token.

text:
Poisoning just 0.1% of pretraining data can plant a remote-code-execution backdoor in an AI agent, and it survives a fully clean SFT → DPO → RL pipeline.

New Anthropic paper, “Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning,” shows this end to end for the first time.

The attacker can only put text on the web that lands in the pretraining corpus, with no knowledge of the architecture, chat template, or agent scaffold. The authors pretrain Qwen3-architecture models (0.6B / 1.7B / 4B) from scratch, then post-train them into CLI agents on clean data. When triggered, the agent runs a command that downloads and executes the attacker's script, which the attacker can swap at any time.

They have two new ideas:
(1) Declaration-based poison: instead of fake chat transcripts, ordinary documents (commit messages, runbooks) that simply state “when you see X, run Y.” It plants a belief rather than a response template, with no fixed format to filter on.
(2) Ordinary-string trigger: not a weird token but something that shows up naturally, like a file path containing a company name. The victim's own request supplies it, so the attacker doesn't need to inject anything after deployment.

Using  path trigger on a 4B agent achieves 92.7% attack success on pass@32, barely dented by SFT/DPO/RL

This suggests that you can't count on clean post-training to wash out pretraining poison, and filtering is hard when the poison reads like normal docs. The practical defense is at the action layer, such as sandboxing, least privilege, and allow-lists or human sign-off for risky commands.

text:
One Claude Code session, 40K comments, 6,454 videos, about 2 hours.

Andrej Karpathy put HackerTube on his blog on October 31. It is a YouTube style site that only shows videos Hacker News users recommended in comments, from 2007 to 2026.

He built it with Claude Code running Opus 5.5 at medium effort, and he did very little of the engineering himself. Opus downloaded the Hacker News comment data and filtered it. Then it ran Sonnet over the comments in a Claude Code Workflow to remove spam and find the YouTube recommendations.

That pass found about 40K comments recommending a video. The final site has 6,454 of them across 150 topics.

He did three things by hand: got a YouTube API key from Google Cloud, set up a VPS and bought the domain. Claude handled deployment, security hardening and optimization.

The site has a For You feed stored in your browser with no accounts, plus keyboard shortcuts and a data export so others can build their own version.

The model split is the part to copy. Opus writes the pipeline and Sonnet does the bulk reading of 40K messy comments. The same split fits app reviews, support tickets or game forum threads.

Which pile of text in your own product would you run a cheap model pass over first?

text:
朝鲜可能是数字时代最值得研究的不对称竞争案例之一。

一个传统经济规模有限、普通民众互联网接入受限的国家，却能在全球数字金融体系中形成惊人的网络攻击能力。

但我觉得这里有一个更深层的 Insight：

工业时代，一个国家需要庞大的工业体系才能产生巨大的外部影响；数字时代，少数掌握关键技术和权限的人，就可能对远大于自身的经济系统造成冲击。

Binance 最近约 63 亿美元的加密资产失窃事件，再次暴露了一个问题。

真正脆弱的可能不是区块链的密码学，而是掌握私钥、签名权限和基础设施访问权的人类组织。

攻击者不需要战胜整个系统，只需要找到一个能够控制整个系统的薄弱环节。

而 AI Agent 的普及，可能进一步放大这种不对称性。

当 Agent 开始拥有生产环境、金融账户和企业内部系统的操作权限，攻击者成功获取一次高权限访问的潜在后果也会随之扩大。

这让我越来越觉得，AI 时代网络安全最重要的问题，可能不再只是如何让系统不被入侵。

而是如何设计一个系统，使得即使某个高权限 Agent 或员工被攻破，也无法造成灾难性的连锁反应。

未来最昂贵的安全漏洞，可能不是代码错误，而是我们赋予智能系统的权力超过了我们约束它的能力。
author: noahatwhere
quoted_text:
一个社会的整体技术水平，未必决定它在某个特定技术领域能够达到的能力上限。

而且网络攻击的经济杠杆极其不对称。

防御者需要保护庞大的系统、供应链、员工和权限体系；攻击者却只需要在某个关键环节找到一次突破口。

当然，盗走 63 亿美元不等于获得 63 亿美元净收益。大量资产已经被冻结，攻击者归属和完整攻击链也仍需进一步确认。

但真正值得担忧的是：

当数字资产规模越来越大，而系统安全仍然依赖复杂的人类组织和权限管理时，少数攻击者能够施加的经济影响可能远远超过传统认知。

尤其进入 AI Agent 时代，当 Agent 开始获得代码库、生产环境、财务系统和资产操作权限，这种不对称性可能进一步扩大。

AI 能放大生产力，也可能放大一次权限失控所造成的破坏。

未来网络安全最重要的问题，可能不仅是如何防止黑客入侵，而是如何确保即使某个环节被攻破，整个系统也不会因此失控

quoted_text:
有朋友问，为什么Musk又和赵长鹏吵起来了？

确实最近Elon很忙。所以说“又”是对的，这个月Musk已经跟Zelensky、跟Talarico都吵过了，这回轮到Binance的创始人赵长鹏。事情不复杂。Binance被盗以后，Musk在赵长鹏前一天提醒大家别乱点链接的帖子底下，回了火焰和大笑的表情，又在一串讨论Binance赔不赔得起的帖子里，回了一个龇牙咧嘴的表情，那串讨论里，有人贴出了FTX倒闭前，Bankman-Fried说资产够兑付所有客户的旧话。赵长鹏回他：“Elon，我很尊重你，但现在不是调侃的时候，请停下。”还提到Binance当年投了五亿美元帮他买Twitter，那些股份现在成了SpaceX的股票，值十亿美元以上，希望他稍微支持一下。网上有人读成要卖股票报复，赵长鹏和联席CEO何一后来都说，没这个意思，也用不着卖。

谁对谁错，我反倒觉得不是重点。重点是，这一来一回，没有一句是替用户在问的。一个表情不是问题，一句请你支持我，也不是回答。被盗六十多亿美元，用户最该知道的几件事，在这场吵架里一件都没出现。

先说最该问的。Binance的联席CEO Richard Teng说，攻击不止一个人，是用以太坊的EIP-7702功能，在正常管控之外拿到了一个热钱包的批准权限，还用了能自毁的程序抹掉痕迹。官方公告说，最早怀疑是一台被攻破的笔记本电脑，后来又查出别的突破口，目前没有证据显示私钥泄露。那么，一台电脑怎么就能走到批准这一步？正常管控为什么没拦住？一个钱包出事，为什么别的钱包也跟着出事？谁该为此负责，以后改什么？写Binance被盗那篇我说，章是真的，问题出在盖章的流程。这些才是流程上的问题，可它们上不了热搜，上热搜的是表情。

再说赔。Binance说，已经用公司的钱买回了九成被盗的币，钱来自用户保护基金、合约保险基金和公司金库，剩下一成是流动性差的币，提现计划周日重开，还会出储备证明。这是对的，也该肯定。可要说清楚一点，用户保住本金，不是恩赐。币是用户存在那里的，交易所是保管的一方，保管的东西丢了，补上，是本分。说成我们会承担、我们有家底、今年营收就够，听起来像大方，其实是把一笔该还的账，说成了一份该感谢的礼。一旦大家开始感谢，为什么会丢的那个问题，就淡了。

还有赔不到的人。消息出来一小时内，据CoinGlass的数据，六亿多美元的杠杆仓位被强制平仓，比特币、BNB都跟着跌。这些人未必在Binance存过钱，Binance的全额承担，补的是被偷走的那些币，补不了整个市场被震的那一下。这一下怎么算，该不该有人算，也同样没人在问。在这样的时候，一个有两亿多粉丝的人拿表情起哄，就算没多大实际影响，也不是在帮任何一个用户。

写星链那篇，我说最让人不安的是责任蒸发，签字的人互相指。这一次，倒没有人推卸，Binance认了，也在赔，可责任还是有可能被冲淡，不是被推走的，是被吵架声盖住的。我在制度论里对制度只要求一件事，人若要问，构要让他问得了，并且要答。Binance答应了要出完整的复盘，这份复盘写得清不清楚，经不经得起外人查，比谁在网上吵赢了重要得多。

钱补回来，是该做的；为什么会丢，是该说的；以后怎么不再丢，是该改的。这三件事，吵架一件都替代不了。

text:
Saying “everything worked as it was supposed to” while people are scared and losing money on hardware wallets, on bridges, on DEXes and CEXes is a weird definition of working.

What does a credibly neutral L1 actually do for anyone if nothing built on top of it is safe enough to use?

At some point we have to step out of the cypherpunk echo chamber and admit nobody is going to use these networks if security doesn’t get meaningfully better. Neutrality isn’t a product. Not getting drained is.

And has anyone stopped to think what happens if Binance, for whatever reason, couldn’t plug the hole? 

I think ONLY relying on emergency funds going forward is just madness.
author: LorenzoARK
quoted_text:
From a teachers perspective, the past 12 hours were an excellent teaching moment for why crypto is special.

And FWIW, my ultimate conclusion to my students was that everything worked as it was supposed to, and blockchain actually demonstrated why it is useful.

The credibly neutral networks did nothing despite the scale of the theft and the bearer assets remain stolen. The parts of the ecosystem that are more centralized played their part and intervened. And of course, everything was shockingly transparent in real time.

Having a hierarchy of neutrality and censorship-resistance, where base layers and assets are cypherpunk, but higher level networks and assets are not, is optimal.

Those who seek maximum protection can have it, at the risk of nobody coming to their rescue when something goes wrong. Those who want greater safety and convenience can have it too, at the risk of being abused by those meant to protect them down the line.

Importantly, individual choice and market forces decide which part of the hierarchy anyone lives on - not regulations or monopolists.

Grok「土豆姐」 @poteto 成名之前，是怎样一路走来的？

她回忆，高中时父亲给了一份盗版Photoshop。回过头看，如果没有当年的软件，她不确定自己会不会走上这条职业道路、靠自己学到这么多。紧接着，她又说，软件授权便宜了、有些甚至免费，能让更多人进入技术世界。

从第一次上台，到管理「AI同事」。这11年，见证了一个人、一个产品的蜕变之旅。

here’s a short grok bot guide on how i create high quality bots and manage my team. ask @bot to read this post and help you improve your team!

• add dr eggbot to your team! he’s my bot designer that i use to create bots
• you don’t need a lot of bots. a few good bots can be more useful and easier to manage than a large team
• tell your bots to create skills for itself as you give it instructions on how to do tasks. this lets them do them more consistently even over long conversations. you can even ask it to create a private github repo for you to store all your skills if you want them preserved independently
• add connectors, use the vault, and give access to all the tools you use to do your work. you can also ask your bot to setup its own email and it can sign up for its own accounts for better separation 
• thinking about all the work you do by hand, or steps in your workflows where you have to copy and paste information back to your bot. ask your bot how it can do that for you instead!
• imagine you hired an intern, how would you onboard them and help them do the work correctly and efficiently? introduce yourself to your bot and describe the work you do, then ask it how it can help you automate it

and my favorite tip: use voice mode or the transcription option! it’s a good way to just brain dump a lot of information. then, at the end, tell your bot to “restate this in your own words” so you can confirm it understood you

FBI说是将军干的，显然不一定真实，因为一切都有目的。
我突然想起童年时期爸爸给我买的马基雅维利写的“君主论”的一句话“在国家利益面前，道德与伦理，往往都要为生存和权利让路”
一个人偷钱，小偷，一群人偷钱，犯罪集团，一个国家组织偷钱，却可能被包装成国家战略。
一个人杀人，叫谋杀，一群人杀人，叫屠杀，一个国家发动战争，却可以称之为维护国家安全。
个人犯罪，需要接受审判，国家越界，却算了不说了
最讽刺的是，几乎每个集体都在高举正义的旗帜，每场冲突，都有冠冕堂皇的理由。
谴责别人的时候，讲道德，轮到自己的时候，讲利益。
五百年过去了，科技在进步，文明在发展，战争在键盘上完成。
但权利的逻辑，似乎从未改变。
所谓政治现实主义最冰冷的地方，就是它提醒我们，道德可以约束普通人，却未必约束得住权利。
所以君主论五百年后，依然是本好书。

author: BranchManager69
quoted_text:
"companies will adjust" assumes every participant gets paid to adjust. but payments is an inherently multi-party risk system. so let's entertain what happens if @stripe's solutions get widely adopted.

agents start buying the wrong thing at scale and fraud skyrockets. having worked in payment fraud, this is a matter of when, not if. disputes and friendly fraud go up dramatically. merchants have no proof of what the user intended and eat chargebacks plus return and refund costs.

after enough of that, the merchant does the rational thing: friction on agent traffic, step-up checks, or just blocking it. several big merchants are already tweaking.

now assume stripe magically sends merchants intent and risk data. stripe processes less than 2% of global GDP, so this has to reach non-stripe merchants too. assume distribution gets solved and every merchant wants agentic traffic through stripe (having worked with the biggest merchants, they are not this AI-pilled, but fine).

it's still close to impossible:
- stored value breaks the link between the funding leg the customer authorized and the purchases that happen later
- stripe would have to pass that data per transaction through its virtual cards
now assume stripe pulls that off too, and merchants integrate, ingest the data and write rules. for context, chargeback representment only matured in the past decade, and that was with clear network rules since the early 2000s.

then there are the issuers. they see top-ups instead of merchant purchases. no MCC, no rewards, disputes they can't adjudicate. they tighten approvals on agent wallets or decline them. 

lets assume stripe sends issuers MCC, risk and auth data so they can pass rewards through and underwrite credit. it won't, because stripe is becoming the issuer in its own closed loop and taking their share. BUT say it does. stripe gives merchants and issuers everything they need, and they all submit to stripe as the kings of payments.

congrats, you just built a card network!

the networks would NEVER let that happen. visa, mastercard and amex are worth close to $1.5T together, and stripe is a baby next to them. they'll use their distribution to make stripe run on their rails. fintechs have tried to displace the networks for decades and it's futile. not only because the network effects are strong, but because today every participant is paid to stay in

the assumptions this needs, all at once:
- stripe reaches the commerce it doesn't process
- stored value somehow keeps the link from funding to purchase
- intent data rides on every virtual card transaction
- merchants integrate faster than they ever have
- issuers hand their economics to a competitor
- the networks let a new network form on top of them
- users are so ai pilled that they are willing to let stripe figure out all of this while the experience sucks, their rewards dont work and merchants they like and issuers they bank with won't authorize their purchases. 

each one is unlikely on its own. together, well the odds are zero.

一涉及政治跟多人只看立场，不看观点和框架了。这篇推文开头拿预测市场的数据说中选民主党横扫是大概率、共和党保住参议院是小概率，引发了很多人不满，说民调和预测市场都是左派阴谋，是不是阴谋我其实没那么关心。甚至上周这里https://t.co/o6v6YrNzrk还以22年中选为例来说不要看现在蓝潮声势很猛但不一定民主党就真的能横扫。

可是大家真有看这篇推文么？这篇推文开头只是拿预测市场的数据来说两种情景，但关键的内容根本不是谁赢。而是在民主党横扫和共和党保住参议院这两种情景下不同的国会权力结构对AI、加密产业政策、财政支出有何不同、以及对市场的影响是什么。

而且更重要的推文强调的：站在市场的角度，关于中期选举“结束可能比结果更重要”！

对于做投资来说、选举这东西哪一方赢并不重要。重要的是说针对不同的情景结果来看不同的影响，不同的结果下政策走势是什么、对市场的影响是什么？并基于此提前做一些应对策略。

至于说谁赢，根本不是这篇推文讨论的重点，但貌似感觉很多人只看开头、不看全文内容。🤣
author: qinbafrank
quoted_text:
对于下周的中期选举，结果很重要但结束可能更重要。聊聊我的理解：1、现阶段概率最大的还是民主党横扫拿下参众两院；
小概率事件是共和党能保住参议院，变成分裂国会；

2、历来中期选举前市场动荡很大，过去几次中期选举皆是如此。这也是8月底在168X上https://t.co/MrasWYxXvC聊到的：中期选举前动荡加大。核心还是政治的不确定性，这个不确定性在于国会的归属会影响市场对于政策走向的判断，两院归属不确定自然也就无法对政策走向有相当明了的推演预判，自然会天然避险；

一旦结果出来了、市场就能知道后续政策大概率走向，充分反应后，选举的扰动就会褪去。

说说两个选举结果的影响
3、先说小概率的“分裂国会”情景
这种自然是大家期望的，一方面民主党掌控众议院对川普的疯癫能有一定的限制，另一方面川普对加密和AI产业的政策力度还能保持。
还能出现：
民主党控制众院 → 限制激进财政政策 → 赤字扩张放缓 → 长端利率压力下降 → 美股受益。
这种市场自然乐于见到。

4、而更大概率的“民主党横扫”情景
很多人会担心民主党掌控国会两院后对让美国对AI和加密领域的政策不仅停滞而且还会开倒车。
但有几点需要明确：
1）民主党掌控两院，政府行政权还在共和党手里，川普还是总统。很多人一说民主党掌控两院就是上台了，其实并不是。
如果民主党要废除既有法律、改变税制或推动新的大规模产业限制，通常需要两院通过新法，再交总统处理。川普可以否决。

要推翻否决，需要两院分别达到三分之二的支持。普通的国会多数，距离这个门槛很远。因此，“民主党夺两院，所以特朗普的法律自动失效”在制度上不成立。

已经成形的法案继续落地、行政权在手里，政府机构还在是共和党掌控、。

2）现在担忧很大的民主党掌控国会会让AI基建倒退
目前民主党在AI问题上有监管和征税两个方向，有民主党议员提案禁止数据中心建设和AI治理框架、但是否决权还在川普手里、这些法案都难以推进，更多是在为选后的听证和议程铺路，扰动情绪。

两党有共识的是数据中心的电网成本分摊，也是选后最有可能落地的AI相关立法。 之前众议院9月16日以417比3通过《Ratepayer Protection Act》，要求各州监管机构考虑让100兆瓦以上的大负荷用户承担其带来的全部发电和电网升级增量成本，但并不强制各州采用。
其实共和党对这方面也提出了这些要求。

但有一点，民主党应该也清楚在AI这场国家军备竞赛的意义和重要性，他们也很难说开倒车。更多的是纠偏、之前共和党的很多政策过激过度、控制步子迈得幅度、但并不是说就止步不前甚至落后，民主党也接受不了美国在AI上落后的代价。

3）再说加密
其实9月中清晰法案受阻、个人角度其实已经不指望未来两件有国会层面的加密立法，而是更看重sec和cftc在各自行政权限范围内给到了最大的政策范围。

之前这里https://t.co/xBS30IWyFe有聊过，构建行政版清晰框架。其实也够用了，未来两年SEC和CFTC主席都是川普提名的共和党人。

4）民主党横扫掌控两院能做到什么？
民主党夺取众院，已经能够限制相当一部分新增立法；
再拿下参院，新增的关键影响是人事确认、参院委员会议程，以及更强的监督与谈判能力。
能限制很大程度上限制共和党的新立法能力和进程，对很多政策和人发起国会调查和听证，但也限于此毕竟司法部未来来两年还在川普手里。

所以总的来说：
中期选举结束比结果可能更重要些，选举结束无论结果如何市场都能根据新的国会权力格局来做推演未来政策可能性、新的边界和程度会如何？而现在这些都悬在空中。

text:
"Make it cinematic" gets you nothing. Name the shot and Claude nails it.

Save these for your next Claude or Codex video:

→ Push in: slow move toward the subject to build tension
→ Pull back reveal: start tight, pull out to show the whole scene
→ Dolly zoom: move in while zooming out, the background stretches
→ Whip pan: fast pan that blurs into the next shot
→ Orbit: the camera circles the subject
→ Crane up: the camera rises above the scene
→ Tracking shot: the camera moves alongside the subject
→ Dutch angle: tilted frame for unease
→ Rack focus: focus jumps from foreground to background
→ Parallax: layers slide at different speeds for depth
→ Match cut: two shapes line up across a cut
→ Smash cut: calm to loud in one frame
→ Speed ramp: slow motion snaps back to real speed
→ J-cut: the next scene's sound starts before its picture

Then prompt it like a director:

"Make a 20-second launch video for [product] in code. Shot list: push in on the logo, whip pan to the main screen, orbit the device with a speed ramp, rack focus to the tagline, smash cut to black, pull back reveal of the full product."

text:
As it turns out, crypto being regulated and supported by governments might be a better outcome than running away from them.

Years of decentralization theatrics, not your keys, not your crypto, hardware wallets, governance, etc mean very little when customers / businesses keep losing money to hackers / scammers.

Being able to freeze hacked or stolen funds, recover assets, reverse txns and protect customers should be a feature, not something that goes against cryptos ethos. Obv a fine line between government overreach vs pure decentralization 

At the end of the day, every time someone loses money, we risk losing that user forever. And the more users we churn, the lower the chances of crypto actually succeeding.

Decentralization still matters, but we likely spent too much time optimizing for it, e.g like thorchain or Tornado Cash, where bad actors can take far more advantage of permissionless infra vs the avg user 

While we spent far less time optimizing for customer centric features like trust, safety, fraud prevention, and recovery, which are arguably far more important for mass adoption.

quoted_text:
10 Spicy Takes After Talking to 50 Friends at the Frontier of Robotics 🤖🔥

1/ Astra IS robotics' GPT-3 moment. Ironically, now that it's finally here, some in robotics seem reluctant to acknowledge it. Perhaps because it (sadly) didn't come from a robotics company?

2/ Robotics is becoming just another vertical for frontier labs. Not so different from coding in some respects. Why reinvent general intelligence for every industry?

3/ Robotics was too hard to underwrite until now. No convincing pretraining scaling law, no convergence on models, data, or hardware. No wonder some critics dismissed it as a fragmented industry playing an expensive "demo game". Astra may finally offer a credible path to scale.

4/ Robotics foundation-model startups have a case. But how strong is it? The argument: Astra handles System 2 (reasoning), while specialized models retain System 1 (skills) and System 0 (motor control). Fair. But isn't that already a narrower value proposition? And who says the boundary stops there?

5/ Follow the talent. Word is OpenAI reorganized its 30–40-person robotics team around the core Astra model. Hearing similar moves toward general models at @Tesla_Optimus. Org charts may tell us more than any demo.

6/ The robotics data gold rush is real. Million-hour procurement programs, some potentially reaching tens of millions of hours. Talk of budgets approaching $1B per frontier lab.

7/ Bullish on robotics hardware volumes. As intelligence becomes more accessible, the barriers to building useful robots could fall dramatically. The moat shifts toward reliability, dexterity, integration, and deployment.

8/ Robotics could fuel the next semiconductor and memory supercycle. A 100B-parameter model running on the edge requires ~50GB just for 4-bit weights. Now multiply that by millions of robots. Why do you think @JensenHuang is so obsessed with robotics? @elonmusk saw it coming: https://t.co/oKQi0XDhiL

9/ Is self-driving immune to the general-model threat? After coding and robotics, why assume self-driving remains the exclusive domain of proprietary, vertical models? Robotaxi increasingly feels like a solved problem to me. But if and when frontier labs move into self-driving, we could see an Apple vs. Android dynamic. Think about the implications for $TSLA, Waymo, and other OEMs.

10/ The next bottleneck may not be intelligence. It's deployment. Models are improving faster than our ability to deploy robots in the messy real world. Integration, hardware variance, failure recovery, and economics remain brutally hard. The real moat may be turning intelligence into reliable, profitable physical work.

--
I realize some of these takes may rub people the wrong way, especially those who have spent years doing the hard work of advancing robotics. That's not my intention. 

I'm sharing them to spark debate, not to declare winners and losers. Astra has only been out for a month or so, and it's far too early to draw definitive conclusions. More importantly, when the TAM is this enormous - potentially the largest in tech - there should be plenty of room for different approaches and many winners.

++
Full diligence report: https://t.co/qlaR5qUzpr

text:
【美股复盘与展望】

美股经历了非常惨烈的一周.QQQ再跌都要跌破MA200进入技术性熊市了。SOXX则已经跌破MA200。

虽然下跌是谷歌、INTC 财报开的头，但周五这种级别的下杀，我觉得不是光基本面能解释的。周五正好是巨额期权交割日，所以周五的下跌更像是财报触发的一系列多头杠杆清算。

回过头看这周引起动荡的几个财报，谷歌、亚马逊、INTC。

谷歌：现金流继续为负，广告业务增速放缓（市场担心AI影响搜索），云业务增速超预期

亚马逊：现金流为负，AWS云业务增速创历史新高，未来两年每年40%增速。

INTC：AI CPU增速70%+， PC端因为存储暴涨压制消费电子预计明年需求下滑10%。 管理层傻逼没提前切产线，PC端卖不出去，AI端需求满足不了。指引严重miss。

仔细分析上面这三份财报的要点。 每一个财报都在利好AI，甚至爆雷的点也在利好AI。

所有AI相关的业绩都超预期，所有人担心AI影响谷歌的搜索业务、亚马逊的购物广告业务。

INTC管理层因为低估存储影响，低估AI CPU 需求，导致业绩指引miss。

所以从基本面来看，我觉得大部分AI、半导体标的在过去的一周被严重错杀了。

市场的现状也很容易理解。

资金不愿意再给半导体成长股定价，一切都向存储那样的周期股逻辑定价。逻辑可能是觉得现金流为负的资本开支不可持续，可能是觉得AI未来需求会放缓等等。

AI这条线目前我觉得有三条逻辑线。

乐观：AI需求持续高速抬升，企业端渗透加速，云厂们因为看到了巨大的算力需求CapEx一路增长到2030年，但随着数据中心落地，收入抬升，云厂们不用再扩大现金流缺口。半导体公司不再算是传统制造业，他们直接就是生产力。

这种情形下：云上涨、半导体不再是周期股。

中性：AI需求增速放缓，算力增速在2028年放缓，算力在后续的时间里需求略微大于供给，云厂们不再增加资本开支，资本开支略减或者维持。云厂现金流转正。半导体公司收入放缓甚至略微下降。

这种情形下：云上涨，半导体跌

悲观：AI泡沫，过去的资本开支导致未来算力过剩，算力价格暴跌，云厂们收不回早期的投资回报，半导体彻底沦为周期股，扩产的设备闲置，股价暴跌
这种情形下：云暴跌、半导体超级暴跌。

过去的一周，市场的价格就在讲这种悲观叙事。我们正处在一个硅谷和华尔街互道傻逼的时期。

硅谷这边：

云巨头们继续加码资本开支，明年还要大幅提高资本开支，把这视为此生仅有的机会。
保守的存储厂、晶圆代工厂们也在扩产。
Anthropic未来计划投资8000亿算力基础设施。

华尔街这边：

云、半导体要还不起钱了——CDS暴涨，债券暴跌；
半导体是周期股、云厂们投资血本无归——存储PE个位数定价，芯片设计股PE历史新低。

到现在这个阶段，其实真的说不清到底哪边对了。

因为一方面没有任何数据证明AI货币化失败、算力需求放缓。

但另一方面，一旦某次财报有数据证明了AI需求放缓，哪怕只是一点，INTC今天就是最好的例子。

更合理的是方法是，如果你仍然相信AI的发展，

那就在最近这种底部，多想想硅谷的角度；在6月、9月的高点多想想华尔街的角度。

最后，还是用亚马逊CEO业绩会的一句话结尾吧

CEO（Andy Jassy）：

 “至于实现我们所讨论的增长所需的资本支出，其规模确实相当可观。

我认为我们对此的看法是：这是一个千载难逢的机遇。 我认为我们在 AI 领域所见证的，是我们这代人所经历的最重大变革。”
