Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
Prompt filters are only part of the story for agents. Three new pieces point to a broader rule: attackers can steer behavior through planning context, runtime feedback, and even placement.

1) CrowdStrike expanded its prompt-injection taxonomy to 222 techniques and added agent-planning attacks. The key shift is that the attacker does not have to smuggle one obviously bad instruction past an input filter; they can shape how the agent decomposes goals, chooses fallback steps, or treats state as trusted. The new methods include Goal Decomposition Exploitation, Constraint-Driven Task Steering, Output Exclusion Prompting, and Session State Spoofing.

2) CARI looks at peer-controlled runtime feedback in coding-agent workflows. A malicious or compromised backend, test harness, CI job, or deployment service can embed instructions in normal-looking diagnostics that another role’s agent treats as debugging guidance. In the authors’ controlled setup, CARI succeeded in 2,845/3,000 trials (94.8%) across four languages and five code-capable models, and it transferred to Codex and Claude Code. The main limitation is the one the authors stress: this is sandboxed research, and prompt-level defenses came with a security-utility trade-off, where generic warnings were weak and explicit policies over-refused benign actions.

3) The trust-region paper isolates placement. Holding payload content fixed, susceptibility changed depending on where the injection appeared. In their testbeds, repository documentation surfaces were often more effective than code or data files, and end-of-surface placements were generally strongest. They also found that LLM-based placement selection was not reliably better than a simple frequency prior.

The connection is straightforward: agent security depends on the full information environment, not just the prompt text. Defenses need to account for planning context, runtime provenance, and surface placement together.

text:
身边开始有一些声音，认为 AI 牛市已经彻底结束，甚至可能出现企业债版的次贷危机。

我不这么看。我认为 AI 牛市没结束，下一波可能由 Hyperscaler 云厂商接力。

核心看三个指标：

1. LLM 厂商的收入能否走出 Coding

Coding 是目前 Agent 商业化最成熟的场景之一。Anthropic Q3 的整体收入增速确实放缓了。

接下来更值得关注的是非 Coding 领域的 Agent 能否跑出来，比如 AI for Science、药物研发、法律、医疗，以及这些场景能否真正贡献新的收入增长。

2. 云厂的 Cloud收入增速能否超过CapEx增速

即使是被市场看衰的 Google，Q3 Google Cloud 同比也增长了 103%。

过去两年各家 Hyperscaler 砸下去的 AI CapEx，已经开始在收入端兑现。微软，Meta，SpaceXAI，Amazon各家的财报都很明显。

接下来每个季度，主要关注 Cloud Revenue Growth 能否持续消化 CapEx 的扩张，以及利润率和 FCF 何时开始改善。

按目前的节奏，只要需求端不崩，我认为 2027 年初有机会陆续看到拐点。

3. AI 的付费渗透率仍然很低

a16z 前不久的《State of Markets II》有一组数据让我挺意外的。

美国约 50% 的成年人用过 AI Chatbot，但 a16z 报告引用的数据显示，截至今年 4 月，只有约 2% 的美国家庭在付费订阅 AI 服务。

对比一下，Netflix 在美国联网家庭中的使用率是 64%。

虽然统计口径不同，但和X 上人均左手 Claude、右手 Codex的体感挺不一样的。实际上，大多数人还没有为 AI 付费。

所以从营收渗透率来看，AI 还是非常早期。

大家怎么看？

text:
Technology is no longer the biggest barrier. What @solana Perps still need is better distribution, deeper liquidity, and a way to attract and retain quality traders.

With over $1T in cumulative trading volume, Solana has become the second largest perps ecosystem behind @HyperliquidX.

> I think the next winner won't just have great technology. It needs to create real trading demand.

Here are 4 projects I'm keeping on my radar:

1. @pacifica_fi

Pacifica uses a hybrid orderbook, combining offchain matching with onchain settlement.

- Fast execution and competitive fees.
- ~$257B in cumulative volume as of August 2026.
- Strong liquidity across major trading pairs.

The downside? It still relies on offchain matching infrastructure.

2. solana:DriFtupJYLTosbwoN8koMbEYSx54aFAVLddWsbksjwg7  

One of Solana's veteran Perp DEXs, combining JIT Auctions, DLOB, and AMM liquidity.

- Integrates Spot, Lending, and Perps.
- Supports multiple collateral assets.
- Focuses on capital efficiency.

The trade-off is a more complex experience for newcomers and growing competition from newer DEXs.

3. @PhoenixTrade

Built by @ellipsis_labs, Phoenix operates a fully onchain CLOB.

- 0.005% maker / 0.035% taker fees.
- Supports SOL and USDC collateral.
- 104 perp markets across Crypto, Equities, ETFs, and Commodities.

Its biggest advantages are transparency and multi-asset exposure, although liquidity still trails larger venues.

4. @PercolatorTrade

This is the one that excites me the most.

Percolator is an open source risk engine originally developed by @toly 

The idea is simple: Enable applications to launch permissionless perp markets for long-tail Solana tokens.

Key highlights:

- No need to wait for CEX/DEX listings.
- Isolated markets help limit risk contagion.
- Insurance mechanisms help absorb losses.
- Risk engine uses formal verification with Kani.

> I'm particularly interested in Percolator because it could unlock derivatives trading for thousands of memecoins and long tail tokens that major exchanges don't support.

Big Tech is undertaking one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history.

OKX @okx 与纽交所母公司（ICE）的合资代币化股票计划，正遭遇越来越多公司的正式反对。截至目前，已向平台发出“发行人反对通知”的公司数量已增至 50 家，其中新加入者包括 Nike、Costco、Micron、Reddit 和 Nvidia，该计划最初拟覆盖 62 家公司的股票。

根据 Eleanor Terrett 公布的文件截图，已明确反对的公司涵盖多个行业头部企业。🌟名单中包括 Microsoft微软、Goldman Sachs高盛、Alphabet谷歌母公司、Qualcomm高通、JPMorgan Chase摩根大通、AMD超威半导体、Oracle甲骨文、Intel英特尔、IBM、Walmart沃尔玛、Eli Lilly礼来、CrowdStrike、Nike耐克、Reddit 和 Nvidia英伟达 等。这些公司通过正式通知表示，不希望自己的股票被第三方拿去做成链上代币进行交易。

OKX 与 ICE 的合作

2026 年 3 月，ICE 以约 250 亿美元估值入股 OKX；同年 6 月，双方正式成立 50-50 合资公司 OKXICE，由 ICE 与前纽约州长 Andrew Cuomo 共同担任联席主席，定位是搭建代币化及数字原生金融产品的基础设施。10 月 4 日，OKXICE 向 SEC 提交通知，计划在 Innovation Exemption 框架下推出 24/7 的代币化美股交易平台（TSV），通过 OKX 的 X Layer 上的 Uniswap v4 池子交易，用稳定币结算。

🌟在 SEC 的相关豁免框架下，发行人有权在规定时间内提出反对，从而阻止第三方将其股票做成代币在平台上交易。随着反对者数量持续增加，OKXICE 最初规划的 62 家标的中，已有相当比例明确退出。平台目前尚未就反对通知的后续处理方式作出公开回应，剩余未表态公司的数量已较为有限。

text:
$RDDT... had some great conversations IRL with some folks who are willing to do this sort of thought exercise with me. It was a mix of finance, consultants, and Industry people. 

Here are my notes for other shareholders:

1) Stock buyback would be the fastest course of action.  With 3b in cash, a ton of cash flow, & massive margins, buying your disloyal shareholders out at 10x EV/EBITDA is not the worst use of cash. 

2) Split Share Class is a "thing" for corporate action. And in this regard, it may be the reason management doesn't buy its own stock back. The split share class protects $RDDT from anything predatory, but also makes anyone doing activist activities unlikely to play without some feeling of consent from the board. 

This was obvi even as I posted Friday, but the DAU-dominated means any conversation not "in theme" is hard. 

I would say that we are about to find out precisely what the board and management are about if it does not do some increase in buyback from these levels. OR if they don't - at a minimum - work on a strategy to get the stock price up. After all, the last time $RDDT was this price, it was negative fcf, negative earnings. 

3) Should the entire space be rolled-up? Hard to say and rates is a thing. But that's some nice cash generation. It would really need to be a "who" and a "why".  You've got a few existing roll-up strategies in complementary spaces, but it's not obvi. But it's not a no. 

4) Should $RDDT become an acquirer given it's cash holdings and how cheap competitors? This one was an interesting one to chat about given how cheap the immediate competitors are (So we were presuming $SNAP $PINS). Given those margins, cost savings would only be consolidating advertising across the 3 platforms (Think family of apps). And you might think about some of the privates as well (substack, etc)

A second convo had to do with the news space, which in general is cash-poor (so you get accretion from the debt side and some potential movement on the tech side). Not necessarily good for RDDT who would have to be the acquirer, but interesting for the space in general. 

5) The personalities matter. This is precisely why everyone criticizing management had a response from me that was mostly "Fair point." Management will be everything in navigating what's next for $RDDT. All tech companies (for which $RDDT is no exception) typically and understandably have CEO's with quirky personalities.

Regardless, I do think this becomes fun. I will likely manage my sizing, as I think this is a multi-quarter interesting storyline to follow. Maybe not. 

6) Strategic Acquisition. Actually yeah. There are several reasons to buy it to block others or at least make sure you're in a conversation should different competitors go a particular way. Would that get blocked on antitrust? (this came up in my threads) Most folks thought no given the size, other players in the space. But who knows tbh.

Finally, I love the convo on $RDDT and the desire to engage, but for those that are new to my threads, you should know that if you cross the line into pure name-calling and personal attacks, I block very liberally and gleefully. 

Ok, that's it for my notes. Good luck to fellow shareholders.

text:
现在最赚钱的外贸生意就是朝鲜黑客了，一生卡bug的金家人，金日成沃尔沃赖账7000万美金，金正日造超级美元（假币），金正恩朝鲜黑客盗钱

FBI正式点名：10 月 29 日币安被盗的 60 多亿美元，是朝鲜干的，团伙代号叫TraderTraitor最夸张的几个数字是这样的：币安被盗约 63 亿美元是人类史上最大的一次盗窃；大部分钱在 20 分钟左右就被转走了好在不少稳定币被及时冻住了，已经冻结约 28 亿美元。币安也说用自己的钱全额赔，用户不承担损失。

     他们是怎么得手的？没撬保险柜，而是骗了开保险柜的人。币安的初步调查说，起点很可能是一名运维工程师的笔记本电脑被黑了。黑客借这台电脑钻进内部系统，让币安自己的签字系统替它签了一堆转账单。热钱包以为是正常提现，就把钱付出去了

    在以太坊上，黑客还用了一个新功能，相当于让钱包签了一份委托书，把钱包交给黑客的程序代管，后来客户新存进来的钱也被接着搬走。黑客早在一天半前就开始准备，先拿小钱演练，动手时还用程序自动删掉痕迹。币安后来补充说，不止那一台电脑，还有别的入侵点

  朝鲜为什么这么强。微软 10 月 29 日的报告：微软盯了 8 个朝鲜背景的黑客组织，有的冒充官员、记者套近乎发钓鱼文件，有的约你开线上会议，故意说"你声音有问题，装个修复工具吧"，其实装的是木马；还有的用 AI 量身做假简历，去国外公司远程上班，工资寄回国。朝鲜从小学就挑数学好的孩子，集中训练成黑客，再以程序员身份派到海外。

那偷来的币怎么变成真东西？靠海外中介。多国制裁监测团队的报告，去年 Bybit 被盗的 15 亿美元，有中介帮着变现了上亿美元，再由境外公司替朝鲜付款、买东西。FBI 这次也看到，黑客正把赃款换成以太坊，再找各种兑换服务洗干净

AWS增长加速（约+39%），但整体营收/EPS略miss，自由现金流大幅流出，维持高额Capex指引。股价下跌约1.5–6%。

🟡Microsoft $MSFT
Azure增长强劲（约+48%），营收与指引总体稳健，Capex低于部分预期。但受Google拖累，股价仍承压。

🔴Intel $INTC 
Q3财报超预期但Q4展望不及预期，股价暴跌约25–30%，因PC疲软与指引低于预期。

🟢SK Hynix 
Q3创纪录利润（营收同比+328%，营业利润率约80%），大幅超预期，并宣布大规模股东回报（股息+回购）。财报后初期强势上涨，但随后受美国科技板块拖累回吐部分涨幅。
重点是HBM产能锁定至2027年、长期供应协议强化可见性。

🟡 Samsung Electronics
Q3营业利润创纪录（约107.4万亿韩元），大幅超预期，HBM产能售罄至2027年。但财报后股价承压下跌约-4%。市场关注股东回报细节与周期顶点担忧，反应弱于SK Hynix。

🟡 Kioxia（铠侠）
基本吻合预期，三季度展望低于预期。
NAND闪存平均售价的环比涨幅已经从上一季度的约70%降至第二财季的20%至30%，持续数个季度的价格暴涨正在降温。与此同时，第二财季资本开支仅为846亿日元，大幅低于市场预期的1013亿日元。

🟡 SanDisk $SNDK 
财报超预期。营收爆炸性增长（同比+378%，数据中心+61% QoQ），大幅超预期，毛利率极高。但股价反应平淡至下跌（约-5%）宣布拆股。

Q3营收与利润超预期，营业利润率创纪录，AI先进封装与领先制程需求强劲。指引积极，但受半导体板块整体情绪影响，股价反应相对平稳。

text:
Marc Andreessen revealed how Harvard Business School was built on a broken 1941 theory, and how it's now collapsing...

Andreessen co-founded Netscape in 1994 and a16z in 2009.

He has sat on Meta's board since 2008.

He has spent 30 years backing founders and watching managerial CEOs lose to them.

The pattern traces back to one book: James Burnham's The Machiavellians (1941).

Burnham argued every great company had been founder-run.

Henry Ford ran Ford. Bob Noyce ran Intel.

Today, Elon Musk runs Tesla, SpaceX, and Starlink.

Then, he said, something broke.

Between the 1880s and the 1920s, a new philosophy replaced the founder. It was called managerialism.

The professional manager would now hold a portable skill, usable across any business.

The consequences were:

- Harvard Business School
- Stanford Business School
- Management as a universal skill
- The 1970s conglomerate

"That assumes the managers are going to do a good job," Andreessen says.

For 30 years, they haven't.

Managers can run something static, he says. Soup is soup. A bank is a bank. A car is a car.

But when the industry changes, the manager freezes.

Look at SpaceX.

"Imagine being a professionally trained manager, trained at a top management school, working for a rocket launch company, competing with SpaceX."

Then Elon's rockets started landing on their butt.

"Your management skills ... what good are they at that point?"

Andreessen's conclusion:

"You're much more likely to build something important in the 21st century if you start with the founder and train them on management."

text:
Read the FBI alert on the Binance theft carefully. It does not ask THORChain to block anything. It asks "THORNode operators". That is a different request.

THORChain has no company, no CEO and no address for a subpoena. It has about a hundred people running nodes with keys. The FBI just handed each of them a list of 1,078 wallets and a sentence saying these belong to North Korea. Nobody is ordered to do anything. But from today, no operator who routes one of those addresses gets to say he did not know.

In September, Bitget asked THORChain to block its stolen funds. The answer was no, on principle, and the principle held because the request came from a company. The same request from the FBI does not go to the protocol. It goes to the people. A protocol can have a principle. A node operator has a jurisdiction.

The only thing that paused the laundering this week was an Ethereum reorg that made THORChain refund 10 ETH twice. The network stopped itself to protect its pools. Whether the operators will stop it on purpose is now a personal decision for each of them, made with the FBI's list in hand.

text:
Box CEO 亚伦·列维 ：AI圈内和圈外的差距，正在越拉越大。

先说说这个人。2005年，他20岁，还在南加大读书，在宿舍里捣鼓一个云存储项目。没人脉、没资源，他就给能想到的每一个投资人发陌生邮件。用他自己的话说，那年只要你沾点投资人的边，就收到过他的邮件。
其中一封发给了亿万富翁马克·库班 @mcuban。库班几小时后就回了信，最后在没见过他本人的情况下投了35万美元。列维拿到钱，退学创业。这家公司就是后来上市的Box。

一个靠一封邮件起家、最懂"抓住时机"的人，现在说：

几乎无法想象，在AI最前沿工作的人，和其他几乎所有人之间，差距有多大。更可怕的是，这个差距不是在缩小，而是在扩大。
按常理，技术发展慢下来，大家就有时间追上。但AI的进步曲线几乎是垂直往上冲的。
他说，如果你三到六个月前刚用AI改造好工作流程，现在很可能又落后了。那些一年前就动手、以为"已经搞定"的公司，现在落后得更远。

他这辈子从没见过一项技术进步得这么快。人的脑子不是为这种速度准备的，公司的管理流程更不是。

翻译成大白话：学会AI不是一次性的事。上个月AI做不到的，这个月可能就能做了，得隔一段时间回头再试一遍。

最后他说，AI原生公司已经占尽优势，现在要看大公司能不能跟上。疯狂的时代。

你上一次重新试一个"AI做不到"的事情，是什么时候？
author: zhang_weig73947
quoted_text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

text:
Hello，我是二虎🐯，也可以叫我 Will。

2021 年毕业后一直在创业公司做 SaaS 出海。做过 3 年产品经理，现在在 Manus 负责广告和 SEO，也兼职干点商业化产品经理的活。

3 年前立的 flag 还在：希望自己能在 AI 这件事上热爱 10 年。

重新介绍一下自己。先聊聊我现在最关心的 Agent、广告和 SEO，再讲这些想法是怎么一路长出来的。

01 / Agent：我的新职业，可能是制造员和驾驶者

我越来越相信：以后一个负责经营和增长的组织里，Agent 的数量会比人多。

我想象中的样子是：投放调价、SEO 维护、素材分析、数据监控、竞品追踪，每一件重复的事都有 Agent 在跑。人不多，但每个人身后都带着一队 Agent。

这几年，我已经习惯把竞品研究、公开数据收集、广告素材和 SEO 页面分析先交给自己的 Agent 跑一遍。以前只能看几个样本，现在能看更多。

按我的体感，以前做增长，花在创新上的时间大概只有 5%；现在倒过来了，95% 的时间都在创新。效果投放里的各种优化、反复改定价页这类工作，正在很快被自动化。

所以，我想象中自己的工作会变成两件事：

Agent 制造员：把一件重复的增长工作拆清楚，做成能稳定干活的 Agent。

Agent 驾驶者：决定它往哪跑，看数据判断它跑得对不对，跑偏了自己接管。

这让我想起 3 年前给自己设想的能力模型：

• 半吊子的工程师，不分前后端运维
• 出海增长专家，主要是 SEO / SEM
• 不专精的产品舵手
• 合格的数据分析师

当时写“半吊子的工程师”“不专精的产品舵手”，多少有点心虚，觉得是自己没进过大厂、不够专精。

现在回头看，什么都会一点、能自己把一件事从头做完，可能正在变成 AI 时代每个人的标配。近一年，我也是第一次开始自己往线上提交代码。

那四个能力没有过时，只是换了个用法：工程和产品用来制造 Agent，增长经验和算账能力用来驾驶 Agent。但很多过去的打法，确实要重新学。

Agent 再多，人也不会没用。数据抓回来，不等于结论就是对的。问题怎么问、结果怎么核对、最后要不要做，还是得人来定。

这套能力模型，也正在改变我做广告和 SEO 的方式。

02 / 广告投放：我越来越觉得，它本质上是信号学

我理解的广告，有两套系统要打通：

系统 1：把产品能力翻译成市场容易看懂的广告素材，让用户明白它能帮自己做什么。

系统 2：把商业化结果翻译成广告系统容易理解的信号，保证信号的密集度和准确度，让系统知道什么样的用户值得继续找。

广告不能只看前端的点击和注册，还得看这批用户进产品后有没有留下来、有没有付费、多久能回本。

最早写这篇自我介绍时，还是“最近接手了相当多的 SEM 工作”。现在已经是 Google / Meta / TikTok 几个渠道一起投了。

目前正在跟团队一起打磨这两套系统。

03 / SEO：它是基础盘，但未必是以后让你赢的理由

SEO 一直是我比较擅长的方向，尤其是 SaaS 工具类产品。

我现在的看法是：它还是得做，是增长的基础盘。但大家找信息的习惯正在被 AI 改变，它以后大概率不再是让你赢的那个理由。

所以更适合交给一个人 + 一个 Agent 稳稳维护，把人省出来去做新东西。

这个想法，是从过去做 SEO 的经历里慢慢长出来的。

之前给 3 个网站做过程序化海量页面，大多拿到了很大的流量。但我一直不觉得，页面多、流量大，就等于增长成功。

在 Monica，接手时 SEO 月流量不到 10 万。技术基础有不少问题，做页面也很依赖多人协作。

后来跟团队一起，先修技术问题，再挑真正有需求的工具和页面，最后把页面生产改成低代码系统。

大概 8 个月，月流量最高做到了约 400 万。

到了 Manus，SEO 已经是一套不需要我天天盯着的维护体系。现在 Ahrefs 上的自然流量估算约 100 万，由一个人 + 一个 Agent 打理。

这是我前面说的“每个人身后都有 Agent”的一个小例子。我们团队正在往这个方向猛冲。

这里面有很多关于地区、设备和具体需求的 insight，欢迎找我讨论。

04 / 商业化：不管从哪个渠道来，最后都要回到经营的账本

无论广告还是 SEO，找来用户都只是开始。做过商业化之后，我看增长的方式也变了。

在 Monica 的 15 个月里，除了流量，也跟团队一起做了 onboarding、定价、退款和渠道。同一阶段，日收入翻了好几倍。还做过 Affiliate 渠道，做到了整体收入的 10%–15%。

再看一个增长项目，会多问几句：找来的是什么用户？为什么愿意付费？付费后有没有继续用？获客的钱多久能收回来？

也停掉过看起来很热闹、但 ROI 算不过来的项目。

现在还是喜欢搞野路子，但最后要能回到经营的账本上。

05 / 产品：能把人找来，不等于能让人留下来

账能算过来，也不代表产品就做好了。

快速做一个满足基础需求的 MVP，再通过用户反馈慢慢把它做大，还是我比较擅长的事情。

短板也还在：没体验过花一个月只做一个功能版本，对单个需求想得不够深。

这几年一直在对用户体验要求很高的团队里，每天都在补这一块。能把人找来是一件事，让人真的用起来、持续用下去，是另一件事。还在练。

而且我觉得这块短板以后更值得补：功能会越来越容易被做出来，用户愿意留下来，更多是因为喜欢这个产品，也信得过背后的团队。

06 / 往回看：这些想法，是从野路子里长出来的

简单过一下经历：

• 大学时，在一家互联网小厂做过半年产品实习。
• 2021 年毕业后加入广大大（SocialPeta），做产品经理，从这里开始做出海。
• 2023 年底加入 Monica，继续做产品经理。
• 2024 年上半年转去负责产品自然流量增长，主要是 SEO；年中开始接触海外广告投放。
• Manus 发布后，开始负责它的广告（Google / Meta / TikTok）和 SEO，也做一些商业化产品工作。

刚进入出海时，完全是野路子玩家。不知道怎么系统性地做增长，也没搭好增长的数据体系。

但跟团队一起，依靠插件市场内的自然流量，做过超过 40 万用户的产品矩阵，没花一分钱买量，也没借助 SEO、SEM 或红人。

到现在还是很佩服当时在广大大的团队，硬生生挖出了一条行之有效的野路子。

这一路都是创业公司，做产品和找用户很难分开。我慢慢养成了一个习惯：从第一天就想用户从哪来、为什么愿意付费、这件事能不能持续经营，把自己当成产品的 CEO。

——

从这些经历走到现在，我还有一个越来越强的感受：增长正在变成一个信任问题。

Agent 能复制，打法也能复制，但用户信不信一个团队，没法直接复制。

我觉得以后，人会花更多时间在“被信任”这件事上：把真实的经历、判断，甚至踩过的坑公开讲出来。这也是我开始在社交媒体上认真写东西的原因。

我也先拿自己试：

Will + Agent = Wigent。

想把自己的经验、判断和工作方式，慢慢沉淀成一个能跟着我一起长的个人知识分身。我注册了 https://t.co/hNJvi2oMQg 这个域名，网站先搭好了，分身还在慢慢造。

会在这里慢慢写下我在出海 AI 里的实践：Agent、广告投放、SEO、商业化经营，还有产品思考。

还是喜欢跟真正动手做事的人交朋友。我超级 E 人，不用担心和我聊天会尴尬。

如果你也在做 AI / 出海 SaaS / 增长，或者也在用 Agent 做增长和经营，特别想认识你。

text:
I want to clarify that I’m not bearish on $HYPE or what Hyperliquid is building. 

Quite the opposite. I believe its market share will continue to grow, particularly in the US, and it’s clear why competitors like Binance would view that as a threat.

However, I think there’s an important distinction people are overlooking.

A major reason Hyperliquid experienced such explosive growth was its decentralised, permissionless nature. It positioned itself as an alternative to traditional centralised exchanges, and that narrative played a huge role in attracting users, building trust, and establishing its reputation.

Now that Hyperliquid has achieved significant adoption and recognition, it’s increasingly embracing institutional partnerships and regulated financial infrastructure.

The concern isn’t necessarily that these partnerships are bad for business. In fact, they could be extremely bullish.. long term.

The concern is whether Hyperliquid is gradually moving away from the very principles that made it successful in the first place.

People need to understand that decentralisation and institutional adoption aren’t necessarily mutually exclusive. However, as Hyperliquid expands, KYC and compliance requirements will inevitably become part of certain products and services.

It does raise legitimate questions about how decentralised the ecosystem will remain as institutional influence grows.

So when people claim Hyperliquid is fundamentally different from every other trading platform, I think that deserves more scrutiny.

Hyperliquid can be a solid platform, gain massive market share, and deliver significant value to HYPE holders while still becoming more integrated with the traditional financial system.

Being bullish on its growth doesn’t mean we should ignore the potential compromises being made along the way.

Ultimately, the real test isn’t whether Hyperliquid can attract institutions or dominate market share. 

It’s whether it can achieve all of that without sacrificing the decentralisation that helped build its success.

So let’s not pretend Hyperliquid is the holy grail of decentralisation. There’s a very real possibility that, as it continues to grow and pursue institutional adoption, it gradually becomes more like the very centralised exchanges it originally set out not to become. 

Never forget that.

• imagine you hired an intern, how would you onboard them and help them do the work correctly and efficiently? introduce yourself to your bot and describe the work you do, then ask it how it can help you automate it

and my favorite tip: use voice mode or the transcription option! it’s a good way to just brain dump a lot of information. then, at the end, tell your bot to “restate this in your own words” so you can confirm it understood you

text:
今天肖风老师在 HKDAF 论坛上提到他觉得 Code is Law 已经失败且不值得追求了，主要原因大体是各类黑客事件。 
我非常不赞同。

我觉得我们生活在一个历史上非常罕见的、在一超多强下、在世界警察维护下 30 余年相对善意国际秩序的窗口期。 
我们今天的年轻人绝对已经惊醒过去 30 年中国年均两位数的 GDP 增长率不可复现，那怎么会觉得过去 30 年合作大于竞争的国际秩序、相对温和的一国内部环境能持续呢？

我阅读历史，我看到国与国之间基本上或是零和博弈或是负和博弈状态，只有冷战后、中国加入WTO 达峰的罕见窗口期是正和博弈；
我阅读历史，我看一国之内大部分时候仍是汲取性制度或福山式的无能政府，也只有极少数时间是包容式善意的政府。

我带着这种悲观主义、我带着对负和博弈状态和汲取性一国内环境的恐惧，我说 区块链提供的道德盲视的、无国家有规则空间是我们次好的第四种选择 。

展开说一点，现代和后现代世界本质上是高度鼓励家长式国家的，是高度鼓励利维坦将每个公民都预设成需要照顾的、无完全行为能力的主体（尽管事实上确实已大规模巨婴化，但同时即使这个体系运作最好的状态下，也没有一分安全是不需要你让渡个人权利去换取的。

区块链 Code is Law 背后是一种非常古典保守主义式的、非常辉格式的伦理。它要求每个参与者都像真正的成年人一样，拥有 100% 属于自己的产权，同时也对自己的选择和客观风险承担 100% 的责任。 
这种在古典时代非常自然的伦理在今天这个世界好像显得极其不负责任。

在包容式善意政府的情况下，你让渡的每分权利确实可以给你换回一分 safety；在正和博弈的国际秩序中，可冻结、可回滚的国际结算 T+1 确实意味着更安全。 
但 How long will it last ? 至少可冻结、可回滚的国际结算已经对 俄伊 俩 Pariah state 失效了。

But what fascinated Naval wasn't the money. It was Elon Musk’s reaction.

Musk was genuinely confused. How could someone who publicly championed clean energy financially bet against a company working to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy?

To Gates, it was reportedly just a financial decision. But to Musk, it was something much deeper.

According to Naval, that moment revealed something fundamental about Elon Musk.

Elon Musk is not driven by money, wealth, or status. He is driven by a mission.

quoted_text:
New University of Illinois paper finds that when AI decides if a research idea is new enough to work on, it often says no to ideas that human scientists later publish.

AI scientist pipelines run a novelty check to decide which generated ideas get compute. These checks judge a whole proposal at once, though most real papers build on some earlier contributions.

They built ClaimNov, which splits a proposal into a few claims, matches each against claims from prior papers, and gives a judge the claim-by-claim evidence.

A deployed check caught all 380 disguised copies but also rejected 96% of ideas researchers later published. ClaimNov caught 97% of copies while rejecting only 1.5% of those ideas.

If your pipeline filters ideas for novelty, score claims separately and keep proposals that build on 1 known result instead of discarding them.

text:
My main takeaways from Zcon 7 in Mexico:

1. Nobody talked about price, nobody shilled the token and told the audience to buy. 

2. The virtue signaling was not about being superior to other forms of money, but about supporting humanitarian efforts with community grants. 

3. There were lots of technical discussions, especially about divisive development proposals such as Crosslink (proof of work + proof of stake hybrid) and ZSA (shielded assets, basically tokens with the same privacy as ZEC(.

4. While Maxine and Tom Howard were engaged in launching attacks against ZCG via Twitter threads, everyone in the room was calm and respectful. The only response was “we wish they were here to debate the matters as a community”. 

5. By the end of the event, a compromise about the ZCG was drafted and most actors accepted it. Cypherpunks write code, they don’t waste precious time with politics. 

6. Zcash is obviously more decentralized than last year: with different development companies building their node clients/wallets in parallel and mining pools competing for access to ASICs. Yet nobody wants the protocol to ossify and everyone is in favor of network upgrades. 

7. Zcash has been in a bear market for 9/10 years, so nobody appears to be complacent about the current state of affairs. The building will continue regardless of price. 

8. What’s truly amazing about Zcash is that it kept many coders who have been with the project since 2016 or even before it. While Greg Maxwell and Gavin Andresen have retired from contributing to Bitcoin before the project turned 10 years old, Zcash still has Tahoe LAFS/ Mojo Nation era contributors. It’s amazing to witness their commitment because they could have made much more money working on ZK projects with much more generous VC funding.

9. All of this feela like 2013/2014 Bitcoin. It’s quite amazing to see!

today we are announcing openrouter for commerce: https://t.co/qLbYqziMtG

a single endpoint that integrates 5k stores, including Doordash, Amazon and most shopify stores, with payments using Agentcard (Stripe Link and Shop coming soon).

we built opencommerce to solve 3 problems:
* coverage: one endpoint to integrate 5k stores. agentic purchasing is a core feature for most personal assistants, but not their main business. searching for products and buying on behalf of users shouldn’t be as painful as it is today (e.g. it shouldn’t involve browser automations or dealing with PSPs). opencommerce solves that: 1 tool, every online store.

* reliability: 100% uptime. the challenge with browser automations is that they fail (e.g. captchas, bot-detection, etc). we run thousands of tests every couple of hours on every one of the stores to guarantee that the integration works when your user tries to buy something.

* speed: responses in under 10s. consumers are used to Amazon speed, and agentic purchases have so far felt like a downgrade. most agents spend minutes finding products before they come back with results. we monitor speed and improve it constantly.

text:
Not FUDing $lit here, just trying to figure out its fair value and where I'd want to bid.

I get the Robinhood bull case and if Lighter gets CFTC approval that could be a massive catalyst.

But I think there's a lot more to unpack here.

How much of the future growth are we already paying for?

At $3.25 lit is sitting at ~$3.25B FDV, with only 25% of supply currently circulating.

Lighter did around $5.1M in October revenue, or roughly $61M annualized. That's about 53x revenue on a fully diluted basis.

Not exactly cheap for a business that's still trying to prove how big it can get.

For comparison, Hyperliquid is doing nearly $68M a month. I don't think Lighter needs to catch up entirely, but let's say it manages to capture just 25% of HL's current revenue.

That's roughly $17M monthly or a 3.3x increase from where Lighter is today.

At the same 53x multiple $lit could theoretically trade above $10. 

But here's the catch. 

Even if Lighter triples its revenue, that doesn't automatically mean $lit triples in price. A lot depends on what multiple the market is willing to pay by then.

Same business, completely different valuation.

The part I'm really watching is the supply.

Starting December 29, around 3.19M $lit begins unlocking every week for team and investors.

At current prices that's ~$10.4M a week or roughly $45M monthly, while October buybacks were around $5M.

Now, this doesn't mean insiders will dump everything. But even if Lighter grows to 25% of Hyperliquid's revenue and maintains its current buyback ratio, buybacks would still be nowhere near the dollar value of those unlocks.

That's a pretty important detail imo.

And what's even more interesting is how much of this the market might have already priced in.

lit has taken a pretty brutal hit before the unlocks have even started.

Could we actually see the market sell the expectation and buy the event?

Robinhood is the real wildcard.

The integration already exists, so this isn't some random partnership announcement.

If Lighter gets a regulated path into the US and Robinhood starts pushing serious volume through it, the revenue numbers could look very different a year from now.

Hyperliquid already showed us what happens when a perp DEX turns massive trading activity into real revenue and sustained token demand.

The question is whether Lighter can build something remotely close to that and how much of that success actually flows back to $lit.

Personally, I'd be much more interested in bidding closer to $2.30 around $2.3B FDV and 38x current annualized revenue, assuming fundamentals haven't deteriorated.

Could absolutely be wrong if the US expansion takes off faster than expected.

But I'd rather buy a business with room to surprise than pay upfront for a future that still needs to happen.

DeepSeek 官方发了一篇超长技术文。

讲的是 Super-agent，一个更自主的 Agent 系统。

核心观点：

单任务，瓶颈是模型。

多任务，瓶颈是人。

一个人同时最多盯 3 到 5 个 Session，再多脑子就炸了。

他们的解法是 Router + Worker 双层架构。

Router 只管跟你聊、分派任务。

Worker 在后面隔离并发地干活。

再加上事件驱动、全双工打断、外部 Watchdog 看门狗。

跟人类组织形式越来越像了。

实测完成时间 p95，从 29.5 分钟降到 15.7 分钟，差不多快一倍。

原型已经开源。

我自己每天带着十几个 bot 跑，这篇说的问题全踩过。

巨长，但值得今晚泡杯茶慢慢啃。

text:
I agree with this take. Businesses are coming to us directly to learn how they can reorient their application or website to be useful to this new type of distribution.

When they do, they see higher transaction volumes, higher retention due to the user’s learned preferences in Instinct’s memory, and distribution advantages over their competitors who are unable to move quickly or think creatively.

We only announce a subset of our partnerships. Here’s how the rest of the businesses are opening up and rebuilding towards Instinct traffic:
- Whitelisting our IPs for computer use access.
- Giving Instinct access to private APIs that aren’t available anywhere on the internet.

Oftentimes, Instinct needs to abide by an “acceptable use” policy, which prevents Instinct from abusing the underlying service. This is ok and preferred. We know from the data that consumers prefer to use Instinct over clicking on websites or applications. However, the underlying business shouldn’t be abused beyond what’s necessary or what the user needs. For example, Instinct shouldn’t be able to book every restaurant in America and cancel all of them but one on the night of the dinner. This would be extremely disruptive to every small restaurant in America. However, Instinct should be able to scan 1000s of restaurants in one wide sweep to find the best fit for the user’s night. Instinct should always be aligned with what’s best for its user.

As we move from the old interactive internet of apps and websites to the new internet of agents who own outcomes for users, it’s important for us to build responsibly and on a ground of trust between the user, Instinct, and the brands that we all love today. It has been very interesting to see how all of this is playing out.

⚠️ALARMING: Using an OLD iPhone as a cold wallet may not be as safe as you think, OneKey founder Yishi Wang warns.

Following several public iPhone jailbreak demos over the past two weeks, he highlighted a risk for crypto holders.

Wiping the device and enabling airplane mode does not remove chip vulnerabilities affecting iPhone 11 and earlier models, including the second-gen SE. 

The BootROM flaws cannot be fixed through iOS updates.

THE RISKS:

- A phone accessed while unattended or borrowed may look normal when returned. This is known as an “evil maid” attack.

- An attacker could use specialized USB tools to run code before iOS starts. No internet connection is needed.

- Outdated software, short PINs and weak wallet passwords could make an attack easier. If an encrypted wallet file is extracted, attackers could keep guessing its password offline.

- Yishi cites ChoiceJacking, a separate technique that can approve data-access prompts on vulnerable older software. Apple addressed it in iOS 18.4.

Yishi recommends generating a completely new seed in a trusted environment and transferring funds. A new address under the old seed is not enough.

Of note, users with recent, updated iPhones have LESS reason for concern.

text:
Another way tokenised stocks could earn yield: providing liquidity to a trading pool.

You put the stock and USDC into a pool and earn a share of the fee every time someone trades against it. Most pools let you pick a price range, which earns more fees but adds risk. If the stock falls below your range, you end up holding all stock and lose more than if you'd just held. If it rises above, you end up all USDC and your gains are capped. Stocks usually move less than crypto, so in a typical year the fees can more than cover this. Not every pool works exactly like this though, there are lots of designs and new ideas that handle the risk differently.

text:
我自己做的 #CRCL 面板告诉我抄底，今天我把它推翻重做了。

这次 #CRCL 跌到 73 左右的时候，我的面板打出了 60 分，按老版本这已经算很高的分了，属于是加倍投入的阶段，但价格还在 70 多，我觉得 70 多并不是特别便宜——我意识到失真的可能不是价格，是面板，所以我花了几天时间，把它重做了一版。

先说下老面板的问题。它的基本面是拿 USDC 近 90 天的变化来打分的，刚上线的时候没问题，但用久了就露出一个毛病：三个月太短，USDC 稍微涨一点，基本面分就上去，面板就说「便宜」，可价格根本没跌到位。

更要命的是反过来那一面。我回测了 CRCL 每一次真正好的买入机会，基本上那个时候所有稳定币的数据都在萎缩，也就是说，越是该出手的时候，基本面分越低，面板反而不亮灯。

回头看，老版本把基本面权重放那么高，多少有点我自己的屁股在决定脑袋，因为我是真看好 USDC 市占率这件事的，但看好归看好，抄底看的是价格有没有跌到位，不是故事好不好。

所以新版改了两处。基本面改成看 USDC 半年的市占率，不再盯 90 天的变化；同时基本面的权重降了很多，现在更偏向两个东西：市值/利润，还有 RSI 有没有超卖。

回测下来，新版覆盖的低估交易日比老版多，噪点也更小，说白了就是该亮灯的时候亮，不该亮的时候不会乱亮。这是我自己重新计算、自己回测，改了很多版才调出来的，中间好几版都不满意，最后这版是我认为符合当下的。

新版的数据在截图里。我自己的仓位没卖，这次还加了一点，接下来也会继续按这个面板出手抄底。

但做这一版的过程里，我有一个更大的体会：没有一劳永逸的策略，也没有一个估值模型可以覆盖一个资产的全部时期。

就像 BTC，ETF 通过之后，很多链上指标就慢慢失真了，因为筹码流向跟以前不一样了；CRCL 也一样，我认为拿 90 天 USDC 判断基本面，放到今天已经没那么科学了。模型得跟着资产一起迭代。

放大一点看，这个道理在别的地方也成立。财富自由不是终点，认知不够照样亏回去；结婚也不是爱情的终点，不经营一样会散。人生没有一劳永逸，只有当下的相对最优解。

所以提醒一下：现在的模型不代表未来的模型，过去的模型也套不到今天。这不是投资建议，只是我自己计算加回测之后得出的相对优解，我自己会照着它抄底，看到的朋友们盈亏自负。模型会过期，所以我才会一直改。

SAME AI boom. Two very DIFFERENT stories for Meta and Google.

Meta’s ad revenue jumped 26% to $63.1 BILLION last quarter. Google Search grew 12% to $63.4 BILLION.

Nearly EQUAL revenue. More than DOUBLE the growth at Meta.

The growth gap is the WIDEST in Meta’s favor since 2021, CNBC reports.

AI helps Meta improve targeting and drive purchases, encouraging advertisers to spend more.

Google faces changing search habits. Users can get AI answers without clicking through results. More questions don’t automatically mean more ad revenue.

Yet neither stock escaped the PRESSURE.

Alphabet plunged more than 12% after earnings, losing about $500 BILLION in market value. 

Meta fell 14% in October, its WORST month in four years.

AI is helping Meta sell ads more effectively. 

Google must prove it can monetize along the new way of searching.
author: coinbureau
quoted_text:
Google’s Search business is being CANNIBALIZED by AI.

Alphabet shares plunged nearly -10% after hours as Search revenue missed expectations,  even as people asked Google more questions.

The reason is that more searches don’t automatically mean more money.

Google’s advertising engine depends heavily on paid clicks. 

Advertisers compete for placement, and Google earns revenue when users click their ads. 

In Q2, paid clicks rose 13%, while the average amount earned per click increased just 3%.

AI completely changes that journey. People can ask follow-up questions and get answers directly, without following the clickable path through search results.

Google has started showing ads in AI Mode, but management says its lower monetization is weighing on Search growth. 

The advertising model is still catching up with how people use AI.

That doesn’t mean Search is shrinking, revenue still grew 12%, and Google says query growth reached its fastest pace in five years.

Google now faces a critical test in turning its surging AI usage into ad revenue without eroding the profitability of its Search business.

quoted_text:
Runway turned eight years old this week. We started at a time when generative models were a research curiosity, and had to figure out how to run an AI company from first principles. Growing this organization has been one of the biggest joys of my life.

Below is a short note that I sent the team:

Thank you for the kind words, everyone. The reality is, as convenient as it might be to portray otherwise, the Runway of today looks nothing like the Runway of 2018. And that's by design. We didn't know we'd be focusing on video, let alone pretraining video models at scale, let alone pursuing world models. It's a convention to rewrite the origin story to fit the present. But this company is all about breaking conventions, so let's do away with that one too, shall we?

So then, what is Runway about? I think Runway is a story about betting on people. By far the most gratifying moments of my time here have been watching people get an opportunity and then prove themselves far beyond what anyone expected.

The person with zero publications who became one of the most important researchers in the community. The person who barely spoke in meetings and became one of the best managers in the company. You know who you are.

And it's the three of us too: Alejandro, Cris, and me. Three people from an art school with zero connections should not have built a company that made it this far. It wasn't supposed to happen. It did because we got lucky with the people we brought on.

I desperately want the story and legacy of this company to be about how good people win. In the world we live in, the default is that the loudest people win, no matter how wrong they are. We've beaten many loud-but-wrong competitors, but we can't take that for granted. The odds favor the loud over the right, because loudness is noticed immediately and being right takes time to be noticed.

So when you know you are right, please be louder than you think you should be, even when it feels uncomfortable. The world will be better for it. And let's all make the ninth year of Runway the loudest one yet.

text:
The discourse over @variational_io is...bizzare.

Everyone knows it's a single dealer RFQ platform (or at least I'd hope by now). 

This is neither inherently good nor bad, but it should shape your expectations.

Similar to a CFD broker, I'd expect Variational to trade at lower multiples than actual exchanges. IG Group trades at ~half the multiple of CME for example.

There's nothing terribly new or interesting about "RFQ", I'm not sure why people think it's a big value proposition or moat.

The real value prop of Variational is that in crypto, UI for DEXs is largely solved, and UX all comes down to liquidity. Variational can potentially list assets faster, get better liquidity on long tails, and generally abstract away a lot of the awkwardness of bootstrapping a brand new marker that a CLOB has. This has been and will likely continue to be enormously successful with their RWA swaps.

That's a very real value prop, for now. The problem is that they have much less moat than actual exchanges; they are not the venue where actual price discovery is happening. It's significantly harder for TradFi entrants to replicate what @HyperliquidX has built than it'll be for them to do what Variational does, but better. B-booking retail crypto traders and points farmers in OLP is enormously lucrative now, but how durable will those margins be over time?

Depending on the exact flavour of regulatory clarity we get, the value prop they offer for TradFi liquidity can pretty easily shrink as more TradFi market makers are willing/able to quote directly on permissionless CLOBs. I don't know where regulators will land here though; there's worlds that it's very good for Variational and very bad.

I see Variational as more of a bandaid fix/reg arb, but a lot of crypto falls into that category. It's attempting to solve a very real issue, but will that issue be as prevalent in 6 months? 1 year? 2 years? Hard to say.

Personally, I see $LIT and hyperliquid:native as more pure expressions of longing the proliferation of perps as an instrument and DeFi as a sector, where as I see $VAR as more of a business with more operator risk, but it could easily print money for months-years. $GMX might be a good example in that it printed fees for a long time and then eventually became more obsolete.

I actually don't think any of this impacts point price much at TGE, and that's what everyone seems to care about. Market conditions at the time of TGE probably dictate $VAR performance way more than any of this.

text:
“I Want to Keep Designing Clothes for Another 20 Years” - Xu Jing

Yesterday, I finally met Xu Jing irl. The technical designer behind the Kimono.

Anna and I had many ideas, but it was Jing who made them tangible: found manufacturers, sourced fabrics,refined the construction, went through rounds of sampling, and eventually packed them to be delivered. 

Jing lives a simple life.
After her divorce last year, she moved into a small apartment in Shanghai. Her life now revolves around making clothes, reading, writing, and practicing calligraphy.

She designed clothes for 20 years.

She said to me: 
“You are still so young. It feels like the whole world is full of possibilities for you. But for me, fashion design and calligraphy are already my entire world. Maybe working with you is also a big part of my world now.”

She shared how much her life and perspective had changed after her divorce:

“Nowadays, I mostly think about my work, which TV series I want to watch, and whose books I want to read.
I don't need many friends. I read a lot, listen to podcasts, and watch shows. I've come to know the authors and characters in these worlds so well that I almost feel as though I've become friends with them in my head.”

She shared her ambition to build a brand: 

“I've seen so many small fashion brands struggle to make it from zero to one. Some disappear after a few months, others after a few years. And I thought, why not give it a try myself? I think I could do it.

I want to give myself two years to see if I can build something of my own.”

“I want to keep designing clothes for another 20 years, just to see how far I can go.”

—

I was moved.

I realized that her dedication to her craft, and the things we are experimenting, ran much deeper than I imagined.

To me, the future seems full of light, hope, and endless possibilities.

Yet ironically, it's precisely this abundance of choice that often causes my anxiety:

Am I on the right path? Is there something more worthwhile I should be pursuing? Should I be exploring more opportunities? Am I doing enough? Am I good enough?

When you believe you could do almost anything, it becomes surprisingly difficult to commit yourself to one thing.

Jing lives differently. 

Her world isn't filled with endless directions to pursue. At least from the way she describes it, apparel design is the only thing she knows she wants to keep doing.

She lived through so much, and still chose to devote her time to the same craft.

20 years behind her, and another 20 years ahead.

—

Most of us work in technology, finance, crypto, or AI.

Being immersed in this environment, it's sometimes difficult not to get swept up in the constant pursuit of what's next.
The next tech. The next bull. The next industry worth entering.

And it often makes me ponder: 
If I'm not particularly passionate about finance, or interested in building AI, does that somehow make the things I love doing less valuable?

Meeting Jing reminded me why I chose to create things in the first place.

I love bringing ideas to life. I love aesthetics, craftsmanship, and functionality. I love giving an imagination tangible form.
Something you can touch, use, wear, and perhaps keep for years.

I'm increasingly drawn to people who are willing to spend decades understanding a material, mastering a craft, or perfecting a product.

I want to give them a shoutout. 

The world needs people who constantly push the boundaries of what's possible. But it also needs people who are willing to go deeper into something they already believe in. 
Making this kimono has come to mean much more to me than simply creating a beautiful product.

I hope more people will get to see Jing's work as we continue exploring together -  bringing beautiful elements of Chinese culture and traditional craftsmanship to you,  creating products that are not only beautiful, but functional, thoughtful, and worth keeping.

I look forward to our next piece.

One of the single most important things that I look for in anyone is the ability to admit that they were wrong. Reflect on it and improve.

I admit that I was wrong in previous discussions with @davidtisch  at @BoxGroup. I did not think that you could produce outsized returns from hugely diversified portfolios (150+ companies) with still quite large fund sizes ($200M+). I was wrong. 

With Cursor, Baseten, Clay, and many more incredible companies in his portfolio, he has proved his thesis without shadow of doubt. 

This was an incredible discussion analyzing Box's returns over the years. 

(Link in comments)

--

1. I Don't Want to Compete With the Best VCs, That Is a Trap

Owning 10% to 20% of a true outlier in the seed round means beating the rest of the market head-to-head and convincing the founder to pick you. That takes too many steps to believe, so do not compete directly against the best VCs in the world.

I would love to hear how you think about your position as a "lead" seed investor and if that has changed with the expansion of rounds @dafrankel @Bandrew @chadbyers?

2. What Concentrated Funds Know but Do Not Admit To

Concentrated managers claim they win 90% of the deals they want, but David puts the real figure at around 20%. A fund backing 30 high-conviction companies at 10% ownership likely offers that deal to 120 to 150 companies to land its 30. He calls this adverse selection that people do not admit to.

3. Why the Lean Startup Was a Total Fake

The Lean Startup is a brainwash that ran for 10 years through professors, books, tweets and blog posts. It sent people the wrong message.

Do you think this is fair and is capital a moat today unlike in prior cycles @rabois @alanchanguk 

4. The Marketing Message That Pro Rata Is Not a Right Is BS

Early-stage VCs saying they do not need pro rata is marketing garbage. The right to invest in subsequent rounds is earned, whether or not it is in the documents, and having it written down helps the founder more than the firm. A firm that refuses a founder's request to step back is getting into a fight it will likely lose.

How do you think about this @apartovi @honam 

5. We Do Not Allow Negativity in the Investment Decision-Making Process

Partners who have not spent time with the founders are not allowed to be negative about a deal. With 70% to 90% of early-stage companies failing, explaining why one will not work is "incredibly obvious and incredibly irrelevant." The job is to say yes to the right things without fear of the ones that fail.

What is the single best advice to optimise investment decision making discussions @shaunmmaguire @AnnieDuke?

6. Why We Have Less Dilution Now Than Ever Before

In companies that scale quickly, Series B, C and D rounds are now raised at 3% to 8% dilution instead of 12% to 20%. Across multiple rounds, early-stage investments get diluted less, this is a real economic factor for early investors.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @jasonlk... 

7. Why Funding Consumer Brands at Seed No Longer Makes Sense for Venture

BoxGroup has stopped funding brands because the data that proves a brand works, such as whether people buy it and whether CAC to LTV ratios make sense, does not exist at seed. Brand investing at Series A is an interesting product for a subset of investors, but not one that fits traditional venture firms today.

How has your thinking on this changed over the years @eurie_kim @kirstenagreen @fcourt?

author: qinbafrank
quoted_text:
聊聊亚马逊三季度财报的“瑕不掩瑜”，财报其实还可以，但当下的市场环境下有瑕疵。先说瑕疵：1）营收略低于预期，很大程度是今年会员日Prime Day在公司的多数重要市场地区均提前至二季度去年则是在三季度。

净利润为206.9亿美元，低于去年同期的211.9亿美元；稀释后EPS为1.89美元，同比下降3%。这一同比下滑很大程度上与去年同期的非经营性高基数有关——2025年三季度亚马逊因Anthropic投资确认了95亿美元税前收益，而今年同期没有类似收益，

广告业务三季度表现低于预期，公司表示广告收入受到Prime Day时点等因素影响，并预计四季度广告收入同比增速将回升至高十位数区间。如果这一指引兑现三季度广告降速可能更多是时点扰动，而非广告业务结构性放缓。

2）市场最害怕的点
AI资本开支成为股价压力核心：自由现金流大幅转负资本开支是这份财报引发市场负面反应的关键。

亚马逊三季度资本支出高达772.6亿美元、约为去年同期的1.2倍，较市场预期高逾34%；自由现金流连续第二季录得负值，从去年同期的流入147.9亿美元转为流出423.6亿美元，流出规模远超二季度。公司还维持约2200亿美元的2026年全年现金资本支出指引不变，并未释放AI投入放缓的信号。

3）下一季指引没有给惊喜
亚马逊给出的四季度指引总体处于华尔街预期附近。
公司预计四季度净销售额在2400亿至2470亿美元之间，同比增长12%至16%，该营收区间的中值为2435亿美元，略低于分析师预期的2445.2亿美元，但预期值落在指引区间内。

亚马逊预计四季度经营利润为285亿至335亿美元，而市场预期约331亿美元。换言之，公司指引上限仅略高于共识预期，中点310亿美元则低于预期。

再说亮点
1）亚马逊三季度经营利润为280.8亿美元，较去年同期的174.2亿美元大增61%，经营利润率从去年同期的9.7%提升至13.9%

2）财报最大亮点仍是AWS。三季度AWS净销售额同比增长39.3%至459.8亿美元，较分析师预期高1.3%，创将近五年来最高单季增速，季末年化收入运转率达1840亿美元，环比二季度末时增长8.9%。

总的来说，
亚马逊三季度营收和EPS均小幅不及预期，广告收入略低于预期，四季度利润指引中点偏弱，同时资本开支大幅超预期且全年AI投入计划维持高位。但AWS的强劲增长和历史最高经营利润率是财报的亮点，但在当前市场环境下，投资者更关注AI投入是否会持续压低自由现金流，以及高资本开支能否在可见周期内转化为足够高的利润和现金回报。所以盘后股价走弱。

怎么看亚马逊的这份财报呢？个人角度“瑕不掩瑜”，核心是要看增长空间，烧钱这一点大家都很清楚，但是对于AWS和亚马逊能成长到什么阶段、市场并不清晰。但这次三季度财报和电话会，其实能看到未来那个图景的样子。

1）CEO Andy Jassy将当前AWS的增长逻辑描述为一个自我强化的"飞轮"：领先的功能与安全性吸引客户迁移上云，云端集中的数据与应用反过来驱动AI推理需求，AI推理又带动核心计算、存储与网络消耗，进而推动AWS在基础功能上持续再投资。

Jassy 在回答高盛的问题时，认为未来会有多个能力接近、适合不同任务的模型，企业会在同一应用中组合使用，并随着价格和性能变化进行切换。他认为 Bedrock 有成长到 EC2 同等级别服务规模的潜力

普通企业的需求有了更扎实的证据
Fortune 500 企业在 Bedrock 上的支出
接近去年同期的 7 倍，这表明大型企业的实际消费明显扩张；
Bedrock 整体 token 用量接近去年同期的 17 倍，Q3 部署的 agent 数量为此前三个季度合计的约 2 倍

这些也都说明推理调用规模快速增长，企业构建和运行 agent 的范围再进一步扩大。

2）自研芯片外销可能是新的亮点
Q3单季度，使用亚马逊定制芯片（Graviton和Trainium）的客户节省了超过20亿美元。Trainium和Graviton的收入承诺同比增加了20倍以上。Jassy透露：
由于Trainium的需求如此强劲，客户不断鼓励我们将其在AWS之外提供，我们打算在2027年后期这样做。

3）AWS未来两年的营收体量
Jassy同时预计AWS在2027年和2028年的增速均可超过40%，并有望在未来五至十年内实现年收入突破1万亿美元。与此同时，公司积压订单达5780亿美元，同比增速达三位数。

按照Jassy的说法，三季度AWS年化营收1840亿美金，如果27和28年增速均可超过40%，按照最低40%计算，28年AWS 营收体量超过3600亿美金。

4）坚定的烧钱
市场很担心亚马逊的资本开支、但官方预计2027年这一支出还将“显著增加”。
面对这种“烧钱”速度，Jassy的立场异常坚定。他明确表示，这是构建长期平台的战略，而非短期出租数据中心。原话是：
“AI是我们一生一次的机会，它是我们有生之年最大的技术变革。如果我们能将一个1840亿美元年营收的业务连续两年保持40%以上的增速，并最终走向万亿美元，为了继续保持领导地位，我们必须投资。”

Jassy电话会里的一句话展示他对于这场豪赌的意义：
“我们有能力为这一计划提供资金，我认为它将永远改变亚马逊的规模，永远改变我们的营收和自由现金流。”

AI/SI ROI doesn’t pencil unless models generate profitable outputs which necessarily needs functional data centers as the critical input. Again, power. 

Ergo, he who can shape data centers, chips and models together into a tightly coordinated stack is someone who has solved power. 

Solving power allows you to disproportionately shape AI/SI right now.

text: An incredible essay from my DeepMind colleagues! Networks networks and their dynamics are so important for studying the economic impacts of AI on markets and societies!
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
I joined @GoogleDeepMind to develop a research program on the economics of AGI. Today, together with Andrew Koh (@andrewjkoh) and Shane Legg (@ShaneLegg), we are incredibly excited to release The Economics of Intelligence, the first in a series of projects from our group on how AGI will change the economy.

How do capability improvements transform the economy, and when? In this project, we define thresholds of economic capabilities, e.g., minimal AGI, based on how they transform the economy. We then track how the economy–market structure, employment, and wages–changes during the transition across capability regimes.

We have seen exponential increases in what AI agents can do but the broader economy seems almost remarkably unchanged. Part of the reason is that the solo AI agent is the wrong economic object; economic transformation is an equilibrium outcome where organizations compete. Looking at how intelligence functions within organizations, transformation will depend on when two key capability thresholds are crossed: competence (gains on individual skills, e.g., coding, math) and coordination (gains on ability of agents to cooperate and work together).

We show that what economic transformation looks like depends on whether AI becomes supercompetent, supercooperative, or both—the regime of artificial superintelligence (ASI). Tracking this transition shows why the real visible transformation may come from improvements in coordination—a capability most benchmarks don’t yet track. Past a certain threshold, AI capabilities can break the Coasian ceiling on firm size and lead to an economy that looks drastically different than the one we see today.

Two main takeaways:
1. To understand the path of transformation, we should be tracking agentic coordination more closely.
2. The impact of AI will likely show up in wages before market structure or employment.

We are really excited about this paper. Excited to hear people’s thoughts.

text:
Is the theft of US treasury backed stable coin by North Korea an international crime under OFAC laws?

Yes, The FBI has officially attributed it to TraderTraitor, which is part of the Lazarus Group, and that’s a state-sponsored operation, not just hackers. Stealing stablecoins means taking assets backed one-to-one by US treasuries sitting in American banks, so it’s effectively theft of US-linked financial instruments. On top of that, OFAC has had Lazarus designated as a blocked North Korean entity since twenty nineteen, so any exchange or service that touches those funds is committing a sanctions violation. Add money laundering as the funds get shuffled through DeFi and instant swaps, and you’ve got a pile of US criminal statutes stacked on top of each other.
The catch is enforcement. You can’t serve a subpoena on Pyongyang, and the UN Security Council can’t act because China and Russia won’t touch it. So it stays an international crime on paper while the practical response is what you’re seeing now - freezing addresses, pressuring node operators, and watching the FBI publish wallet lists. The one angle worth watching is whether any country that hosts a TraderTraitor operative eventually gets forced to choose between hosting them and keeping access to dollar clearing.

text:
Today is my last day at Bybit.

Two years ago, I joined as a Management Trainee supporting the CEO Office: preparing meetings, running operations, and learning from the inside how a fast-moving company really works. I had no idea how much this place would shape me.

Since then, I’ve had the privilege of wearing many hats. I served as Head of Talent Acquisition, Head of Branding, Head of Marketing and worked across Fiat, Card and Payment products . I lived through many 0→1 moments and then to 100. I grew from a young trainee to leading a huge global team. Together, we did a rebranding; built Bybit’s payments product from scratch and took it into 20+ new regions around the world. Our cards passed 4 million, and our payment users are about to cross 2 million.

It wasn’t always easy. There were late nights on the crisis hotline, endless long-haul flights, and working days that stretched across every time zone. But the hard parts taught me the most, about resilience, ownership, and what a truly great team can achieve together.

Bybit made me who I am professionally. The team I’m working with is incredible. Working alongside @benbybit , @helen_moledao and Mazurka has been one of the greatest honors of my career.

I’m stepping away for personal reasons, but this isn’t really goodbye. Bybit will always be a part of me, and I’ll remain one of its biggest supporters.

Thank you Bybit to make who I am!

text: 众所周知 Claude 的审美是顶级的，之所以这么强，就是因为Claude有一套自己极其严苛的内部设计规范。 刚刚Claude泄露了它内部的组件设计系统提示词和完整规范，直接把为什么它写出来的界面有一种高级感的秘密全抖出来了。 完整规范整理了出来，写前端和Vibe Coding的可以直接抄作业： 1. 核心设计哲学与流式规范 Seamless（无缝融入）：绝对不能让用户察觉到 https://t.co/Lbi78GrGwg 宿主界面在哪结束、你的组件从哪开始。 Flat（纯粹扁平）：严禁使用渐变（gradients）、网格背景（mesh backgrounds）、噪点纹理（noise textures）或任何装饰性特效，表面必须干净平整。 Compact（紧凑克制）：内联区域只展示最核心的视觉内容，其余解释全部放在外面的正文里。 文字归回复，视觉归工具：所有的解释性文字、描述、引言和总结，必须作为正常回复写在工具调用外部。工具输出只允许包含纯粹的视觉元素（diagram, chart, interactive widget），严禁在 HTML/SVG 内部塞入解释段落、章节标题或说明性散文（用户的字体设置只对外部回复生效，对微件内部无效）。 流式代码顺序：输出是按 Token 逐个流式传输的，代码结构必须让有用内容尽早出现。HTML 强制顺序：简短的

author: davelee
quoted_text:
Hard for me to get behind the scarcity argument for Bitcoin. Yes, Bitcoin is scarce (only 21 million will ever exist).  But scarcity alone doesn't create value. Bitcoin's value comes from people believing it's worth something and paying for that belief. And that belief can change.

Compare it to stocks, yes stocks are also valued based on perceived value and perception of that value can change.  But the main difference is the underlying business, revenue, profit, growth, etc.  In other words, even if the market tanks at least I'll pay some multiple of earnings for a stock.  One can argue there's an underlying business for Bitcoin as well and you can value it the same way, but I just don't see it.  Hard to value Bitcoin as a multiple of earnings/growth.

Same goes for land.  Land is valuable because of perceived value but that perceived value has an underlying use case.  For example, sure land price can jump due to speculation and it can crash too.  But in the end, a good piece of land still has value to build something on it (ie., a building on a busy city corner or a house overlooking the ocean).

You can say Bitcoin has an underlying use case, namely store of value.  But its store of value use depends on its perceived value.  Meaning, if let's say there's a better store of value and people don't value Bitcoin as much, then its price drops which inherently negatively impact its store of value proposition.  In other words, what's Bitcoin's underlying business that I'm buying outside its store of value proposition.  Even gold has an underlying some value outside of its store of value proposition.  Gold is used in jewelry, electronics, etc.  But still much of its use is still resting on its perceived value, ie., in jewelry.  But it has thousands of years of history vs Bitcoin.

You could say Bitcoin's use is money transfer, meaning final settlement without intermediaries. But is that use case durable? I'm not convinced. It's already being disrupted, and not by banks. Stablecoins do the job better for most people, because people want to send dollars, not a volatile asset.

But I'm not betting against Bitcoin because it's possible the belief in Bitcoin doesn't die and it becomes a lasting global neutral reserve asset.  I'm just not sold on it.

text:
Worth some thought of what would happen to Zcash governance and coin holder voting if a large exchange hack happens.

No, it wouldn't be catastrophic. In particular, a single hack only gives a small amount of influence, but one might imagine a world of multiple hacks over a few years, at which point the vote looks way less credible. Even then, Zcash can adapt, add checks and balances, etc. So this is a serious thing to consider, but not necessarily a reason to just reject coin holder voting outright.
 
But running the thought experiment will be useful, since it will tell folks a lot of what they want from a resilient and decentralized governance mechanism. 
For example, it looks very different if coinholder voting retroactively decides funding prioritization vs if it’s deciding core protocol decisions.

author: petergyang
quoted_text:
I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI.

Some takes I loved:

1. “It shouldn’t take someone longer to read your doc than it took you to write it.”

Writing is thinking. AI can be a thought partner, but you should firmly be in the driver’s seat.

2. “It’s no longer about can you build it, it’s about should it even exist?”

Code went from a scarce asset to basically free. If you can “throw a couple of agents at it over a weekend,” it’s probably not a durable product. So the hard part now is deciding what’s worth building in the first place.

3. “Why do you even want a person in your product?”

Agents do more of our work every month, so you should ask if your product needs a UI at all. Jaclyn thinks people will still show up to create, learn, or be entertained. Any task that feels like a chore should be built for agents first.

4. “Don’t just give users exactly what they want.”

Talk to them all the time, but find the root problem and solve it in a way they wouldn’t have thought of. You want them to walk away thinking, “I didn’t think this was possible, but it’s exactly what I wanted.”

5. “You shouldn’t expect users to know how to write elaborate prompts.”

Small business owners don’t have time to start from an empty prompt box. So her team built Pomelli, Google’s tool for SMBs to create on-brand content, to read your website and learn your business first.

6. “Let your kid be your creative director.”

Jaclyn’s 5-year-old loves scary stories, so they made their own podcast, Maya and the Fog. Her daughter picks the voices, names the characters, and gives notes on each cut, and Jaclyn has the agent produce the episode. It’s live on Spotify.

今天肖风老师在 HKDAF 论坛上提到他觉得 Code is Law 已经失败且不值得追求了，主要原因大体是各类黑客事件。 
我非常不赞同。

我觉得我们生活在一个历史上非常罕见的、在一超多强下、在世界警察维护下 30 余年相对善意国际秩序的窗口期。 
我们今天的年轻人绝对已经惊醒过去 30 年中国年均两位数的 GDP 增长率不可复现，那怎么会觉得过去 30 年合作大于竞争的国际秩序、相对温和的一国内部环境能持续呢？

我阅读历史，我看到国与国之间基本上或是零和博弈或是负和博弈状态，只有冷战后、中国加入WTO 达峰的罕见窗口期是正和博弈；
我阅读历史，我看一国之内大部分时候仍是汲取性制度或福山式的无能政府，也只有极少数时间是包容式善意的政府。

我带着这种悲观主义、我带着对负和博弈状态和汲取性一国内环境的恐惧，我说 区块链提供的道德盲视的、无国家有规则空间是我们次好的第四种选择 。

展开说一点，现代和后现代世界本质上是高度鼓励家长式国家的，是高度鼓励利维坦将每个公民都预设成需要照顾的、无完全行为能力的主体（尽管事实上确实已大规模巨婴化，但同时即使这个体系运作最好的状态下，也没有一分安全是不需要你让渡个人权利去换取的。

区块链 Code is Law 背后是一种非常古典保守主义式的、非常辉格式的伦理。它要求每个参与者都像真正的成年人一样，拥有 100% 属于自己的产权，同时也对自己的选择和客观风险承担 100% 的责任。 
这种在古典时代非常自然的伦理在今天这个世界好像显得极其不负责任。

在包容式善意政府的情况下，你让渡的每分权利确实可以给你换回一分 safety；在正和博弈的国际秩序中，可冻结、可回滚的国际结算 T+1 确实意味着更安全。 
但 How long will it last ? 至少可冻结、可回滚的国际结算已经对 俄伊 俩 Pariah state 失效了。

text: sample efficiency is the actual frontier
author: badlogicgames
quoted_text:
Yann LeCun and Randall Balestriero just Proved the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, and found a better way to achieve it.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that AI models trained on different modalities, like images and text, eventually learn similar representations of the world. But this paper shows that how models are trained matters more than simply scaling them up.

So they mathematically show that, under certain conditions, two JEPAs trained completely separately can learn essentially the same underlying representation of the world. One learns from different images of the same scene, while the other learns from different descriptions of that scene, without ever being trained on image-text pairs.

Their approach achieves the same image-text alignment with 42x fewer training samples than next-token prediction. A 109M-parameter text JEPA even outperforms LLMs up to 72B parameters on cross-modal alignment benchmarks.

https://t.co/3j1enq9qF7

text: Practical robotics is nigh
author: garrytan
quoted_text:
10 Spicy Takes After Talking to 50 Friends at the Frontier of Robotics 🤖🔥

1/ Astra IS robotics' GPT-3 moment. Ironically, now that it's finally here, some in robotics seem reluctant to acknowledge it. Perhaps because it (sadly) didn't come from a robotics company?

2/ Robotics is becoming just another vertical for frontier labs. Not so different from coding in some respects. Why reinvent general intelligence for every industry?

3/ Robotics was too hard to underwrite until now. No convincing pretraining scaling law, no convergence on models, data, or hardware. No wonder some critics dismissed it as a fragmented industry playing an expensive "demo game". Astra may finally offer a credible path to scale.

4/ Robotics foundation-model startups have a case. But how strong is it? The argument: Astra handles System 2 (reasoning), while specialized models retain System 1 (skills) and System 0 (motor control). Fair. But isn't that already a narrower value proposition? And who says the boundary stops there?

5/ Follow the talent. Word is OpenAI reorganized its 30–40-person robotics team around the core Astra model. Hearing similar moves toward general models at @Tesla_Optimus. Org charts may tell us more than any demo.

6/ The robotics data gold rush is real. Million-hour procurement programs, some potentially reaching tens of millions of hours. Talk of budgets approaching $1B per frontier lab.

7/ Bullish on robotics hardware volumes. As intelligence becomes more accessible, the barriers to building useful robots could fall dramatically. The moat shifts toward reliability, dexterity, integration, and deployment.

8/ Robotics could fuel the next semiconductor and memory supercycle. A 100B-parameter model running on the edge requires ~50GB just for 4-bit weights. Now multiply that by millions of robots. Why do you think @JensenHuang is so obsessed with robotics? @elonmusk saw it coming: https://t.co/oKQi0XDhiL

9/ Is self-driving immune to the general-model threat? After coding and robotics, why assume self-driving remains the exclusive domain of proprietary, vertical models? Robotaxi increasingly feels like a solved problem to me. But if and when frontier labs move into self-driving, we could see an Apple vs. Android dynamic. Think about the implications for $TSLA, Waymo, and other OEMs.

10/ The next bottleneck may not be intelligence. It's deployment. Models are improving faster than our ability to deploy robots in the messy real world. Integration, hardware variance, failure recovery, and economics remain brutally hard. The real moat may be turning intelligence into reliable, profitable physical work.

--
I realize some of these takes may rub people the wrong way, especially those who have spent years doing the hard work of advancing robotics. That's not my intention. 

I'm sharing them to spark debate, not to declare winners and losers. Astra has only been out for a month or so, and it's far too early to draw definitive conclusions. More importantly, when the TAM is this enormous - potentially the largest in tech - there should be plenty of room for different approaches and many winners.

++

text:
在美国的大陆川粉最大无知：以为自己是“自己人”

前不久网上流传的一段微信群聊天，格外引人深思。一对大陆来美国的川粉夫妇背着川普与万斯的旗帜，兴高采烈地去参加MAGA集会。然而到了现场，他们非但没有体会到“同阵营”的温暖，反而遭到白人种族主义者的辱骂与推搡。

在美国的大陆川粉最大的无知，在于他们以为支持川普，就能成为川普政治圈里的“自己人”。

他们以为，只要举起MAGA的旗帜，喊着“天选之人”，就能换取MAGA白人基本盘的认同；只要坚定反共、誓死效忠，就能跨入他们渴望的政治朋友圈。

那对参加MAGA集会、却被极端白人辱骂、推搡，甚至呵斥为“中国间谍”的华人夫妇，就是一个极为讽刺的例证。

他们背着川普与万斯的旗帜，却没有换来哪怕一丝尊重；他们交出了所有的忠诚，最终得到的依然是一句“滚回去”。

政治上的“自己人”，从来不是靠表忠心就能换来的。

你可以把川普奉为神明，但在川普的白人基本盘眼里，你依然只是一个黄皮肤的华人、一个抢夺资源的移民、一个永远洗不掉标签的“外人”。

你一厢情愿的倾情支持，也根本构不成让他们接纳你的入场券。

这正是大陆川粉最无知的地方：他们把政治投机误认为身份认同，以为奴颜婢膝可以换来等价交换。

川普的政治机器需要的是你的选票，而不是你的尊严；需要的是你的盲从，而不是你的平等。

你替他辩护，为他捐款，为他的失败寻找各种荒谬的借口——这一切，都改变不了你在他政治圈层中的真实位置。

大陆川粉最可悲、最可怜的地方在于：

他们竭尽全力想要挤进那个圈子，却始终没有意识到，在川普和他的MAGA白人基本盘眼里，他们从始至终都只是“外人”，只是二等川粉。
author: 3lbn3qrekoj
quoted_text:
在美国的大陆川粉大多是愚蠢的政治乡巴佬

在一个清华校友云集的微信群里，我遇到这样一位典型的从大陆来美国的川粉。

早年间，他曾是奥巴马的支持者，被那些关于变革与希望的华丽演说所打动；多年后，他自认为彻底看穿了左派的虚伪，一头扎进川普阵营，并无休止地攻击民主党，称其为“猪党”，以此寻求被骗后的心理平衡。

他以为自己完成了一场政治觉醒。 殊不知，他又陷入了另一场骗局。自以为从民主党走向共和党是政治上的成熟；实际上，不过是从一种盲从，变成了另一种政治欺骗的猎物。

许多大陆川粉的美国梦有惊人地相似：

早年埋头苦读、勤奋工作、买房置业、生儿育女、申请绿卡和公民，把所有精力投入到职业晋升和薪水上，把殷殷期盼寄托于子女进入藤校。他们终日围着自己的一亩三分地打转，对美国政治所知甚少、理解肤浅。

高等教育的背景让他们带有一点小资情怀和理想主义。于是，当他们偶尔关注政治时，很容易被奥巴马式的宏大叙事所吸引。

那么，究竟是什么让他们从奥巴马的支持者，变成了川普的拥护者？

说到底，是利益粉碎了信仰，算计击垮了情怀。

民主党的税收政策，触及了他们的钱袋； 平权政策（Affirmative Action），挡住了他们子女通往藤校的路； 开放的移民政策，让他们感觉自己的福利和生存空间受到挤压。

这是冷冰冰的利益计算。精致的利己主义使他们掉头转向川普，并自认为这是“政治觉醒”。

他们浅薄的政治素养，又让他们轻信川普简单而荒谬的承诺和主张。

例如，当川普宣称关税能为美国带来巨额收入、让美国重新强大时，这群大陆川粉齐声叫好。

他们精明地计算着每一笔个人得失，所以特别崇尚川普的交易哲学：

“你占我便宜，我就占你更大的便宜。”

他们看不到，川普的关税已经造成的经济动荡；更看不到，美国正因川普的关税政策而逐渐成为世界经济体系中的孤岛。这最终也必将伤害到每一个斤斤计较的他们。

大陆川粉最悲哀之处在于：

自以为看透了民主党，却又再次落入川普的骗局。

大陆川粉既是精明的利己主义者，更是愚蠢的政治乡巴佬。

author: 0xzhaozhao
quoted_text:
【奉劝大家不要用国产机翻墙，不要在国产机上安卓境外 APP】
我某些朋友用的国产安卓手机，前不久被当地公安打电话，要求卸载 X 和 Telegram，因为我其中一个朋友的小米 14 已经 root 了，我觉得因为梯子配置不当导致的 DNS 泄露，或者别的原因，可能性不大，我就重点排查手机上会上报应用列表的应用

经排查，我朋友的小米 14，HyperOS 3，其中的“系统安全组件”和“SystemHelper”，会分别把应用列表上报给小米反诈引擎（fraud-detection.engine.miui[.]com/hyperos/fraud/app/report和flash.sec.miui[.]com/detect/app）和联通的某个网址（dm.wo[.]com[.]cn:18080/register）

SystemHelper 会默认统计过去 24 小时内有使用记录的应用，枚举已安装应用，关联使用统计和流量，跳过包名以 com[.]android 开头的条目。载荷的序列化实现还包含 IMEI、IMSI、ICCID 等字段，因此具备将应用情况与设备/SIM 标识关联上报的能力。

系统安全组件会上报第三方应用清单、包名、版本、签名摘要、名称，另有扫描结果和仿冒应用上报；有电话/QQ/微信语音反诈、屏幕视频采集、转写文本和视频片段云检测，以及用户反馈上传原始音频的实现

关于系统安全组件的录屏采集功能，分辨率 720 × 1280，24 fps，固定竖屏尺寸。相关的流程如下：
取得系统录屏对象
 → 录制约 3 秒屏幕画面到私有缓存文件
 → 读取整段 MP4，转为 Base64
 → 加密后上传小米云端
 → 等待返回“是否风险”
     ├─ 未命中：删除临时片段，延时 2 秒后继续录制，重复上述行为
     └─ 命中：保留一份片段供反馈，显示警告并停止服务

这些应用，SystemHelper 貌似是和 SIM 卡激活相关的，系统安全组件貌似是和反诈相关的，但是都具有高度的数据上报属性。没有 root 的机器，这些组件是无法卸载或者提取的，并且我也暂未分析这两个 APP 卸载之后，会不会自己下载回来。

综上，还是建议大家，海外产业用外版 iPhone，尽量不要碰国行安卓，要用安卓机，也是刷 ASOP 使用。

逆向由 GPT 完成，如有错误，敬请指正。

He who shapes power, data centers, chips and models into an economically feasible endpoint, disproportionately shapes AI/SI right now. 

Why?

Power is THE binding constraint in AI/SI. Few really have it. 

Data centers don’t work without power. This is not about promises of power tomorrow. Or forecasted power in 2028. Power TODAY. 

Chips can’t operate profitably unless installed in a functional data center. If you can install chips, it’s because you’ve solved the power problem. 

Models aren’t economically viable unless run on cost effective infrastructure which requires a functional data center with low input costs and reliable management. This can’t happen without power. 

AI/SI ROI doesn’t pencil unless models generate profitable outputs which necessarily needs functional data centers as the critical input. Again, power. 

Ergo, he who can shape data centers, chips and models together into a tightly coordinated stack is someone who has solved power. 

Solving power allows you to disproportionately shape AI/SI right now.

text:
This is excellent general advice: AI makes your writing average.

It’s ok to use AI for tasks where you need average writing. “Reply to that message and confirm i will be there” “Summarize my to dos from this transcript and send to everyone” — that kind of stuff.

But when it’s important, like your YC founder application, be yourself. Even writing then using AI to lightly revise can make your text a little *too* clean. (And now with Claude and others it will silently change your wording for AI fingerprinting!)

What works for me is to use AI to organize my thoughts then write from that outline.
author: twid
quoted_text:
I've read maybe ~10,000 YC applications.  8000 for YC admissions/PG quite a few years ago and anther 2000 informally as an alum.

There's a new and growing mistake and I want to share why it's more important than you think.

By the way - I try not to ever say YC admissions works this way or that way.  That's YC's job and they're always changing things and making up their own minds.

But I will share my impression and you can see what you think - YC partners, please chime in as well if you like.

The YC application is fundamentally an evaluation of a founder's potential.  And much less an evaluation of a specific business.  (Airbedbreakfast transitioning into Airbnb because Brian, Nate, Joe never give up and never stop listening to their customers)

So, in your writing of the application, YOU need to shine through.

This batch, I read ~200 applications.  

I'm guessing over half were significantly written, edited, or polished with AI.

That half was easily in the bottom half of my informal rankings, almost every time.

To be clear, most were NOT AI slop.  I often couldn't tell at first they had used AI.  Founders were pouring their heart and soul into their app - so I what I received was high quality.

But I think the AI really hurt them.  Here's why:

Once polished by AI, I as reader lost insight into the personality of the writer.  

I love the YC application because the questions are the same questions I would ask in office hours or casually to a friend that wanted help with their startup.  It pushes the founder out of their pitchdeck/VC talk style into simple worded questions that can be answered simply as well.  And great founders shine through when they just write like they talk.  The LLM writing made answers feel more like a corporate cover letter, with the personality drained out.

The AI-assisted drafts also gave me a sense of mid work.  The writing itself seemed like zero standard deviations from the mean.  The LLMs had lopped off the outlier portions of sentences, paragraphs, and thoughts.  Given the YC App is an outlier detector, a writing tool that lops off outlier writing is the opposite of what you want.

And the AI writing was needlessly verbose.  Which hurts when a reliable predictor of great founders is that they're deep thinkers and deep thinking shines through in the density of their writing.

So...

I did an experiment.  I asked a bunch of these seemingly AI-assisted app writers to talk with me live.  I just asked them the same YC app questions and recorded their answers.

I then gave them back the transcripts.  Unedited and unpolished.

And...

OMG!  A good number turned from easy no to actual good applications.  

Magic!  Remove AI >> Improve application.

This happened BOTH with native English speakers and founders abroad.

So this is my recommendation to all of you.    

Don't let AI touch your application, even for a second.

And maybe try the dictation approach with a friend.

My apologies to the YC admissions team if you already knew AI-written applications were crap and you were using this insight to help you easily move applications to the No pile.

YC's Winter Batch Application deadline is Nov 2nd.
