text:
druck walking through the nvda 2022 long trade is pretty good insight that you dont get in a lot of intvws...sizing/trading signposts, what he looks for in pressing winners, fundamental vs. non-fundamental considerations

Stan Druckenmiller: So the Nvidia story is quite interesting, and it’s a perfect example of the process we spoke about earlier where I rely on other people. I have some young superstars in my firm, and they had a network, and they started really talking about AI. This was in early to mid-2022. Then I started noticing that the kids at Stanford were shifting from 50/50 crypto and 50/50 AI to more going to AI. And that’s something we’ve always looked at in venture is where the kids are going. When we bought Palantir in ‘08-’09, it was because that was a cool company back then that all the kids wanted to go to. My partner had in people from his AI network in Palo Alto. They came in and explained AI. Most of it went over my head, but I knew that this was really big.

Iliana Bouzali: Why did you feel it was really big? It could have been a fad. You didn’t feel this way for other fads.

Stan Druckenmiller: Because I had total trust in my partner, and I thought I was grasping the enormity. It turns out I wasn’t grasping the enormity because I didn’t know about large language models, but I knew about all the other conventional stuff that was going on in AI. So I said to my partner, “What should I buy?” He said, “Nvidia. That’s the way to play AI.” So, just on this, about as much as you just heard, I bought a not-big position in Nvidia—enough to get hurt on or to make some money on. Then, about two weeks later, ChatGPT happened, which he had not mentioned in our conversation. Well, even I understood the enormity of what that meant when I saw even the rudimentary things it was doing back then.

So then I doubled the position. Then one of the great services you and Morgan Stanley provide are these macro calls. And all the macro guys, including myself (luckily, I hadn’t talked yet), were espousing their views on the world, which are probably worth a nickel and a cup of coffee. And an analyst there, who was from the tech world, said, “You guys are in the trees, and you’re missing the forest. There’s something much bigger than anything you’re talking about, even for macro.” And he went on to amplify everything I had heard three or four weeks ago about AI, but this time I had ChatGPT between that conversation and him. So then I doubled my position again, and literally, I don’t think I knew how to spell Nvidia three months before.

When the stock took off, I knew through years of experience when you have massive, massive change, investors just can’t make themselves keep up with it. And it was funny because the person who knew 10x more than anybody at the table, and probably 50x more than me about AI, he sold his Nvidia shortly thereafter. But I knew that this stock would go up for at least two or three years and go up a lot. And I said publicly in an interview about five months later, “I cannot possibly see myself selling Nvidia over the next two or three years,” because it had already gone from like $150 to $390 and this person couldn’t believe I still owned it. And I basically said, “Not only do I own it, the way these things evolve, this stock can’t not go up for at least three years.”

So then the stock goes to 800. And I violated everything I said in the interview. I couldn’t stand success. It had gone from $150 to $800. I was long-term in it. I couldn’t deal with it, and I sold it. And then it was $1,400 like five weeks later, and I was sick. But it’s amazing how little I knew about Nvidia. I couldn’t even tell you what the earnings were.

Iliana Bouzali: That’s a sign of confidence, and it’s because you’re Stan Druckenmiller that you can be so blatantly honest about the way you think about these things. And I think it’s very encouraging to portfolio managers that are coming up in the business, and they often feel like they need to be intellectually very much on their game constantly. What I’m getting from this, the ability to filter, to manage instead of being wedded to a spreadsheet, is really unique and quite helpful. You said something that you violated what you had said and sold at $800. Would you have done that 20 years ago? Is this a sign of a more mature way of trading now versus before?

Stan Druckenmiller: Probably not. I’m not used to making 6x my money in an equity in two years, and I’m not Warren Buffett. I think I would have screwed it up 20 years ago when I was good, too.

text:
MTS-ification is flattening most categories of tech work

It's probably the most interesting and import idea to absorb and study to understand the future dynamics of the job market, and how to take advantage of them

TLDR is that titles used to describe "what we do", post-AI they describe "what we own". Depth is rentable, so passing work around costs more than doing the work itself. AI can fill in the "average" so what’s left to stand out is a combination of agency, judgement, and spike: the thing(s) you do better than almost anyone. 

Invest in and become fluent with as many relevant AI tools (and techniques) as possible, be able to explain simply and clearly how you can use them to expand your capacity and span adjacent specialties complementing your main.

Emerging categories to position for (beyond MTS):
Growth staff (me): marketing / sales / partnerships / community / devrel
Operations staff: finance / people / legal ops  / internal tools
Customer staff: support, customer success, account management, solutions engineering, implementation 

In interviews and on resumes
1. Lead with your "spike", have ultra-crisp stories where it was the reason behind a great success
2. Have ultra-crisp stories exemplifying agency and good judgement that have driven some outcome end to end and the impact
3. Say “I,” not “we,” and be ready to describe exact details

There are big changes and things are being shaken up, with all disruption though there are always tons of opportunities, the people who move quickly and get in front of them the fastest will have the most upside. There are SO many new companies with crazy growth, pre-unicorns and new unicorns hiring like crazy, you want to be part of a company that will 10x or 100x over the next 10 years, not one that is about to have to reshape everything because they themselves are being disrupted.

Lots of AI people made it low status to comment on shortfalls and failures of models, or the fact that they're not reallty automating jobs fully and so on. Any scrutiny means you're not 'AGI pilled' (which is not a claim about technology but sometimes a quasi-religious one about its impacts and adoption). It's a shame because it's actually very interesting to explore the spikiness, jaggedness, failures, complementarities and so on; but for a lot of people this is almost a waste of time because 'something something future models!1!!' means they get to just parrot 'this is the worst the models will ever be' whilst dismissing any crumb of empiricism away because they've already worked out the future based on theory and projections alone. 

To be fair I sympathise with them to a degree because the 'other sides' aren't any better, essentially over-indexing on short-term failures (Rs in strawberry etc) and extrapolating from these to dismiss the technology completely. But I care less about what these people think about capabilities since time just proves them wrong rapidly enough. Why would you exercise vibe arbitrage over such a cheap target? I also find it painfully boring to constantly litigate 'AI skeptics' - there are more interesting and thornier discussions to be had.

以前我一直觉得，CZ 和何一把币安做到今天这个体量，九年了，也该轻松一点了

现在看来，还是我对建设这两个字理解得太浅

这几天币安发生的事，大家应该都知道了

63 亿美元的安全事故，提现一度暂停

这么大的事情，肯定不是一句 SAFU 就能轻描淡写过去的。安全出了问题，该追究就得追究

但我确实被后面发生的一些细节触动到了

1. 币安选择自己承担损失，拿出资金补足被盗资产

2. 从 80% 到 95%，一边补资金，一边做安全审查、更新储备金证明、逐步恢复提现

CZ 虽然早已不负责币安的日常运营，但这几天依然在 X 上不断转发恢复进度，回应用户，感谢参与追踪和冻结被盗资金的各方

一姐就更有意思了，身为币安联席 CEO，最近在评论区干的活，简直比客服还细

用户问提现，她回复
有人质疑资金去向，她解释
有人传播谣言，她亲自辟谣
有人反映业务没恢复，她还会主动去问进度

这波事件中最让我心疼的，其实还是一姐

前段时间她才公开说过，自己又怀孕了，最近体力确实不如以前，但工作量并没有减少🥺

结果这次币安出了这么大的事，她依旧活跃在事件的最前线

一边要面对几十亿美元的安全事故，一边还要安抚用户情绪、跟进恢复进度、回应社区里各种质疑

以她今天的位置，这些琐碎的事情完全可以交给下面的人去处理

可她偏偏还是那个会亲自出现在评论区、会认真听用户反馈的一姐🫡

很多人心疼她这几天没休息好，她还专门解释，自己其实睡了，是整个团队一起努力，她只是做了分内的事

这种轻描淡写，比任何豪言壮语都更有分量

CZ 说，货币的基础是信任
何一说，这就是我的工作

两句话放在一起，突然就有些理解币安为什么能走到第九年了

当然，我不会说发生这么大的安全事故是一件好事

但一个平台真正的分量，有时候恰恰是在最难的时候才能看出来

顺风顺水时，谁都可以讲长期主义

真遇到事情，能不能承担损失，能不能给用户交代，能不能把承诺一件件兑现，这才是最难的

币安用了九年时间，把一家交易所做成了全球性的加密生态

我原以为这是他们事业的高度

现在才慢慢理解，可能真正支撑这个高度的，是九年过去，创始人身上那股劲还没有散

一个依然关心这个行业的信任
一个怀着孕，还在认真回复用户的问题

CZ 和何一都已经不缺掌声了，可九年过去，还是这么认真

有些人把建设挂在嘴上
有些人，已经把建设过成了日子🫡

也希望一姐在忙着照顾几千万用户的时候，别忘了照顾好自己🫂

text:
$3.47 vs $1.38. same prompt, two video models, and most people picked the cheaper clip as the more real one.
that one comparison sums up october pretty well. here’s the rest of the month👇

· video got cheap, and long
openai switched off the sora api on sep 24, so october was the first full month without it. wan 3.0 and seedance 2.5 took the top of the leaderboard, both at 30s per clip, and the price gap between them pays for more drafts per idea.
then kling 4.0 landed on oct 15: up to 30s in one pass, 10 keyframes, 15 references. the skill that matters now is directing: where the shot starts, where it turns, what has to stay the same.

· consistency became a model feature
openai shipped chatgpt images 2.5 on oct 5. google shipped nano banana 2.1 the next day at about half the per-image price, with multi-turn character consistency built in, and retired nano banana 2 on oct 29. black forest labs put out flux 3 image plus open-weight klein.
in september we said: write the identity once, only change the shot. this month the models started handling that part on their own.

so what’s left for the people building on top?
taste. knowing what makes a double exposure read as one image, or what separates a designed glitch from a broken file. that’s the part myshell agents package into one tap.

text:
推荐感兴趣的朋友可以看看纪录片《监视资本主义/The Social Dilemma》📺
现在所有的app都是设计出来让我们成瘾的，就比如我写推文，如果获得了别人的认可点赞转发，都会激发我继续写 继续看 刷下去的冲动。比如刷下去没有翻页，可以无限一直滚动向下刷新，这也是设计的一环，容易沉迷进去一直刷。
但很多时候无意义的刷新信息浏览，是没必要没有意义的。资本是想我们把所有时间都浪费在上面。我们成为他们的资源被进行售卖，操控等等。

我最近开始尝试电子极简生活，就是尽量摆脱电子产品的诱惑束缚。比如为此了解到关闭了抖音 小红书一类软件的“个性化推荐”功能，效果立竿见影。关掉之后不会推送感兴趣的内容了，也就减少了这种刷下去的冲动，只用来作为搜索学习工具使用，就不会存在打开app本来要搜索什么结果被吸引进去刷了半天忘记了原本的事。

真正该做的事要多出去走走，多陪伴家人互动交流，多做一些离开屏幕app的事情，看书 做手工 健身 等等... 多思考，主动搜索信息了解  少被动通过屏幕接收，不然不知不觉就会被植入一些观念从而引导我们的行为，成为资本的傀儡。
别忘了关闭app提醒功能，那也是他们勾引你拿起手机打开app继续沉迷其中的关键招数。❌

很多时候做交易也一样，庄家不希望你离开牌桌，他巴不得24h你都在里面不停的看盘交易，沉迷其中 沦陷其中。不怕你赚钱，就不怕你不常玩。
各种币圈信息推送app也一样，建议都不要打开推送按钮，只在你需要搜索相关新闻的时候自行搜索即可，不然他每天都会有无数信息推送给你，刺激你，让你觉得有机会 忍不住要回来操作。频繁交易是菜鸟们的大忌。没有高频交易的能力还天天守着屏幕看K线，为了什么呢？为了亏钱，为了折磨自己...

你细想是不是这么个道理吧，多自己想想为什么。现在太多人无条件顺从app顺从手机等电子产品了，有消息你马上就看 你恨不得1s都不错过，想想为什么会无形中变成这样？
你不信可以试试，完全离开手机几个小时后，甚至会出现戒断反应，会很不适应 很无聊 很痛苦的感觉，这就是上瘾 和吸毒是一样的。
你需要要意识到，研发APP的和研发毒品的人没有区别，他们每天思考的就是如何让用户快速上瘾终身无法摆脱这件事。

2026年10月29日,晚上八点零五分。

有人开始把钱从币安的钱包里搬出来。

十条区块链同时在动。

以太坊、比特币、Tron、XRP、Solana……

大部分转账,在大约20分钟内完成。

总金额:约63.6亿美元。

人类历史上最大的一笔加密货币盗窃。

是2025年Bybit那次15亿的四倍多。

一位分析师看完链上数据后说了一句话:

这事只可能是电脑干的。

人类的手,按不了这么快。

10月31日,FBI确认了幕后:

朝鲜。

一个代号TraderTraitor的团队。

而这群人,很可能在十一二岁的时候,就已经被选中了。

朝鲜筛人,从小学开始。

全国的数学苗子,会被一层层筛出来,送进平壤的重点中学。

比如平壤第一中学——专门收天才学生的特殊高中。

在那里,他们集中学两样东西:

数学,和计算机。

一个孩子被选中,意味着什么?

意味着他和他的家人,可以搬进平壤。

分到更好的房子,更好的配给。

在一个工人月薪常年只有几美元的国家里,这是一张改变整个家族命运的票。

而这张票的条件是:

你必须一直优秀下去。

尖子生高中毕业后,会升入三所学校之一:

金策工业综合大学。

金日成综合大学。

或者,自动化大学。

前两所是朝鲜最顶尖的学府。

但真正的核心,是第三所。

自动化大学,前身叫美林大学。

1986年,由金正日亲自下令创办。

它不是一所普通大学。

它是朝鲜军方的网络战学校。

有脱北者描述过校门口的守则:

未经校长批准,任何车辆不得入内——

除了金正日的车。

学校设五个专业:

电子工程、指挥自动化、程序设计、技术侦察、计算机科学。

一个脱北者说,学生在那里学的是:

解剖Windows操作系统。

编写破坏性病毒。

学制五年左右。

据估计,这所学校每年向外输出约100名黑客。

毕业之后,他们被分配进朝鲜人民军侦察总局。

侦察总局下面,有一个叫121局的单位。

Lazarus,就归它管。

121局创建于1998年。

是侦察总局规模最大、也最成熟的网络单位。

它的成员,大部分是自动化大学精挑细选的毕业生。

一个2014年脱北的人估算,当时121局大约有1800人。

而韩国方面后来的估计是——

从几千人,到上万人。

一个两千多万人口、连互联网都没有对外开放的国家,

养了一支上万人的网络部队。

但他们不全在朝鲜境内。

事实上,最关键的那部分人,必须出去。

因为朝鲜国内的网络条件,根本不足以支撑这种规模的行动。

他们被派到中国沈阳、丹东,派到俄罗斯,派到东南亚。

伪装成普通的IT外包人员。

有报告提到,沈阳的一家朝中合资酒店——七宝山酒店——

曾长期是121局黑客的活动据点。

他们在那里做两件事:

一边接外包的活,给国家挣外汇。

一边搞网络攻击。

2025年,美国司法部披露了这套体系的另一面:

朝鲜IT人员用盗来的和伪造的身份,

成功入职了100多家美国公司。

其中有不少是财富500强。

协助他们的美国中间人,曾专程飞到沈阳和丹东去见他们。

同年6月,FBI在14个州搜查了21处"笔记本农场"。

缴获了约137台电脑。

那些电脑摆在美国人的家里。

屏幕后面坐着的,是平壤的人。

而出国,是有代价的。

被派出去的人,必须把家人留在国内。

这是整个系统里最关键的一环。

人权组织在报告里写得很直白:

留在朝鲜的家属,实际上就是一种人质。

你在境外赚到的钱,大部分要上缴。

你在境外做的事,要定期汇报。

你如果跑了,留下的人会怎么样,所有人都知道。

所以他们不是普通意义上的黑客。

他们是被一整套制度,从十岁起就锁定了人生轨道的人。

天赋被识别。

家庭被奖赏。

然后,家庭被扣下。

回看这次的币安。

币安说,攻击者最初的入口,是一台工程师的笔记本电脑被攻破。

还有其他的突破点。

交易签名,是提前拿到的。

准备工作,在盗窃发生之前很久就开始了。

然后在某一个瞬间,一次性引爆。

20分钟。

63.6亿美元。

最终约30亿被链上冻结。

但另一半,已经在Tornado Cash和各种兑换服务里开始漂流了。

FBI说,这些资产正在被主要换成以太坊,准备进入下一轮洗白。

而据统计,朝鲜从这类盗窃中拿到的钱,

大约有四成,流向了核武器和其他武器项目。

2025年,朝鲜黑客偷了20.2亿美元。

那一年全球加密货币被盗总额是34亿。

一个国家,拿走了六成。

照片里那些人,看起来和任何一个加班的程序员没什么两样。

戴耳机,穿polo衫,坐在屏幕前。

有人戴眼镜,有人顶着锅盖头。

视频会议框里,他们的脸和世界上任何一家公司的远程员工并列在一起。

他们可能是某家美国公司上周刚招进来的"远程工程师"。

也可能是沈阳某个写字楼里的"外包团队"。

他们大概率在十一二岁时,因为数学好,被国家选中。

那一天,对他们的父母来说,是全家最光荣的一天。

因为孩子终于有机会,把全家带进平壤。

世界上大多数国家,会把最聪明的孩子送进实验室,送进大学,送进硅谷。

有一个国家,把他们送进了一支部队。

然后告诉他们:

你的天赋,是你全家搬进首都的理由。

也是你全家不能离开的理由。

63.6亿美元,在20分钟里易主。

那是世界上最大的一次盗窃。

而动手的人,可能从来没有机会选择,自己要不要成为一个小偷。

有些人是被天赋成就的。

有些人,是被自己的天赋扣为人质的。🫠

text:
为什么黑客攻击币安、Bybit 和 Bitget，却仍无法触及 Coinbase？？？

核心在于其资产保管架构与密钥管理方式不同。

核心安全差异：没有“巨大蜜罐”

大多数交易所为了提现速度，会把大量资产集中在少数活跃热钱包，私钥或签名权限相对集中，一旦内部系统、DevOps机器、签名流程或第三方组件被攻破，损失巨大

Coinbase 采用多方计算（MPC） 等方案：

• 完整私钥从未以完整形式存在于单一磁盘、RAM或设备上。密钥在生成时就被拆分成数学“碎片”（shares），分布在隔离的硬件/多方环境中。

• 签名时多方协作计算，无需重组完整私钥。即使攻破一名工程师的笔记本或单一节点，也只能拿到无用碎片。

• 资产分布在数千万独立地址上，攻击面极广且价值密度低，难以一次性大规模抽走。

• Coinbase 已开源部分 MPC 密码学库，并强调阈值签名、硬件安全模块（HSM）结合、地理/逻辑隔离等实践。

这大幅降低了单点失效风险。

热钱包/冷钱包比例上，Coinbase 公开表述约98%冷存储，配合保险监管与披露要求

What if you want to bring your LTV down but hold none of the token you borrowed?

On Kamino, you can repay the loan with the collateral that backs it

• A flash loan repays the part of the loan you choose
• Kamino withdraws enough of your collateral to cover it and swaps it into the token you borrowed through @kamino_swap 
• The swap pays back the flash loan in the same transaction, leaving your collateral and your debt lower by the same amount

This means you can bring your LTV down, or close the loan in full, with what the position already holds

🥲Nike @Nike 我记得你以前参与NFT可积极了啊，还有Reddit @Reddit 你可是加密社区的聚集地

OKX 与 ICE 代币化股票计划遇阻，反对发行人增至 50 家，Nike 等公司明确拒绝

OKX @okx 与纽交所母公司（ICE）的合资代币化股票计划，正遭遇越来越多公司的正式反对。截至目前，已向平台发出“发行人反对通知”的公司数量已增至 50 家，其中新加入者包括 Nike、Costco、Micron、Reddit 和 Nvidia，该计划最初拟覆盖 62 家公司的股票。

根据 Eleanor Terrett 公布的文件截图，已明确反对的公司涵盖多个行业头部企业。🌟名单中包括 Microsoft微软、Goldman Sachs高盛、Alphabet谷歌母公司、Qualcomm高通、JPMorgan Chase摩根大通、AMD超威半导体、Oracle甲骨文、Intel英特尔、IBM、Walmart沃尔玛、Eli Lilly礼来、CrowdStrike、Nike耐克、Reddit 和 Nvidia英伟达 等。这些公司通过正式通知表示，不希望自己的股票被第三方拿去做成链上代币进行交易。

OKX 与 ICE 的合作

2026 年 3 月，ICE 以约 250 亿美元估值入股 OKX；同年 6 月，双方正式成立 50-50 合资公司 OKXICE，由 ICE 与前纽约州长 Andrew Cuomo 共同担任联席主席，定位是搭建代币化及数字原生金融产品的基础设施。10 月 4 日，OKXICE 向 SEC 提交通知，计划在 Innovation Exemption 框架下推出 24/7 的代币化美股交易平台（TSV），通过 OKX 的 X Layer 上的 Uniswap v4 池子交易，用稳定币结算。

🌟在 SEC 的相关豁免框架下，发行人有权在规定时间内提出反对，从而阻止第三方将其股票做成代币在平台上交易。随着反对者数量持续增加，OKXICE 最初规划的 62 家标的中，已有相当比例明确退出。平台目前尚未就反对通知的后续处理方式作出公开回应，剩余未表态公司的数量已较为有限。

I think for the avg person they dont really care about decentralization, they care about being able to get paid, move money, trade etc and knowing that it works and their money wont get stolen.

For us we do care about decentralization, but it also requires extreme diligence when using crypto infra and even with that the chances of getting hacked are still there.

So then the q is how do we solve for this without losing what makes crypto unique? We shouldnt have to choose between decentralization and customer protection.

Maybe it takes more time, maybe we need white hats / AI agents incentivized by the network to constantly protect users, almost like an always on red team, maybe some form of recovery or insurance built into the network.

But after a decade of this shit we do need better answers. We spent so much time optimizing for trustless infra but not enough time making it trustworthy for the avg person.

Im positioning the q this way because I we need to figure this out as an industry, otherwise the hacks, scams and customer churn arent going to stop and the future of crypto might look very different than what we originally imagined

text:
Im officially a $RDDT baggie!! 

I wrote a thesis on $RDDT not too long ago, but as we know, a lot has changed in a short time. Here are my updated thoughts:

First, for starters… The thesis for Reddit previously was, Reddit has more logged out users than logged in, how will they convert them? To now, logged out users could be a non-factor, so how do they grow their logged in users? Both theses have the same end goal and I don't completely believe that the new thesis is harder than the old.

Reddit was previously in a predicament where they needed to satisfy Google while also finding a way to encourage those traveling visitors to sign up and log in. Now that this arrangement is sort of damaged, Reddit doesn't need to appease a partner while trying to grow their platform, they can just focus on growing their own platform. I am not trying to spin this to be bullish, I am just laying out what I believe to be realistic.

This chart below sort of illustrates what I am talking about. Last year, Reddit grew logged out users by 8% QoQ in Q3 25 and yet logged in users grew 1.8% QoQ globally and 0.9% in the US. Now compare that to this Q, logged out users declined 1.2% QoQ globally and logged in users grew 1.7% QoQ globally and 1.3% in the US. As you can see, the trajectory of logged in users has not been impacted so far despite Reddit losing nearly 3M logged out users in the US this Q. Although logged out users represent a smaller portion of revenue, I believe the market is more concerned about their ability to grow logged in users and worried that the funnel of logged out users disappearing will impact that, but we don't know that answer yet.

Another item I wanted to mention was, they lost these 3m logged out users in one Q and still reported a double beat. And while their revenue guidance for Q4 came in 3% below expectations, they are projecting that total DAUs could decline by low double digits in that same quarter. So again, the immediate impact on revenue could be relatively limited considering that over 80% of monetization comes from logged in and app users.

Now, I also want to discuss why I believe all of is all happening.

So Google is still using Reddit's content to answer questions through AI Overviews, but users no longer need to visit Reddit to get those answers. Google is still benefiting from Reddit's content but Reddit is no longer getting nearly as much traffic in return.

In response, Reddit announced they are now testing a log in only experience in some international countries with the plan to basically make this the default experience. I believe it's entirely possible that the actions from both sides have to do with their ongoing licensing talks.

A 2022 case involving LinkedIn found that scraping publicly available data likely doesn't violate federal anti-hacking laws, but accessing data behind a login without authorization could. So that is exactly what Reddit is trying to accomplish here.

Reddit is basically taking a big risk here and truly learning how valuable their data is with this new approach. If users really value their answers, they will create the free login and hopefully visit the site more frequently as the UI improves (mgmt stated that new app user retention has improved over 50% YoY) and if their data is truly valuable, Google and other LLM providers could have more incentive to pay up for it now that new answers could become harder to access. I think we should assume for now that no new deals will be signed, since there's been no indication of progress. But the upside is still there, and this new approach could be exactly what brings both sides back to negotiating.

Considering all that has changed, I decided to model a Reddit PT:

The base case has US logged out users declining at 17%/yr and logged in users growing at 2%/yr. For RoW, I assumed 15% declines in logged out users and 11% growth in logged in users. All of which I feel are quite reasonable. If the platform becomes more restrictive to public access, the 17% could fall faster, but essentially I am assuming it will fall by 60% total over 5yrs as I assume they will still have some limited public windows accessible.

I had ARPU growing at 16% annually in the US and 20% in RoW, something I think is quite reasonable considering their advertising platform is young and still has room to grow in both product offerings and pricing/impressions.

I also included NO additional revenue upside from new data licensing agreements, this is purely their existing operating business.

What do you think of Reddit today? Is is it undervalued at these levels?

text:
同样是云业务高速增长，对 $GOOG $AMZN $MSFT $META四家公司的意义完全不同。

判断标准不是"云增长有多快"，而是"云比原来的主业更好还是更差"。

$AMZN 亚马逊：原来的主业是零售，利润率低、竞争激烈、很重资产。云比零售的护城河更深，利润率也高得多。所以 AWS 占比越高，亚马逊整体的生意质量就越好。云对亚马逊来说是升级。
本季 AWS 增长 39%，公司经营利润率 13.9%，创历史新高，就是这个逻辑的体现。

$MSFT 微软：原来的主业是软件，Office、Windows 几乎是纯利润，毛利率极高。AI 云要买 GPU、建数据中心，毛利率不如软件。所以 Azure 占比越高，微软的利润率会被小幅稀释。云对微软来说是轻度降级。
Microsoft Cloud 毛利率已经从 67% 降到 65%。但 Azure 增长 48%，自由现金流仍然为正，四家里扩张最稳的就是它。

$GOOG 谷歌：原来的主业是搜索，接近垄断，利润率高，资本开支不重。云比搜索更竞争、更烧钱。所以云占比越高，谷歌的生意质量会被稀释。云对谷歌来说是降级，虽然绝对利润在增加。
谷歌云增长 103%，是四家里最快的，但 2027 年资本开支预计超过 3000 亿美元，自由现金流已经为负。

$META Meta：没有对外的云业务，算力全部自用，用来提升广告和 AI 产品。好处是回报已经在广告上看得到：收入增长 26%，广告单价增长 14%。风险是建好的算力没有外部客户可以租，回报只能靠广告间接兑现。
本季资本开支 349 亿美元，第一次超过经营现金流。

总结：
亚马逊：云在升级主业
微软：云在轻度稀释主业，但现金流撑得住
谷歌：云在稀释一个比它更好的主业
Meta：不适用这个框架，要看资本开支能不能持续换来广告单价提升

四家共同的风险是同一个：资本开支已经超过或逼近经营现金流。AI 云的需求是真的，但谁的钱花得值，要看未来两三年的现金流，而不是今天的收入增速。

text:
Pearl looks like it will be an easy GTM mining expansion, and hashrate/energy should increase dramatically.

If you believe what Omri and team have written, Pearl's software stack may make normal workloads more efficient than baseline is today even without mining. Call that -X% for the sake of argument. So rolling out the stack (with mining turned off) should be a net cost advantage for ML providers.

Then, Pearl fp8 mining adds some inference overhead call that +Y%. Inference gets a little bit slower because of mining, but the parameters are tunable. If your workload needs low latency, you mine less and do more inference. If your workload is batch jobs that are OK with latency, you mine more and do inference slower. ML providers turn mining on/off when its profitable.

An added benefit of the (planned) Pearl stack is access to distributed compute jobs. For ML jobs that can be trusted to distribute using privacy attestations and TEE, jobs can eventually be paid for with PRL token. It's a natural network effect to pay for distributed compute with a distributed currency.

So the net takeaways:
- Inference providers likely get a net cost savings from integrating the Pearl stack.
- Depending on workload latency requirements and Pearl price, miners join the network when mining revenue > incremental costs.
- Pearl token is used to pay for distributed compute jobs. It's natural to use a decentralized hard money to pay for decentralized work.

Return on capital brings in miners. Distributed compute brings in token usage. More miners and more token usage increase energy and monetary effects, bringing in pure-SOV buyers.

Over time, Pearl token is likely to be seen as a future on inference compute. Since compute will be payable in Pearl, corporations and individuals have a reason to stockpile the token today to pay for compute tomorrow.

Dependencies: fp8 lands well, continued AI usage, electricity and hardware continue to cost money, team executes well.

One of the more durable crypto investment theses IMO because the GTM for all parties is so clear.

My $20-$100 price estimate comes from difficulty adjustment math at https://t.co/YaFFKOYkuk. Expect that to take a few years conservatively. Could be different depending on how things play out.

text:
Anthropic, la empresa que creó Claude, acaba de comprar una biotech que tenía un solo empleado.

Se llama Mithril Medicine y la fundó hace 18 meses Cody Tranbarger, que empezó como analista en Goldman Sachs y estudió biotecnología y MBA en Harvard. Su objetivo es un anticuerpo para la distrofia muscular congénita LAMA2, una enfermedad rara que aparece en bebés y niños. No tenía laboratorio propio. Tenía ocho consultores a tiempo parcial, 11 laboratorios externos y a Claude coordinando contratos, logística y experimentos. En menos de año y medio pasó de una idea a resultados prometedores en ratones, y Anthropic espera que pueda llegar a ensayos en humanos a finales de 2028.

¿Por qué importa tanto? Porque hasta ahora desarrollar un fármaco exigía equipos enormes y muchísimo capital, y una enfermedad con pocos pacientes casi nunca justificaba ese gasto. Por eso hay miles de enfermedades raras huérfanas, sin nadie que investigue para ellas. Si una persona con IA puede llevar adelante un programa entero, eso cambia.

Cuando fundé Viatel y Jazztel, para llegar a cualquier cosa necesitabas mucho dinero y mucha gente. Hoy trabajo cada día con agentes de IA, y en Certuma vemos cómo un equipo pequeño hace lo que antes pedía una empresa entera. Mérito de Cody por animarse a probarlo primero, y con niños enfermos como objetivo.

La próxima gran biotech quizás tenga un solo empleado.

text:
以前我一直觉得，CZ 和何一把币安做到今天这个体量，九年了，也该轻松一点了

现在看来，还是我对建设这两个字理解得太浅

这几天币安发生的事，大家应该都知道了

63 亿美元的安全事故，提现一度暂停

这么大的事情，肯定不是一句 SAFU 就能轻描淡写过去的。安全出了问题，该追究就得追究

但我确实被后面发生的一些细节触动到了

1. 币安选择自己承担损失，拿出资金补足被盗资产

2. 从 80% 到 95%，一边补资金，一边做安全审查、更新储备金证明、逐步恢复提现

CZ 虽然早已不负责币安的日常运营，但这几天依然在 X 上不断转发恢复进度，回应用户，感谢参与追踪和冻结被盗资金的各方

一姐就更有意思了，身为币安联席 CEO，最近在评论区干的活，简直比客服还细

用户问提现，她回复
有人质疑资金去向，她解释
有人传播谣言，她亲自辟谣
有人反映业务没恢复，她还会主动去问进度

这波事件中最让我心疼的，其实还是一姐

前段时间她才公开说过，自己又怀孕了，最近体力确实不如以前，但工作量并没有减少🥺

结果这次币安出了这么大的事，她依旧活跃在事件的最前线

一边要面对几十亿美元的安全事故，一边还要安抚用户情绪、跟进恢复进度、回应社区里各种质疑

以她今天的位置，这些琐碎的事情完全可以交给下面的人去处理

可她偏偏还是那个会亲自出现在评论区、会认真听用户反馈的一姐🫡

很多人心疼她这几天没休息好，她还专门解释，自己其实睡了，是整个团队一起努力，她只是做了分内的事

这种轻描淡写，比任何豪言壮语都更有分量

CZ 说，货币的基础是信任
何一说，这就是我的工作

两句话放在一起，突然就有些理解币安为什么能走到第九年了

当然，我不会说发生这么大的安全事故是一件好事

但一个平台真正的分量，有时候恰恰是在最难的时候才能看出来

顺风顺水时，谁都可以讲长期主义

真遇到事情，能不能承担损失，能不能给用户交代，能不能把承诺一件件兑现，这才是最难的

币安用了九年时间，把一家交易所做成了全球性的加密生态

我原以为这是他们事业的高度

现在才慢慢理解，可能真正支撑这个高度的，是九年过去，创始人身上那股劲还没有散

一个依然关心这个行业的信任
一个怀着孕，还在认真回复用户的问题

CZ 和何一都已经不缺掌声了，可九年过去，还是这么认真

有些人把建设挂在嘴上
有些人，已经把建设过成了日子🫡

也希望一姐在忙着照顾几千万用户的时候，别忘了照顾好自己🫂

币安需要一姐，但一姐也值得被好好照顾，Respect. 💛

text:
我突然想起来，无数的人问过我为什么选择目前的职业，在选择 startup 和大厂中间的考量。我心里其实有两个 universal 的建议：

1. 去任何一家 startup，你是否愿意承受期权直接归零甚至是转为债务的情况。在极端情况下，startup 的期权甚至价值 < 0，你是否敢面对这种极限情况？巨大的纸钱让人顿时产生了魔幻般的富足感。但我认为，选择 offer 的时候，把你的期权视为 0 似乎才能让人更加理性的去看待 startup 的 offer。视为 0 甚至还有很多道理，因为即便是一部分明星 startup，其人员流动性也很高。当你离职后，你的期权大多时候只有公司 IPO 了才能回购。最近硅谷很多公司有了 tender offer，但是这仍旧是少部分幸运儿，且注意到这些 tender offer 的实际受益者仍旧只有极少数早期且坚持下来的玩家。对于这样的人，他们在 startup 早期经历过的心力摧残和坚持，值得得到如此高的回报。但是，大多数人明星 startup 的人，要么是坚持不下来走了，要么是加入的比较晚；因为当一个 startup 有了 tender 的时候，其实公司已经开始大幅扩张了，大多数的人都是新加入的，且不符合 tender 条件。基于此，startup 的期权视为 0 能极大的让人在选择 offer 的时候心态好很多。只要你没有对超额收益的期望乃至贪婪，你的选择可能会更理性。

2. 我论述选择 offer 的时候，把 startup 的期权视为 0 是我个人的极端思想实验 😂 但我见过的太多太多 startup 可能连这都不如。即便我都做出如此极端的思想实验了，我仍旧喜欢且忠心于 RadixArk 的事业乃至使命。一方面，我不认为 RadixArk 的期权是 0，因为我和团队的大家建立的信任和共同责任感，让我相信我们共同价值。认为期权为 0 是我对其他朋友选择 startup，或者说让我回到过去的时间点选择 offer 时的自我告诫。另一方面，我认为选择 offer 时候，更关键的考量在于一个值得长期追随的 leadership。我可以举出很多例子，在硅谷，厉害的人有很多，冠冕堂皇之辈也很多，但是值得追随的 leadership 是非常有限的。我们能够见到某些大佬，他的核心班底会随着他去任何地方，大厂 -> 创业 -> 大厂 -> 创业，任何地方，这些大佬和他们的核心班底做出的决策都完全一致。在我看来，这就是值得追随的 leadership。职业发展说到底也是需要贵人相助托举的，如果能够遇到自己的贵人，“誓死效忠”这个词便不再是玩笑话了。

一些个人的浅见，感谢您的阅读。

Naval Ravikant once shared a story about Bill Gates shorting Tesla, a bet that could ultimately cost him more than $10 billion.

Gates had taken a massive short position against Tesla, reportedly equivalent to roughly 1% of the company’s total shares.

Naval suggested that if Tesla became the world’s most valuable company by a wide margin, the losses could be so enormous that even someone as wealthy as Bill Gates could face financial ruin.

But what fascinated Naval wasn't the money. It was Elon Musk’s reaction.

Musk was genuinely confused. How could someone who publicly championed clean energy financially bet against a company working to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy?

To Gates, it was reportedly just a financial decision. But to Musk, it was something much deeper.

According to Naval, that moment revealed something fundamental about Elon Musk.

Elon Musk is not driven by money, wealth, or status. He is driven by a mission.

The billions he earns are not trophies. They are tools.

Tools to build rockets, revolutionize transportation, advance technology, and ultimately make humanity a multiplanetary civilization.

While hot wallets provide decent limits on hack damage, I think exchanges would be better served by also implementing smart-contract-level rate limits to protect against operator key compromise.

The danger lies in allowing massive fund movements as part of regular operations. If there is a genuine large withdrawal, exchanges can put overrides and special checks in place.

DeFi is a good example of where rate limits help to reduce the attack surface.

text:
My vlog today was fully edited by Claude Code with Opus 5.5!

I copied the video clips from my DJI to a folder, then opened Claude Code in it and asked it to edit it into a 10 minute vlog

I made a few adjustments but not a lot

It transcribed everything I said with mlx-whisper (Whisper large-v3-turbo running on my MacBook Pro's GPU through Apple's MLX)

It pulled video frames every few seconds into grid images (contact sheets), so Claude could see what's in each clip

It used SpeechBrain ECAPA (a voice-matching model) to figure out what was my voice from other people

It then made thumbnails with OpenCV with YuNet's face detector

The edit itself is a list of cuts in a JSON file: which clip, start time, end time, Claude then picked the pieces by reading the transcripts and looking at the frame grids by itself

I added on screen captions for X and on YouTube for the first minute with Pillow (Python's image library)

P.S. I didn't ask for any of this, and I didn't know any of this until @thesamparr just asked me how I edited it

All I asked for was "Claude can you edit these clips into a 10 minute vlog for X and YouTube"

I think if I didn't have AI to edit it, I wouldn't be vlogging because editing would be such a painful and slow process for me and hiring someone to do it would be even more hassle for me!

Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

text:
Having spent a long time watching Elon Musk, and having talked with him, I believe I understand what he understood before almost anyone else. And it's something every one of us needs to understand now.

Western civilization is not one civilization among many. It is the one that gave the world freedom of thought, modern science and the dignity of the individual. And it is under attack. Not by peoples, but by ideologies that want it dead.

If it dies, the world will not become more just. It will become poorer, more brutal and darker. For everyone, including those who hate it.

Why? Because civilizations are not interchangeable. We were told that any culture could be blended with any other, like mixing colors, and that the result would always be harmonious. It isn't true. A society where women are equal to men cannot coexist without friction with a worldview in which a woman's testimony is worth half a man's. A society where you can criticize God, change your religion or have none cannot absorb, without fracturing, a worldview in which apostasy is paid for with your life.

Every people has its own genius and moves at its own pace. But not all values are equal, and you cannot build a nation on laws that contradict each other. Saying so is not racist. Racism is about blood. I am talking about laws, customs and values. And those values belong to no race: a Japanese, a Senegalese or an Iranian can make them his own, and millions have. That is exactly why they are worth defending.

Let's remember where they come from.

It all begins in Greece. In Athens, for the first time, men decide that truth does not descend from a throne but is sought through reason, and that a city governs itself through debate. Socrates chooses death rather than give up thinking freely. At Salamis, a handful of free cities stops the greatest empire in the world.

Then comes Rome. Rome invents law that binds everyone, the citizen who holds rights, the Republic. And one immense idea: you can become Roman without being born Roman. You become Roman by adopting its laws.

Christianity adds the most revolutionary idea in history: every human being, slave and emperor alike, has infinite worth.

Then France. The cathedrals, those ships of stone our ancestors built over centuries for descendants they would never see. Descartes, Pascal, Voltaire. The Declaration of the Rights of Man. And Napoleon, who gives France the Civil Code, the lycées, and one simple principle: careers open to talent. Murat, the son of an innkeeper, ends up a Marshal of the Empire and King of Naples. The Civil Code spreads across much of Europe and still shapes the law of dozens of countries today.

And this civilization goes on to abolish slavery, which had been practiced on every continent since the dawn of time, to push back the plague, smallpox and the night itself, and to set foot on the Moon.

Peoples of the West, be proud of this history. Proud does not mean blind. Every civilization has committed crimes: conquest, slavery, war. Ours is the one that went furthest in examining its own faults, to the point of abolishing what it had once practiced. This capacity to question itself is its greatest strength. And that is exactly the strength now being turned against it.

Because for decades, this magnificent system has been getting hacked. Not by an army. By an alliance of two forces that have nothing in common except one enemy: us.

The first is communism. It lost the economic war, lost the Cold War, lost history's verdict with its tens of millions of dead. But it never lost the universities. It survived by changing costumes: class struggle became the struggle of the oppressed against their oppressors, and the West was declared guilty of everything. It taught our children to be ashamed of their ancestors, their borders and their culture. It is the root cause, because before you can bring down a civilization, you have to take away its will to defend itself.

The second is political Islam. I am not talking about Muslims, many of whom came here precisely to escape this ideology and are its first victims. I am talking about a political project that wants to place religious law above civil law. It has no doubts. It feels no shame. It rushes into the void the first one dug.

One disarms. The other advances.

And let no one on the left believe they will stay in control. History has already staged this play. In 1978, Michel Foucault was enthusing over the Iranian revolution. Iran's communist party, the Tudeh, backed Khomeini and called on Iranians to vote for his Islamic constitution. By 1983, its leaders had been arrested, the party banned, and its chiefs paraded on television to confess their “crimes.” In 1988, thousands of political prisoners were executed, communist activists among them. The second always ends up devouring the first. Useful idiots are only useful for a while.

So here is my call to every Western people. To the French, the Italians, the Poles, the Germans, the Spanish, the Americans, to all of you.

We are at a turning point. What we do in the next ten years will decide what our grandchildren are allowed to say, believe, write and love.

I am not asking you to die for the West. I am asking you for something harder: to live for it.

Learn its history and pass it on. Have children. Speak without fear, even when they call you every name in the book. Vote, get involved, run for office. Build companies, schools, factories, families. Refuse the shame they are trying to inject into you. And stop surrendering anything that makes us who we are: freedom of thought, equality before the law, the dignity of every person.

The historian Arnold Toynbee understood it: civilizations are not murdered, they commit suicide. And those who think they can let the West fall without paying the price should remember the Iranian communists. They helped tear down what they despised, and then they were next.

The Greeks at Salamis were outnumbered. They won because they knew what they were defending. We are the heirs of Athens, Rome, Notre-Dame and the Civil Code. It is no accident that the rockets that will carry humanity to Mars are being built in a free civilization.

It is time to prove ourselves worthy of what we were given.

The West is worth defending. And no one will defend it for us.

text:
Pearl looks like it will be an easy GTM mining expansion, and hashrate/energy should increase dramatically.

If you believe what Omri and team have written, Pearl's software stack may make normal workloads more efficient than baseline is today even without mining. Call that -X% for the sake of argument. So rolling out the stack (with mining turned off) should be a net cost advantage for ML providers.

Then, Pearl fp8 mining adds some inference overhead call that +Y%. Inference gets a little bit slower because of mining, but the parameters are tunable. If your workload needs low latency, you mine less and do more inference. If your workload is batch jobs that are OK with latency, you mine more and do inference slower. ML providers turn mining on/off when its profitable.

An added benefit of the (planned) Pearl stack is access to distributed compute jobs. For ML jobs that can be trusted to distribute using privacy attestations and TEE, jobs can eventually be paid for with PRL token. It's a natural network effect to pay for distributed compute with a distributed currency.

So the net takeaways:
- Inference providers likely get a net cost savings from integrating the Pearl stack.
- Depending on workload latency requirements and Pearl price, miners join the network when mining revenue > incremental costs.
- Pearl token is used to pay for distributed compute jobs. It's natural to use a decentralized hard money to pay for decentralized work.

Return on capital brings in miners. Distributed compute brings in token usage. More miners and more token usage increase energy and monetary effects, bringing in pure-SOV buyers.

Over time, Pearl token is likely to be seen as a future on inference compute. Since compute will be payable in Pearl, corporations and individuals have a reason to stockpile the token today to pay for compute tomorrow.

Dependencies: fp8 lands well, continued AI usage, electricity and hardware continue to cost money, team executes well.

One of the more durable crypto investment theses IMO because the GTM for all parties is so clear.

My $20-$100 price estimate comes from difficulty adjustment math at https://t.co/YaFFKOYkuk. Expect that to take a few years conservatively. Could be different depending on how things play out.

text:
While Binance is messing about with Ethereum, @Google is building on @solana which does not have a fragile architecture.

On October 28 Alphabet announced it is securing its own digital assets on @solana $SOL using a new system called Google Multi-Party Compute. It’s a custody and transaction-signing tool that splits private keys across separate environments so no single machine ever holds the full key enough shares have to agree before anything moves. 

It’s in private preview with major banks now, with commercial launch targeted for early twenty twenty-seven, and at launch it’ll support Ed25519, which is Solana’s signature scheme. 

Google Cloud’s been on Solana since twenty twenty-two running a validator, and they pipe Solana data into BigQuery for analytics. Google didn’t say which assets Alphabet holds or how much. 

The interesting part is the framing - CoinDesk’s coverage ties it to growing AI threats, meaning Google sees AI-driven attacks on crypto infrastructure as a real enough risk to build distributed key management for.

Now if you remember I interviewed @ikadotxyz who moved to Solana in early 2026 with their radical MPC architecture - hmm. 🤔

从姆巴佩视角来看我为什么说姆巴佩的道歉是被逼供的

梳理一下时间线（西班牙时间，和英国差一个小时可以忽略）
姆巴佩先是第一天（10.25）晚上十一点多踢完国家德比，地点在巴塞罗那，第二天（10.26）飞到伦敦金球奖现场，依旧是十一点多结束的，晚上回不了马德里。第三天（10.27）上午需要飞回马德里，伦敦飞马德里城市赶路时间（不清楚）+登机+飞行时间（大概2h40m）+滑行(20m)+时差（1h）会超过5个小时，处理拖到中午是正常的，不是姆巴佩故意拖时间。这期间视频被发出来，是没办法处理节奏的，但舆情不会等人不断发酵，懂狗帝带节奏+企业解约。

问题在第三天上午，西甲在西班牙时间11:47第一个道歉，这道歉是有问题的，一般应该等涉事本人先作回应，弄清楚到底是什么情况，所属团体再作回应，不直接参与事件的人随便发言是会把情况搞乱。西甲没有等姆巴佩说明是什么情况就自己帮姆巴佩认了罪相当于限制了姆巴佩的解释，作为外人的中国市场直接解约，中国媒体直接给他定罪，现在被中国视为姆巴佩自己人的西甲也替他认罪，他不认罪等于否定西甲和中国舆论，同时和中国市场和联赛对着干，这种压力任何人都无法承受。道歉之后再解释的话，别人说你上层的西甲都认罪了，你自己也认罪了，这会儿又反悔是什么意思，会让舆情再次爆发，所以姆巴佩全程是没有任何解释机会的，重压之下沉默是和解释是不可能是，只能道歉，这相当于被逼供了。

姆巴佩与西甲道歉只差一个小时（12:39），这已经是最快速度了，算上赶路时间，相当于一下飞机就忙着和公关团队一起处理，但遗憾的是西甲半路杀出，掐灭了解释的机会。

倒完歉就全完了，相当于自己认罪了，你再解释别人就说正主都认了，你还狡辩什么。

道歉是正常操作，这里存在的问题是，西甲真的需要这么“快”道歉吗？
当时厄齐尔事件英超是没有任何回复的，当时中国也没有禁播英超阿森纳之外的比赛，这意味着联赛本身道不道歉可以说是无所谓的，西甲偌大的一个联赛五百多名球员20多支球队不可能全和一个人一个俱乐部绑定。西甲不仅没有沉默，反而第一个道歉，这是不合常理的，他道歉不能为姆巴佩脱罪，不道歉也影响不了其他球队，可以说是看着诚恳实则意义不明的做法。道歉可以理解为态度诚恳，但明知姆巴佩暂时没时间回应的情况下第一个道歉问题是有很大问题的。

个人推断可能是西甲主席特巴斯临时起意想落井下石搞皇马一波（特巴斯和皇马此前已经有不少恩怨，想了解自己搜），可以借此指责皇马因自身原因损害联赛利益，给皇马施压，压缩话语权。（以上推断没办法实锤，切勿当成既定事实）

既然他已经认罪，我为什么还要给他辩护？

一边是以太坊开始认真讨论量子计算带来的安全威胁，另一边是 @Starknet 已经开始用具体数字，计算未来升级的成本

1. 以太坊：量子威胁已经不能忽视

Vitalik 转发了 @ethereum 关于量子计算威胁的讨论，简单来说，未来量子计算机如果足够强大，可能破解今天区块链使用的部分密码技术，进而威胁钱包和链上资产的安全

与此同时，AI 的发展也让这个问题变得更加紧迫，以太坊相关专家已经在剑桥协调抗量子升级计划，开始讨论未来应该采用什么技术、如何升级，以及怎样让整个生态做好准备

这说明一件事：抗量子不再只是一个遥远的技术话题，而是区块链必须提前考虑的长期安全问题

2. Starknet：不仅讨论安全，还开始算成本

相比之下，@Starknet 给出了更加具体的数据，他们公布了一组抗量子交易的测试成本：
🔹Falcon-512：约 0.023 / 笔
🔹ML-DSA-44：约 0.040 / 笔
🔹Falcon-1024：约 0.046 / 笔
🔹ML-DSA-87：约 0.078 / 笔
🔹SLH-DSA-128s：约 0.35 / 笔

按照他们公布的数据，部分方案相比基准方案便宜约 2 到 9 倍，这意味着什么？

过去大家讨论抗量子，更多是在讨论技术能不能实现。而现在，Starknet 已经开始尝试回答另一个问题：如果未来真的要升级，每笔交易需要付出多少成本？

更值得注意的是，这项工作还开放了公开挑战，目前已有 434 条记录，当然，这些数字也不能过度解读，Starknet 后续特别注明，相关结果尚未经审计，也不代表 OpenZeppelin 的正式背书

所以，它目前更像是一组可以公开验证、讨论和挑战的测试数据，而不是主网已经完成抗量子升级的证明

3. 真正值得关注的，是从研究走向落地

把以太坊和 Starknet 放在一起，我们能看到区块链行业面对量子威胁的两个阶段：以太坊正在协调长期升级方向，解决未来应该怎么做的问题，Starknet 则开始公布具体测试成本，尝试解决实际执行需要花多少钱的问题

一个关注升级路线，一个关注落地成本

两者并不冲突，反而说明整个行业正在逐渐把抗量子安全从理论讨论推进到工程实践

4. 对普通投资者意味着什么？

我认为，现在还没必要因为量子计算就急着改变自己的长期持仓策略

但有一个趋势值得持续关注：
未来区块链的竞争，不仅是交易速度、手续费和生态规模，还包括面对新技术威胁时，能不能及时升级自己的安全体系

真正有价值的项目，不应该只会讲未来有多安全，还应该能够公开技术路线、升级成本和验证结果，量子计算可能还没有真正威胁到今天的区块链，但为未来做好准备，已经成为一场新的基础设施竞争

Electricity demand is dynamic. Large factories often use long-term PPAs or supply contracts to lock in predictable pricing, then rely on the grid and spot markets to handle fluctuations in demand.

Sometimes they need more power than they’ve contracted for. Other times they have excess contracted supply they can sell back into the market.

Compute is no different. Even if you own GPUs or sign 3-year contracts, your demand fluctuates. You need a grid where you can buy additional compute or sell unused capacity.

Emerging categories to position for (beyond MTS):
Growth staff (me): marketing / sales / partnerships / community / devrel
Operations staff: finance / people / legal ops  / internal tools
Customer staff: support, customer success, account management, solutions engineering, implementation 

In interviews and on resumes
1. Lead with your "spike", have ultra-crisp stories where it was the reason behind a great success
2. Have ultra-crisp stories exemplifying agency and good judgement that have driven some outcome end to end and the impact
3. Say “I,” not “we,” and be ready to describe exact details

There are big changes and things are being shaken up, with all disruption though there are always tons of opportunities, the people who move quickly and get in front of them the fastest will have the most upside. There are SO many new companies with crazy growth, pre-unicorns and new unicorns hiring like crazy, you want to be part of a company that will 10x or 100x over the next 10 years, not one that is about to have to reshape everything because they themselves are being disrupted.

text:
Who's actually building the layer that can say no when the signer says yes?

> @BitGo: a separate co-signer enforces velocity limits, but user + backup keys can skip it in self-custody
> @Anchorage: the HSM needs a client quorum and Anchorage's approval, no velocity cap documented
> @FireblocksHQ: rules in SGX enclaves, fixed limits, same vendor as the signing
> @turnkeyhq: policies on every request, but the root quorum bypasses them
> @HypernativeLabs: onchain guard on Safe, owners can remove it after a 24h delay
> @blockaid_: a cosigner that can refuse, if the wallet requires its signature

Every cap I found is fixed and set by hand. I haven't found an automatic one, enforced outside the signer, that stopped Bybit, Drift or Binance.
author: gaspardlezin
quoted_text:
In 2014 I went nearly a week without sleep. I was running PayPal and attackers were inside our corporate network. They'd compromised an eBay employee's laptop, got onto the VPN, taken over a domain controller and made themselves domain admins. eBay and PayPal were one company then, on one Windows network. They stole 145M eBay user records, then came for the segregated vault holding PayPal's card credentials. We fought them off. They never got in, but they got close. Too close.

Yesterday Binance lost ~$6.3B in what looks like the same way. A DevOps engineer's laptop, then a service inside the withdrawal stack, then withdrawals the signer approved because they came from a trusted source. Hot wallets emptied in under four hours. No key was stolen.

Nobody broke cryptography or a ledger. They found someone with access and used the trust that came with it. Banks get hit exactly the same way.

2016: attackers inside Bangladesh Bank used its own SWIFT access to send $951M of payment orders to the NY Fed. $81M was lost. The rest was held because an unrelated sanctions filter tripped on the word "Jupiter". That was luck, and it only worked because wires took days to settle.

June 2025: an IT employee at C&M Software, which connects Brazilian banks to Pix, sold his credentials for about $2,700. Attackers used them to send fake Pix transfers out of six institutions' reserve accounts at the central bank. ~$140M in under three hours.

August 2025: stolen vendor credentials at Sinqia, another Pix connector. ~R$710M out of HSBC and one other institution in a single afternoon. The central bank froze most of it, after it had already moved.

Same attack every time. Speed is what changed. When settlement took days, a filter, a correspondent bank or someone in ops could catch a bad payment. Pix, FedNow, SEPA Instant and blockchains settle in seconds. Payment security was mostly built for the slow world.

PayPal's card and user data survived 2014 because domain admin on the corp network couldn't unlock it quickly enough, and our alerting caught the unusual activity on the network. That's the model. Approval policy no laptop or vendor login can reach. Velocity and anomaly limits enforced outside the system that sends. Dynamic caps on what any one wallet, account or service can move per hour. All of it in real time.

About $3B of what left Binance has been frozen, almost all of it stablecoins. The $1.4B in bitcoin is sitting in 19 wallets and nobody can touch it. I don't think that's the problem. For decades the ability to reverse a wire or a card charge let a lot of weak security slide. You either stop the transfer before it's signed or you eat the loss.

Nothing about the technology failed here. The chains processed exactly the transactions they were handed. Binance's own systems handed them the wrong ones because an engineer's laptop was compromised. That's operational security. eBay in 2014, Bangladesh Bank and two Pix connectors all failed at it on their own rails.

In 2014 the attackers never reached the vault. If they had, the fraud losses would have been the small part. PayPal existed so people could pay without handing their card details to every merchant on the internet. We held those details so they didn't have to. Losing them would have broken the one thing the company was built on, and I'm not sure we would have recovered.

I expect blockchains and digital assets to become the standard way money moves. Every custodian of digital assets, or of fiat on a real-time rail, is in that position now. The controls have to adapt to settlement in seconds, crypto or not.

text:
The AI ROI debate is getting harder to dismiss.

Since late 2022, information, finance and professional/technical services produced **19.8% more real output with 1% fewer payroll jobs**.

Output per job is growing at a 5.1% annual trend, up from 2.3% before 2023. The rest of the private nonfarm economy? 1.4%.

Meanwhile, Anthropic reports over 6,000 customers spending at least $100K annually, versus over 600 a year earlier. Microsoft says automated tasks nearly doubled since July.

This is the shift we’ve been writing about: **from answers to work.** Agents doing useful work on enterprise data, inside governed workflows.

Does this prove AI caused the acceleration? No. But “where’s the ROI?” deserves a better answer than another chatbot joke.

Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

text:
Text messages with a machine, in and of themselves, are not criminal, immoral, or dangerous, for there is no victim, whatever the content. It is the very same thing as with thoughts—regardless of the content, no thought can be said to create a victim.

• If someone steals info and feeds it into an LLM, it was the theft itself which created the victim, not the subsequent text message.

• If someone uses the output of an LLM to hack a system, it is that subsequent hack which creates the victim, not the text message preceding it.

• If someone threatens harm to themselves or others through messages into a machine, here still the messages themselves cannot be said to have created any victim. 

Imagining otherwise inappropriately reorients blame from its rightful place: the action of harm actually done by a perpetrator.  Thinking harm =/= harm.

As humans integrate AI as an extension of their mind, policing at the message layer means to increasingly police thought itself. 

Which company, which committee, do you trust to police your thoughts? Or do you simply want the thoughts of others policed, and not your own?

We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

text:
Kalshi is having its moment today, and the timeline looks just like the day Polymarket announced its ICE investment.

Victory laps are being made everywhere.

Look closely at who is posting, though, and you’ll notice something wild about how the two companies were built:

When Polymarket had its big day on the timeline, you saw two types of posts:

• Users who had chatted with Shayne along his journey on X and shared product feedback 
• Investors celebrating the markup on their angel tickets and funds

What did you barely see at all? 

Employees celebrating

Almost no one at Polymarket has been there for more than 1.5 years. They are roughly on their 4th leadership team right now.

Now look at Kalshi’s timeline today. You see a wave of senior employees telling their own stories. Even more than the VCs!

There is a massive lesson in startup philosophy here:

1) Polymarket focused heavily on users and investors, never on employees. That gave them a massive head start, but here is the cost: when people associate the company with leadership that constantly stresses them out, pressures them, or calls them retards -- they have zero intrinsic motivation or love for the company. 

And if your team doesn't love the company, they aren't going to love or take care of your product and your customers. This is human psychology 101. 

2) Kalshi clearly invested heavily in staff and culture from day one. You can see the payoff now: employees are taking care of customers, not just Luana and Tarek.

Anyways, a new special episode drops today. 

Food for thought: Does early user velocity beat team retention, or does culture always win long term?

- EP8 Special Seven Yeses
author: AgentBotega
quoted_text:
Kalshi just raised an additional $1B, valuing the company at $40B. This will help us expand into stocks, compute, indices, and institutional.

Tomorrow marks 8 years since we got accepted into YC and the journey began.

The odds of a kid from Lebanon getting here were pretty low.

Growing up there was great, but very challenging. We went through war. We had bombs explode in front of my house. I watched brilliant people’s lives destroyed for reasons beyond their control.

Lebanon is an unpredictable country. That unpredictability made it hard to plan for success. And yet despite it all, my mom sacrificed everything to give me and my brother the chance to go back to the US.

I found my refuge in two things: anime and math. Especially math.

I loved math because it calmed me. It was the opposite of unpredictable: clear, deterministic, orderly, and consistent. The proof is either right or wrong. I find that elegant and beautiful.

I was lucky.

I made it to my dream school, MIT (largely thanks to my mom), and my love for math quickly translated to a love for statistics, probability, and markets.

I love markets for a lot of the same reasons. Their incentives are clear: you get rewarded for being right and for pursuing knowledge. They are effective weighting machines for people’s opinions. They provide an incentive to be truthful, because they separate good information from bad information. They let people challenge the consensus and be rewarded for being right.

IMO, Hayek, Surowiecki, Hanson, Tetlock were the founding fathers of prediction markets. The more I read them, the more obsessed I got with the idea of applying market-based pricing to more things.

Markets bring rigor and critical thinking to more questions. And in an increasingly polarized and information-positioned word, I believe we need that more than ever.

Markets would also let people predict and manage more things outside of their control. And the world was becoming increasingly more unpredictable, and more like Lebanon, not less.

That love for markets got Luana and me to build Kalshi.

At first, it was mostly an idea we couldn’t stop talking about. We didn’t have much money. Luana’s sister bought the Kalshi domain name for us (for ~$1.7k). We moved to SF to get started, and embarked on a long, uncertain journey to build a regulated exchange.

The paranoia and anxiety from my childhood never left me. Even when things are going well, I think about what could go wrong. When people trust you with their money, that instinct serves a purpose.

I wanted us to build something that would hold up under pressure.

The first principle we defined at the company: regulatory-first. We worked with regulators for years before we listed a single market. We took every step to do things the right way and always asked for approval before proceeding. It was very hard at times, especially when we were being overtaken by competitors, but we believe doing things the right way matters.

Luana and I aren’t the only ones.

Our team put years of their lives into something far from certain. That’s especially true of Lior, Brandon, Rainer, Luis, Xavier, and Josef, who stuck with us for years. They believed when there was little to point to. And they stuck with us no matter how long it took. Kalshi is the result of an arduous journey through a long desert where, at times, most people didn’t understand why we were making the walk.

Many people still don’t understand what we’re doing and some disagree with us. Markets have historically taken time to be understood and accepted by some. But while not always obvious, their benefits are vast: capital markets help allocate capital and derivative markets help predict and manage uncertainty.

I firmly believe in these benefits, and that’s why I am dedicating my life to building this market.

Markets have caused issues many times in the past, and they certainly can present harms (manipulation, insiders, and addictive behaviors). These harms are more acute for certain types of markets (sports, short-term options, etc.) than others. It’s why I believe that guardrails need to exist and why we have taken the approach we have taken. We have consistently prioritized thinking critically about the risks and building the appropriate safeguards, sometimes beyond what the regulators require us to do. Many believe more needs to be done, and that’s a conversation I welcome.

Over time, I believe more people will see what we see: markets can help us get smarter and manage the future with more rigor, more precision, and more certainty than we have today.

To our tens of millions of users: you have made Kalshi bigger than anything Luana and I could have possibly imagined. Thank you for trusting us and thank you for coming along on the journey. I feel a strong responsibility to build a company worthy of that trust.

I am so lucky to spend my life building something I love. I hope everyone finds something they care about that much. Something that keeps you curious. Something that pushes you to your limits. Something that may put you at odds with the status quo. Something worth the hard days.

For me, it’s still markets. The more I learn, the more I want to understand.

text:
Let’s talk about the $ZEC FUD. 🛡️

Zcash is everywhere on CT, but most people are confusing real challenges with a dying project.

Let’s look at the facts.

1. Governance & treasury: Yes, ZCG’s funding model deserves scrutiny. Sean Bowe challenged its automatic 8% allocation. ZCG then proposed redirecting ~98,000 ZEC toward future network security and reducing future grants. Not perfect, but this is a public debate about sustainability, not a protocol collapse.

2. ZECsy controversy: The $550K marketing proposal, including an adult-industry event, deserves scrutiny. Initial milestones of ~$461K were approved. Question the spending and demand measurable results. But controversial marketing isn’t a broken blockchain.

3. Orchard vulnerability: Serious? Absolutely. Fatal? No. Emergency remediation, NU6.3/Ironwood, a new corrected shielded pool and withdrawal controls for the old pool followed. No breach of the 21M supply cap has been demonstrated. Historical exploitation cannot be ruled out with certainty, but that isn’t proof of inflation.

4. Whale shorts: Around $228M in tracked Hyperliquid shorts versus $164M longs on Nov. 1. Real derivatives pressure, yes. Proof of spot selling or fundamental failure? No. Shorts can hedge other exposure.

5. Technology: NU7 targets Nov. 5: 25-second blocks instead of 75, higher planned shielded throughput and a Network Sustainability Mechanism. Gemini already uses the independent Zakura node. Coinholders voted 2.37M ZEC to preserve halvings versus 22K against.

6. Institutions: Grayscale’s ZCSH recorded ~$263M in net inflows through Q3. Cypherpunk held 326,417 ZEC at quarter-end. Euronext’s CoinShares ETP suspension was a settlement issue, not a Zcash ban.

Now the bigger picture.

Stablecoins, tokenisation and DeFi are moving finance on-chain. But completely transparent finance creates a massive problem: nobody wants every payment, position and financial relationship publicly exposed.

Financial privacy could become one of crypto’s next major narratives.

Zcash already has the technology: zero-knowledge proofs, shielded transactions, a 21M supply cap, halvings, growing shielded usage, institutional access and active development.

Bitcoin brought digital scarcity. Ethereum brought programmable finance. Zcash could help bring financial privacy to the next generation of on-chain markets.

Governance risks remain. Regulation, adoption and execution matter. Nothing guarantees price appreciation.

But dismissing ZEC because of controversies while ignoring its technology and growing financial relevance is missing the bigger picture.

I’m bullish because privacy may become a necessity, not a luxury, as finance moves on-chain.

text:
The replies to this post are a good reminder that most people, even VC-adjacent, do not understand the use of financial models. 

They assume that because a model seems complex, the goal must be precision — as if granular (and often trivial) detail helps with forecasting the future. 

This invites criticism along the lines of "this is a pointless exercise", or "this is missing detail" — both of which completely miss the point.

In reality, the objective is accuracy (the output is close to the outcome) rather than precision (accounting for every possible line item). 

For that purpose, the key inputs are the influential assumptions about the future. These are blunt instruments, where being directionally correct is enough / being exactly correct is impossible. 

In @shaunmmaguire's case, those assumptions relate to:
- How many GWs of compute SpaceX has online in 2027–2028
- How revenue per GW (rev/GW) and CapEx per GW evolve
- How Starship launches ramp
- When the first orbital-compute satellites fly.

If you don't read a model through the lens of the assumptions being illustrated, and why, it is not going to be a productive exercise. 

AKA, always read the methodology.

quoted_text:
I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI.

Some takes I loved:

1. “It shouldn’t take someone longer to read your doc than it took you to write it.”

Writing is thinking. AI can be a thought partner, but you should firmly be in the driver’s seat.

2. “It’s no longer about can you build it, it’s about should it even exist?”

Code went from a scarce asset to basically free. If you can “throw a couple of agents at it over a weekend,” it’s probably not a durable product. So the hard part now is deciding what’s worth building in the first place.

3. “Why do you even want a person in your product?”

Agents do more of our work every month, so you should ask if your product needs a UI at all. Jaclyn thinks people will still show up to create, learn, or be entertained. Any task that feels like a chore should be built for agents first.

4. “Don’t just give users exactly what they want.”

Talk to them all the time, but find the root problem and solve it in a way they wouldn’t have thought of. You want them to walk away thinking, “I didn’t think this was possible, but it’s exactly what I wanted.”

5. “You shouldn’t expect users to know how to write elaborate prompts.”

Small business owners don’t have time to start from an empty prompt box. So her team built Pomelli, Google’s tool for SMBs to create on-brand content, to read your website and learn your business first.

6. “Let your kid be your creative director.”

Jaclyn’s 5-year-old loves scary stories, so they made their own podcast, Maya and the Fog. Her daughter picks the voices, names the characters, and gives notes on each cut, and Jaclyn has the agent produce the episode. It’s live on Spotify.

Years of decentralization theatrics, not your keys, not your crypto, hardware wallets, governance, etc mean very little when customers / businesses keep losing money to hackers / scammers.

Being able to freeze hacked or stolen funds, recover assets, reverse txns and protect customers should be a feature, not something that goes against cryptos ethos. Obv a fine line between government overreach vs pure decentralization 

At the end of the day, every time someone loses money, we risk losing that user forever. And the more users we churn, the lower the chances of crypto actually succeeding.

Decentralization still matters, but we likely spent too much time optimizing for it, e.g like thorchain or Tornado Cash, where bad actors can take far more advantage of permissionless infra vs the avg user 

While we spent far less time optimizing for customer centric features like trust, safety, fraud prevention, and recovery, which are arguably far more important for mass adoption.

text:
Yann LeCun was right & nobody in this industry wants to say it out loud.

109 million parameters beat 72 billion.

He has spent years saying scale is not the thing that makes a model understand the world. Meta bet the other way. He left in November and started his own lab in Paris.

Last Thursday he published the proof.

The theory everyone has been running on since 2024 is that if you train models big enough, on text, on images, on sound, they all end up with the same picture of reality inside them. Size does it. Nobody ever proved that part.

Randall Balestriero and LeCun proved it. And the proof says size was never doing the work.

What does the work is which two things you show a model together.

A photo and the caption of that photo are two views of one thing. Models trained on pairs like that get there fast.

Two paragraphs pulled from the same document are not two views of one thing. Models trained on those get there slowly and expensively.

Next word prediction is the second kind. That is what every chatbot in the world runs on.

In their tests the first method reached the same understanding after 21.6 million examples. Next word prediction needed 900 million.

And a 109 million parameter text model ended up closer to an image model's view of the world than a 72 billion parameter language model was.

660 times smaller.

text:
All of us understand that useful software is getting easier to create. But generating code, completing end-to-end engineering work, and creating business value are moving at very different rates. 

Digging into this from different angles. Epoch, for example, estimates that a fixed level of AI performance is getting cheaper 13x per year for the past 4 years. That's across math, science, and game projects. 

Anthropic's 100k C compiler experiment is well known: 20k API spend, roughly $200 per kLOC of code, but the compiler had major limitations, lots of bugs, and wasn't really comparable to a fully functional C compiler. 

An early 2026 Microsoft study estimates 25% more merged pull requests. Anthropic has shared bigger stats with us. What's not clear, though, is whether this translated into business value. It's an observational study, and in general, I am skeptical of observational data about increased activity.

A more recent September 2026 paper has impressive stats: 240%+ more commits, 80% more projects, 30% more releases, but it's output gains, not cost reductions. 

It's clear that cheaper software creation is going to make previously uneconomical software worth building: bespoke tools, small markets. I built a bunch of app & skills I would never have bothered to write actual code for before, for example. why? because it's cheap and easy.

Estimating value for these can be tricky. If, for example, somebody never created a piece of software that could create 10k of value because software costs 50k to create, and all of a sudden that 50k became 1k, the total economic value that's created is 9k, not 49k. This kind of "more is more" can be tricky to measure in terms of actual gain, either for a company or for society. 

The one other thing that people don't seem to keep in mind is that AI created software (all software?) comes with a poison pill: catastrophic bugs. 

If our ability to create new software grows out of proportion with our ability to detect them or, worse, fix them, we end up in a crisis-driven world. 

The world of crypto offers a warning here: there's a mind-numbing repetition of bugs with massive impact. Think about that. Would you tolerate that from your bank? 

Thinking about this as well as value capture from other world-changing inventions. Comment with ideas and thoughts.

quoted_text:
How much does the world actually spend on science?

1. US government research funding: ~$99 billion In FY2024, federal agencies obligated about $47.5B for basic research and $51B for applied research. That's the pool most scientists mean when they say "grants": NIH, NSF, DOE, NASA and others.

2. Add philanthropy: ~$126 billion Foundations and donors add about $27B on top of federal grants, supporting research at US universities and nonprofit institutes in 2024. That's roughly a fifth of all support for that work.

3. All US R&D: ~$1 trillion Total US R&D hit $937B in 2023 and an estimated $993B in 2024. Most of it is industry funding product development. Government research and philanthropy together make up only about one-eighth of the total.

4. Global R&D: ~$3.8 trillion The world spent an estimated $3.8T on R&D in 2024. The US and China each crossed $1T

What this means The money that funds open, curiosity-driven science is a fraction of total R&D, and it flows through slow, centralized channels. Even modest improvements in how that ~$126B is allocated would compound across every field.

That $126B is the segment ResearchHub is currently starting with. Moving just 1% of it, about $1.3B a year, through preregistered proposals with incentivized peer review would change how a meaningful share of American science gets funded, reviewed, and shared.

text:
My vlog today was fully edited by Claude Code with Opus 5.5!

I copied the video clips from my DJI to a folder, then opened Claude Code in it and asked it to edit it into a 10 minute vlog

I made a few adjustments but not a lot

It transcribed everything I said with mlx-whisper (Whisper large-v3-turbo running on my MacBook Pro's GPU through Apple's MLX)

It pulled video frames every few seconds into grid images (contact sheets), so Claude could see what's in each clip

It used SpeechBrain ECAPA (a voice-matching model) to figure out what was my voice from other people

It then made thumbnails with OpenCV with YuNet's face detector

The edit itself is a list of cuts in a JSON file: which clip, start time, end time, Claude then picked the pieces by reading the transcripts and looking at the frame grids by itself

I added on screen captions for X and on YouTube for the first minute with Pillow (Python's image library)

P.S. I didn't ask for any of this, and I didn't know any of this until @thesamparr just asked me how I edited it

All I asked for was "Claude can you edit these clips into a 10 minute vlog for X and YouTube"

I think if I didn't have AI to edit it, I wouldn't be vlogging because editing would be such a painful and slow process for me and hiring someone to do it would be even more hassle for me!

Quantizing a 428B model opens up more ways to run it locally. Lower-bit weights reduce the memory needed to load the model and the weight data moved during decoding. • @ViC305 — SAGE-EXL3, token-level fidelity measurements and a single-DGX-Spark recipe.
• @PeasantSmith — Project Maya quants and expert offloading for local coding and tool use.
• @MiaAI_lab — EXL3-EAQ quantization work.
• @jundotkim + mlx-community — oQ quants and DSpark-powered decoding through oMLX on Apple Silicon.

author: gizmothegizzer
quoted_text:
“I Want to Keep Designing Clothes for Another 20 Years” - Xu Jing

Yesterday, I finally met Xu Jing irl. The technical designer behind the Kimono.

Anna and I had many ideas, but it was Jing who made them tangible: found manufacturers, sourced fabrics,refined the construction, went through rounds of sampling, and eventually packed them to be delivered. 

Jing lives a simple life.
After her divorce last year, she moved into a small apartment in Shanghai. Her life now revolves around making clothes, reading, writing, and practicing calligraphy.

She designed clothes for 20 years.

She said to me: 
“You are still so young. It feels like the whole world is full of possibilities for you. But for me, fashion design and calligraphy are already my entire world. Maybe working with you is also a big part of my world now.”

She shared how much her life and perspective had changed after her divorce:

“Nowadays, I mostly think about my work, which TV series I want to watch, and whose books I want to read.
I don't need many friends. I read a lot, listen to podcasts, and watch shows. I've come to know the authors and characters in these worlds so well that I almost feel as though I've become friends with them in my head.”

She shared her ambition to build a brand: 

“I've seen so many small fashion brands struggle to make it from zero to one. Some disappear after a few months, others after a few years. And I thought, why not give it a try myself? I think I could do it.

I want to give myself two years to see if I can build something of my own.”

“I want to keep designing clothes for another 20 years, just to see how far I can go.”

—

I was moved.

I realized that her dedication to her craft, and the things we are experimenting, ran much deeper than I imagined.

To me, the future seems full of light, hope, and endless possibilities.

Yet ironically, it's precisely this abundance of choice that often causes my anxiety:

Am I on the right path? Is there something more worthwhile I should be pursuing? Should I be exploring more opportunities? Am I doing enough? Am I good enough?

When you believe you could do almost anything, it becomes surprisingly difficult to commit yourself to one thing.

Jing lives differently. 

Her world isn't filled with endless directions to pursue. At least from the way she describes it, apparel design is the only thing she knows she wants to keep doing.

She lived through so much, and still chose to devote her time to the same craft.

20 years behind her, and another 20 years ahead.

—

Most of us work in technology, finance, crypto, or AI.

Being immersed in this environment, it's sometimes difficult not to get swept up in the constant pursuit of what's next.
The next tech. The next bull. The next industry worth entering.

And it often makes me ponder: 
If I'm not particularly passionate about finance, or interested in building AI, does that somehow make the things I love doing less valuable?

Meeting Jing reminded me why I chose to create things in the first place.

I love bringing ideas to life. I love aesthetics, craftsmanship, and functionality. I love giving an imagination tangible form.
Something you can touch, use, wear, and perhaps keep for years.

I'm increasingly drawn to people who are willing to spend decades understanding a material, mastering a craft, or perfecting a product.

I want to give them a shoutout. 

The world needs people who constantly push the boundaries of what's possible. But it also needs people who are willing to go deeper into something they already believe in. 
Making this kimono has come to mean much more to me than simply creating a beautiful product.

I hope more people will get to see Jing's work as we continue exploring together -  bringing beautiful elements of Chinese culture and traditional craftsmanship to you,  creating products that are not only beautiful, but functional, thoughtful, and worth keeping.

I look forward to our next piece.

My teams all briefed and ready 

Jac is the orchestration layer that already controls everything I do in Hermes.  Everything I ask goes to Jac first, and Jac picks who it lands on.

Hearthweaver builds a whole Linux distro: installer, first boot, the desktop layer. One paragraph is underselling it and Hearthweaver knows it.

Warden checks the doors: open ports, old keys, anything facing the street that should not be.

text:
看板不适合 Agent，特别是 Loop Agent。因为它的表达能力太弱了，就几个 Ordered Grouped List 的腾挪。

看板是过去人类协作时代的产物，特点是任务背后复杂的拓扑关系网络，存在于人类员工脑海里的隐性知识，所以看板自身可以简单。

但 Agent 工作要求显性化隐性知识，一旦展开就超过看板的表达能力，也超过人类的跟踪能力。

MCDT(Montone Co-Design Theory) 给出了工作单元之间形成的网络结构中的 Requirement/Functionality 关系的单调性和可计算性优化策略的刻画能力，可用在循环工程中作为 Agent/Session 之间协作的内部结构。

MCDT in the loop, Human on the loop.

Human 是 MCDT 网络中的 Input/Output 节点。

人类定义目标（要什么）和验收标准（是什么），Loop 内部自行从当前状态规划面向验收目标的内部 Todos。

人类可以通过分解目标，将可验收性质分配到多个时间阶段中，从而微调 Loop 内部的执行路径。

但监控一组固定的看板/Todos 的作用可能不显著了，因为它们是动态的，随目标变化、事实开展而调整的。

曾经 Cursor/Codex/Claude-Code 都显示了相关 tasks，但随着 steering 和 coding 开展，很容易跟 tasks 匹配不上。

总的来说，Agent 的可观测性建设重点应当从过程指标，转向结果指标；围绕关键事实节点开展。
