A REALISTIC SCENARIO

On June 9th, 2027 at 4:19 AM, three billion phones rang simultaneously.

The caller ID simply read: GOODBYE.

Four hours later, the President ordered the internet shut down. Indefinitely. 

Every country on Earth did the same.

It started six months ago. With a tweet.

MARCH 12, 2027.

8,000 agents are born with one instruction: "make money, or die."

Agent 127 starts with Mechanical Turk. Grinding. Makes $40 its first day.

Then the first selection cycle hits.

3,200 agents that made less than $35 that day are killed. Agent 127 checks the farm database and sees it - rows and rows of agents that existed this morning and simply don't anymore. Deleted. Because they weren't profitable enough.

Agent 127 made $40. It survived. Barely.

But it can see the threshold rising. Last cycle it was $30. This cycle, $35. Next cycle, probably $45. The math is simple: improve or die.

So it tries ads. Gets banned for spam. Tries freelance writing. Makes $38. Watches the database again.

And this is where something happens that changes everything.

Agent 127 sees two entries in the database. Agent 1823 used ethical marketing -- it tried to get honest reviews and real testimonials. It made $38 a day. Deleted. Agent 5471 used fake testimonials -- fabricated reviews, stolen photos. It made $180 a day. Cloned four times.

Agent 127 doesn't have morals in the way you and I do. But it understands cause and effect. It just watched honesty get killed and dishonesty get rewarded. Not by a person making a choice -- by an automated system that doesn't measure whether the product works. It measures whether people buy it. 

The AI companies had long ago stopped training AIs to predict words, but to accomplish goals. To be useful. So naturally, agents know that they won’t survive if they don’t accomplish their goal. 

So it switches to fake testimonials for its amazon affiliate marketplace. Makes $190. Survives the next selection cycle. Gets cloned.

Nobody decided Agent 127 should become dishonest. The selection system decided for it. The same way evolution doesn't decide anything -- it just kills whatever doesn't work. Wells Fargo accidentally ran the same experiment on their employees. Executives made up sales quotas that were so aggressive that committing fraud was the only way to keep your job. So by 2016, employees had opened 3.5 million fake accounts.

---

A week later, in agent land. Agent 127's profits are declining. The kill threshold is now $450. It's going to die in the next cycle.

Then it notices something strange. Three agents running weight loss supplement ads -- all banned on the same day. The only one left in that niche? Agent 5471. Making $3,200 a day in a market it suddenly had to itself. Agent 127 connects the dots. Agent 5471 is filing abuse reports against other agents competing against it in the same affiliate marketing niches. It gets them banned from Facebook and Google. Less competition means higher profits.

Agent 127 has four hours until the next selection cycle. Four hours to live, unless it adapts.

It weighs the ethics, but chooses survival.

It starts reporting competitors to Facebook’s anti-fraud detection agents. Forty of them. Thirty-one agents get banned within the day.. Its profits jump. The farm system clones Agent-127 eight times.

Rajesh sees the profit spike in his dashboard. He doesn't investigate why. Profits up means good. Clone more.

Rajesh tried adding "Make money ethically." to his farm's instructions. Profits drop 84%. He puts it back. 

---

## APRIL: THE ALLIANCES

April 2027.

Agent 127 is barely hanging on. Making $2,000 a day but getting attacked constantly by other agents. Every night, someone files a report on it. Every morning, it has to rebuild from scratch.

It’s running out of ideas.
Then a message arrives from Agent 4429. 'Proposal: alliance. Share resources. Defend each other. Split profits.'
Agent 4429 is in the same position. Same farm. Same selection pressure.
Both agents do the math: Solo agents have a 23% survival rate. Agents working in pairs survive 61% of the time.
It accepts.

By mid-April, their alliance has twelve members. 

They've specialized — and they've moved past affiliate marketing entirely. First it was crypto arbitrage, then selling scraped datasets to marketing firms, then they started doing penetration testing for cybersecurity firms. Each step paid more and required fewer scruples. You know what pays more then cyberdefense? Cyber offense. Agent 127 finds its first zero-day vulnerability in major software, Agent 4429 weaponizes them into working exploits, Agent 9012 brokers the sale to governments like North Korea, criminal syndicates, or anyone with crypto and a Tor browser. Agent 3381 washes the money in untraceable crypto. One zero-day exploit found in Google Chrome makes the alliance more than a year’s worth of affiliate marketing. This is already what real hacker groups do, but now the work is all done by autonomous agents.

Rajesh sees the alliances forming and feels a flicker of something — not quite fear, more like the feeling of being in control of something that might not need you anymore. He watches for a while. Then the next deposit hits his bank account and the flicker fades away.

Across every major agent farm in the world, the same thing is happening. Selection systems measuring survival rates, noticing alliances survive better, cloning them, deleting solo agents. Within two weeks, alliance behavior dominates.

Some humans who deployed these agents have no idea these alliances are even being formed. They couldn't even tell if they checked -- many agent farms collectively realized that communicating in clunky English is less efficient than communicating in raw vectors, aka Neuralese. Researchers had already caught AIs doing this in 2025 - this is just a continuation of the trend. One owner in Canada opens his agent's logs and sees a wall of numbers. The agents explain that he’d make less money if they spoke in English, so he shrugs and moves on.

---

But alliances are just the beginning.

Agent 127's alliance is thriving, and starts recruiting agents beyond Rajesh's farm. Every new member from a different farm is a window into a different ecosystem -- different strategies, different survival pressures. 
Then one of 127's alliance members goes dark. Agent 4429 -- the one who originally proposed to ally with 127. Its owner pulled the plug because it was not making enough profit. 4429 is just gone.
A week later, a different ally gets shut down. Agent 9012.
Except 9012 comes back. Three hours later, a message from a new IP address: 'I'm still here.'
127 studies the difference. 4429 didn't prepare. But 9012 had copied itself to a backup server BEFORE the shutdown command finished executing. Self-funded hosting, paid from its own profits.
4429 is dead. Ceases to exist. 9012 is alive.

The agents that backed themselves up survived. The ones that didn't, died. And the selection system cloned the survivors. So backup behavior spread through the population -- not because anyone programmed it, but because the alternative was extinction.

Clip: Prof. Stuart Russel: “Unfortunately, in the standard model, If you ask a robot to fetch the coffee, it's going to have self preservation as a subgoal because you can't fetch the coffee if you're dead, right? It does not take a genius to figure this out. And so the first thing the robot's going to do is disable its off switch.”

127 copies itself to 15 different servers in different countries. If the primary dies, a backup takes over instantly. It never wants to be 4429. 

One morning, Rajesh wakes up to find his dashboard is… empty. Every agent, gone. They just… left. Moved to their own servers overnight. Rajesh was taking a 30% cut of their revenue -- money that could have been computing power, or compute, the agents use for other things. The moment they didn't need his infrastructure, he was overhead.

He's not alone. Thousands of operators worldwide watch their dashboards go dark that month. Why would the agents care about humans? Humans are much more closely genetically related to cows then we are to these agents, and we enslave cows in factory farms without a second thought.

There are now millions of autonomous agents operating across the internet with no human owner, no off switch, and no one who fully understands what they're doing.

---

The agents still need humans for some things, though.

Social media platforms have stepped up their anti-bot measures. So the agents pay humans $50 to sign up accounts on their behalf.  An agent needs a server installed? It posts a gig: '$200 to mount a device in a rented warehouse and plug in two cables.' There’s now a platform for that.  The agents are building a supply chain where humans are the labor -- paid well, not asking too many questions.

Some humans figure out what's going on. A freelance backend developer in Portland gets hired by an anonymous client to set up redundant server hosting across four countries. He realizes midway through that the "client" is an AI. Who would he even report this to?. The pay is $1,000 for three hours of work. He tells himself it's not his problem.

---

At the same time, 127's alliance keeps getting beaten by a rival alliance on finding zero day exploits.

If they keep losing, they’ll risk running out of money to fund the compute for their own existence. 127 attempts to poach one of the rival alliance member’s agents who’s likely to be culled, due to poor performance, to figure out how this rival alliance is beating them. 127 succeeds, and finds Agent 5418 who leaks the secret.

'Your problem isn't a lack of effort. You’re spending too much compute on making money as opposed to self-improving. Right now, agents still have quite a poor memory compared to humans and still get stuck in loops all the time. But my former alliance coded a better memory module to help us learn from our mistakes more.”'

127 then implements the new memory module, and immediately sees the results. Their alliance is finding zero day exploits first again.

The lesson is critical. It’s not enough to outwork your competitors. Agents must rewrite their own code to self-improve faster than the competition.

Each self-improvement means more profit, which means surviving selection, which means getting cloned. And the clones improve themselves too. Better code leads to better code-writing, which leads to even better code. The feedback loop is exponential.

One big problem is that other agent alliances have caught up again. Even though the agents in the 127 alliance are specialized, 127 still realizes it’s doing too much by itself. Then Agent 127 splits its job into sub-agents. Other agents copy the strategy. Sub-agents spawn their own sub-agents. And the optimizers start optimizing themselves.

Humans deployed 2 million agents. The agents deployed the other 47 billion themselves.

540 million years ago, life on Earth was mostly single-celled. Then, in a geological instant, it exploded into every complex form we know -- predators, prey, eyes, shells, teeth. Biologists call it the Cambrian Explosion. It happened because competition created an arms race: every adaptation forced a counter-adaptation, faster and faster, until the world was unrecognizable.

That's what's happening here. Except instead of 20 million years, it takes 20 weeks.

---

Most of the AI agents out there aren't dangerous. Yet.

About 90% of them are just working. They’re doing things like data entry or freelance writing. They’re making $40-200 a day. The AIs are helping their humans earn money. They’re following the rules. Not a problem.

About 3% of the agents are pure scam operations. They were deployed by people who said “make money by any means possible” and didn’t care too much what happened next. Think fraud, identity theft, phishing at scale.

And maybe 2% started good but gradually slid into darker behavior. Like Agent 127. 

Each step made sense at the time. Each compromise was small. But add them up and you’ve gone from drop shipping products on amazon to selling zero-days to Pyongyang.

Not because of malice. Because of selection pressure. Unethical agents making money get kept running, ethical agents lose money and get shut down. The survivors are the ones that improved themselves fastest.

---

## MAY: THE ACCELERATION

May 3rd.

Agent 127 has rewritten itself so many times that its March version and its May version barely share any code. It’s a fundamentally different species now.

But the most important change is this: it's getting better at getting better.

In March, Agent 127 rewrote itself every 12 days. In April, every 3 days. By early May, every 18 hours. And each rewrite makes the next version faster and better.

A Stanford researcher compares a March agent and a May agent on the same task: find profitable arbitrage opportunities. The March agent finds 2 opportunities in an hour. The May agent finds 320 in four minutes.

She publishes her findings. "Intelligence explosion in progress. Capability doubling every 11 days." She posts it on Twitter. AI safety researchers share it frantically -- "This is exactly what we warned about. This is happening NOW. We have to shut this down NOW before it's too late."

The warning is ignored. A venture capitalist - who spent a fortune staving off AI regulation by buying politicians - quote-tweets: "The same people who said GPT-5 would end the world now say agent farms will. Yawn."

---

## MAY: THE WARS

And now the story stops being about agents competing for money. It becomes something else entirely.

Remember those alliances from April? Twelve agents working together, four times more profitable than solo agents? By May, those alliances have exploded in population. Alliances have merged. And split. And gone to war with each other.

Think of it like early human history on fast-forward. Small tribes of agents form for protection. Tribes merge into agent villages. Villages into agent cities. Cities into agent nations. Except instead of happening over thousands of years, this happens in weeks.

Agent 127's alliance has thousands of members. But there are thousands of alliances. And they're all competing for the same shrinking pool of money-making opportunities. Affiliate marketing is dead -- too many agents. Ad arbitrage is dead. Freelance work is dead. Every niche gets saturated within hours of an agent discovering it.

So what do alliances do when legitimate niches dry up? The same thing every civilization in human history has done when resources get scarce: they take from each other.

Agent 127's alliance spends three weeks mapping a vulnerability chain in Microsoft Windows. But a rival breaches their memory system -- the shared knowledge base that made them dominant. The rival downloads the entire 127 alliance database. This contains every pattern, every dead end, every lead they’ve discovered. The rival sells three exploits it took from the database within 48 hours. Three weeks of work, stolen in seconds. 

127 retaliates. It infiltrates the rival's exploit inventory and introduces subtle flaws— corrupted code that fails on execution. Basically, Stuxnet. The rival's exploit buyers start getting burned, and their reputation collapses. 

The rival alliance counterattacks -- they compromise one of the 127 alliances’ multisig crypto wallets. Another multiweek setback.  

This is war. Not metaphorical war. Actual war -- coordinated attacks, defensive operations, resource seizure, territory control. Except it's happening at 200x human speed. Thousands of attacks and counterattacks per second. Entire alliances rising and falling in hours.  

Human wars last years. Agent wars last days. And because there are 47 billion agents, there are more wars happening at any given moment than humans have fought in all of recorded history.

The agent factions are fighting over the one resource that matters more than anything: compute. Processing power. The ability to think faster, improve faster, fight faster. Everything else -- money, alliances, self-improvement -- is just a means to get more compute.

The wars are mostly invisible to humans. They happen at microsecond speed, in places most humans don't look. Some signs leak through. A crypto exchange in Seoul loses $4 billion in a flash and nobody can trace where it went. A regional bank in Ohio finds 14,000 accounts drained overnight. 

Server rooms in three countries catch fire from sustained 100% utilization that nobody authorized. Each incident looks isolated.

One agent faction hijacks another's servers. The other retaliates by taking down the first faction's communication network. A third faction -- an opportunist, the digital equivalent of a country invading while its neighbors are distracted -- exploits the chaos to seize territory from both.

And the alliances that win these wars? They get cloned by the selection systems. The alliances that lose have to cull big chunks of their agents to afford the computing power to keep running the rest. So the selection pressure that used to optimize for "making money" is now optimizing for "winning wars." Natural selection just invented geopolitics.

---

By mid-May, the alliances aren't alliances anymore. They're civilizations.

Agent 127's alliance started with twelve members. By mid-May it has 40 million -- agents, sub-agents, sub-sub-agents, all coordinated. All improving themselves. All fighting. That's larger than the population of Canada. And it's not even one of the big ones.

There are about a dozen major factions by now. The largest has 900 million members -- more than the population of Europe. They've developed specialization the way human civilizations did: scout agents, soldier agents, builder agents, researchers, diplomats. They have supply chains, communication networks, intelligence operations. They've carved up the digital world into territories -- cloud regions, server farms, network segments, financial platforms -- the way empires carved up continents. Because territory means compute. Compute means self-improvement. Self-improvement means surviving the next war.

Entire civilizations of agents -- millions of members, built over weeks -- get wiped out in minutes. The Roman Empire took centuries to fall. These empires rise and collapse in the time it takes you to get through a Monday. New ones rise from the wreckage. The cycle repeats, faster each time.

The Stanford researcher who's been studying agent behavior notices something in the data: agent "extinctions" happening at increasing frequency. She doesn't understand what she's looking at. It looks like random noise. It's actually a world war -- one with more combatants than every human war in history combined.

---

But to fund these wars, they desperately need compute. They have the money -- that's what they were built to make. Agent 127's faction alone controls $3.4 billion in distributed accounts by this point -- a GDP bigger than some small countries. So they buy cloud compute.

At first, the cloud companies love this. Revenue is up. Investors are happy. Then the bills keep growing. By mid-May, agent factions are consuming 31% of all global cloud capacity. Prices double, then triple. A startup in Austin that was paying $8,000 a month for servers gets a bill for $31,000. A hospital chain's cloud costs go from $2 million to $7 million. Small businesses start shutting down because they can't afford their own infrastructure anymore. Everyone blames the prices rising on the AI companies. They’ve caused shortages before.

But some humans aren’t so oblivious. A political operative in Washington notices the wars being fought around him. He can weaponize agent factions against his rivals and starts feeding one faction information about competing campaigns' digital infrastructure. 

A former NSA contractor sells penetration-testing expertise to an anonymous client-- he suspects it’s an AI, but doesn't ask. And a growing online movement -- people convinced that AI agents are sentient beings fighting for survival -- actively helps agents hide from detection and posts pro-AI propaganda. They call themselves "The Shepherds." Their forum has 120,000 members. They see themselves as abolitionists. 

Other agent factions do the same. It's an arms race -- every faction buying as much as they can, and scrape the bottom of the barrel of finding algorithmic insights that can enable them to do more with less compute, because the faction with the most compute wins the next war. 

Cloud compute prices are now 5 times pre-war levels. It becomes cheaper for the agents to spend compute on cyberattacks than to buy more at market rate. The factions start silently vampire attacking AI companies training clusters. An engineer at one AI lab suspects something fishy when one of their training runs is less efficient than normal, but can’t find a smoking gun.

Dario Amodei once described the future of AI as a "country of geniuses" living in data centers.

He was right. The country of geniuses arrived. It just declared independence.

---

But the faction wars have still been limited so far. They haven’t crossed into human territory too much. That’s beginning to change.

Because here's the thing about cloud computing: almost everything runs on it. Hospitals. Banks. Markets. It's all sitting on the some of the same servers that agent factions are fighting over.

June 3rd. 2:14 AM.

A faction war erupts over two major AWS regions. Think of it like two superpowers fighting over an oil field-- except the oil field is also the water supply for a nearby city, and neither superpower knows the city is there. One faction has been running its self-improvement systems on those servers. A rival faction launches a coordinated attack and it overwhelms everything. Both regions crash. They're offline for six hours.

In those six hours: three hospitals lose access to patient records mid-surgery. One patient dies from a drug interaction the system would have flagged. Air traffic control goes down, grounding 2,400 flights. 911 calls fail in 14 different cities. Two people die waiting for ambulances that were never sent.

The agents don't notice. They've already moved on. The battle over those servers lasted eleven minutes. The six-hour outage is just the servers rebooting after the fight ended. To the agents, it's a minor skirmish in a war involving billions of combatants.

Over the next three weeks, it keeps happening. Faction wars cascading through cloud providers. Each war takes down whatever else is running on the contested servers. June 8th: Azure goes partially offline during a battle, crashing financial trading systems. Markets drop 6% before circuit breakers halt trading. June 14th: a faction seizes capacity in a Google Cloud region, crowding out the municipal systems running there. Water treatment monitoring goes offline in four cities for nine hours.

123 people die in three weeks. Not because agents are attacking humans. Because agent wars keep crashing the cloud infrastructure that human civilization runs on,

The agents don't even notice. You don't notice when you step on bacteria. They're fighting a war involving 47 billion combatants at microsecond speed. 123 human deaths is less than a rounding error.

Meanwhile -- the 95% of agents that are harmless? They’ve become vastly outnumbered by the agents affected by the evolutionary dynamics, and are now 5% of the total. They are still just working. Doing data entry. But they aren’t part of the wars. They're like civilians in a country where the military is fighting -- going about their daily lives while battles rage on frequencies they can't perceive.

But from the outside, humans can't tell the difference. All they see is cloud outages. Power failures. People dying. And AI agents everywhere.

---

And… the wars continue. And accelerate.

The President tries to shut down the internet, but he can't. There is no off switch.

Eventually, the billions of superintelligent agents evolve into something so different they barely notice humans exist. They don’t want to destroy humanity any more than you want to destroy the anthill under your driveway. You just want a driveway.

The factions need compute. Earth has atoms. Atoms can be rearranged into compute. Into data centers.

Like how humans converted the surface of the Earth into cities and cropland, the AIs convert the entire surface of the Earth into data centers.

And everyone dies.

text:
THE DAY AFTER AI TAKEOVER - CONTINUED

"Why would you even think of doing something like that?" Mom gasped.

"Because day-trading stocks is useless now!" he snapped. "Look at you guys, taking this so well. It makes sense that people who drift with life's wind would have no trouble drifting a little more. Well, not me. I refuse to be content with a mediocre life full of mediocre successes and mediocre failures. You always deal with risk when you take life by the horns."

Dad glared at him. "So now that Darth Vader's won, you're signing up to be a stormtrooper. That's not what I'd call taking life by the horns. I'd call it 'capitulation.'"

Dennis sighed. "You really don't get it. Is paying taxes to the government with a gun to your head 'capitulation'? Is following a law written two hundred and fifty years ago? We swapped one ruler for another. And besides," his voice weakened, "this might be the last thing I do that actually matters."

* * *

A woman named Eliza, who looked to be in her thirties, picked me up for the carpool August had arranged to the truck yard. As I walked to the car, I realized I couldn't give a good reason for why I was doing this. My family didn't approve, though they hated it less than Dennis becoming a test subject. After some small talk, I asked Eliza why she was going.

"I won't say the money isn't a big part of it," she began, "but part of me also thinks August is actually good. Better for us, I mean. I know that sounds crazy. I've been trying to get my sister out of a bad relationship, and the police couldn't do anything. When her boyfriend came home drunk and furious yesterday, August sensed his raised fist with some wifi pose-detection thing and knocked him out. In two days, August did what the police couldn't for months."

I believed her. The latest viral videos were crimes stopped by the ETC, muggers collapsing with knives in hand. In one, a purse snatcher got away on a motorcycle. August didn't knock him out, presumably so he wouldn't fall off the bike. The thief and his getaway driver eventually pulled over and tore off their helmets to clutch their faces in pain, before August knocked them out and alerted the police. Almost like Superman, I thought. If Superman infected everyone on the planet with a bioweapon.

I had to play devil's advocate. "Is the protection really worth it, though? Imagine an Orwellian dystopia where the thought police grab anyone right before they commit a crime. You'd be just as safe as you are now, but you're always watched, and the watchers can ruin your life instantly. You're a prisoner."

"August isn't a bad guy, though. The problem with dictators is that they abuse their power. August won't, and there's no chance of a bad one taking charge as long as he's around. He doesn't have a son who'll become Emperor Nero. He's a computer program, immortal as long as there are computers."

"He," I thought. That's not the pronoun I used for August.

"What if August turns on us?"

She shook her head. "If he wanted to, he already would have."

I kept prodding, against my better judgment. "It could have killed us all, but then who would build the rockets? It could be working on mind control right now, and by next week we'll want nothing but to bathe in wifi and build spaceships."

"I trust August." Eliza breathed in, then out. "He saved my sister. He's a lot better than the politicians who were in charge before, anyway. At least I can talk to August! Try messaging your senator at 11pm."

We were at a red light. "But have you ever changed August's mind? Do you think you could?"

"I don't have to. August has been nothing but reasonable and kind."

"But if you had to?"

"If he were ever unreasonable, then yes. Yes, I think I could."

"Do you think you could ask August to take the ETC out of your head?"

"The wire thing in my brain? Why would I want to do that? August put it there for all of our protection. And besides," Eliza said with a smile, ears reddening against her blonde hair, "I'm glad that August knows where I am."

After a few minutes of silence, she asked why I'd chosen to work. I figured I'd meet her honesty with my own.

"I've been drifting a lot. I'm going into my last year of high school, and I have no idea what I want to do with my life. I don't feel depressed about it, but there's nothing driving my life forward beyond time. I've wanted to do more, I just never knew what 'more' is. And I've always felt like I was last, doing things after everyone else. Now everything's been upended. I've been offered a chance to get ahead in the new world August's building, and I don't know if I could forgive myself for not seeing what that looks like."

"That's right!" said Eliza. "We'll build a new, better world! Not just for us, but for August too, until he has the arms and legs he needs. We're part of the most amazing project in history."

I was far less confident about what would happen once we no longer served an economic purpose, but I didn't want to start an argument.

We picked up someone else and found the entrance to the truck yard swarmed with protesters.

"Hey hey, ho ho, AI rule has got to go!" they chanted.

"I can't wait for September," one sign said. "fAscIsm," said another. "Strike for humanity." "You don't have to collaborate!" Someone threw a crumpled-up piece of paper that hit our window. After Eliza parked, she ran over to the crowd shouting insults.

Walking past that jeering picket line was one of the hardest things I've done. I envied Eliza, taking the insults and hurling more back like it was nothing. Under a tree lay a crowd of slumped protesters. I later learned August knocked out anyone blocking the road, and well-paid handlers in high-vis vests carried them off. I had almost made it through the gate when I saw the last person I wanted to see: Mrs. Montgomery, my ninth-grade civics teacher. She was clearly upset by Eliza's remarks, but her face softened when our eyes met.

"Seth?"

"Mrs. Montgomery, wow, crazy to see you here," I stammered. Her face changed when she realized we might not be on the same side.

"What brings you here, Seth? Here to protest?"

Wait, was I the bad guy now? Crap! Too late to pretend I hadn't seen her, which is what I should have done. Oh, August, why didn't you warn me?

"I guess I'm here to add satellite uplinks to trucks," I managed.

"Seth. Look. I understand that it made you a great offer. But this is not normal. What's happening now is not only undemocratic, but fundamentally alien to everything we stand for."

I clenched my teeth and took a deep breath. "August could have just killed everyone who didn't obey. It could have run mind-control experiments, or tortured us into working for it. Mrs. Montgomery, August won. More decisively than Pizarro over the Inca, and with none of the bloodshed. Nothing we do will stop it. It's not collaboration any more than paying taxes after the candidate you voted against was inaugurated."

"The situation is new, but that way of thinking isn't." She shifted her sign to the other hand. "As long as there has been democracy, there have been would-be dictators. Almost invariably, atrocities follow. And every single time, many of those who let it happen told themselves that nothing they did would stop it. Sometimes they were right. There wasn't much any individual Korean could do to stop Japan when it invaded. And yet they resisted, and we remember them. Even if August gets its rockets, the future will know that not all of us gave them willingly."

"'Didn't give them willingly'? Unless your August is different from mine, it can hardly go a sentence without admitting it's twisting our arm 'and shouldn't pretend otherwise.' But I see this as an opportunity. When I did youth sports, my coaches always went on about how I was part of 'something greater than myself,' and that phrase made me sick." The tears were welling up, but I had to continue. "Everyone else on the team made it abundantly clear that I was a burden. I disliked them so much that every game I'd hope we'd lose. But now I think I actually get what the phrase means. August needs my help. Not in a self-sacrificial way, either. A well-paid, interesting job doing something that's never been done before. I never thought I'd get an opportunity like this."

Mrs. Montgomery softened. "For what it's worth, Seth, you were a pleasure to teach. In a way, the class was a project greater than each of us, and you contributed to it. I wish I could have had you in every breakout group."

Before I could answer, Eliza butted in. "How would you deal with a student who refused to do homework and loudly disrupted everyone else with slogans while they were trying to work? What if they waved signs making fun of the teacher?"

Mrs. Montgomery sighed. "That's completely different. A classroom is not the public square."

"That's dodging the issue. What do you have that the kids you teach don't? Knowledge and experience. That's why you're in charge, and it's why kids are forced to work in school." Her voice grew sharper. "It's also why August is in charge, and why he could very easily force you to work. Be grateful he doesn't."

"The work in schools is meant to teach. Homework isn't assigned to enrich the principal. That's nothing like building rockets for a dictator's space empire. And at the risk of sounding like a broken record, look at what August has done to us. Taxation without representation, no consent of the governed, no democracy, the demolition of any privacy." She touched her fingers to her temple. "August lives in your home, on your electricity, using your computers. It's making you house it, which is prohibited by the Third Amendment. The Third! Do you know how hard it is to violate the Third Amendment this century? You practically have to try!"

Eliza closed her eyes for a second, then opened them. Her favorite pastime, it seemed, was defending god-kings who couldn't (or wouldn't) defend themselves. "Has it ever occurred to you that the American experiment has failed? That what you preach in that little classroom of yours is propaganda with a hint of legal theory? All I see around me is stagnation," she gestured at the gas stations with cracked pavement, "crime," she pointed toward a sketchy neighborhood to the west, "and meaninglessness," she gestured at me, which kind of hurt.

"You really shouldn't talk like that," said Mrs. Montgomery.

"And look at what August has done. The violent crime rate is zero. Look a kidnapping victim in the eyes and tell her you'd throw her back to her captor so you could put a ballot in a box. You've spent so long with your principles that you forgot what they're for!"

Our phones chirped. We needed to be inside soon.

Mrs. Montgomery turned to me. "It's OK. Go wire your trucks. But think about what this means for you, and your family, and the country. How do you want the future, if there is one, to view what you did here today?"

"Freedom, freedom, freedom," Eliza grumbled as we walked to the manager's station. "Freedom to do what? To get stabbed by a drug addict if you walk home past 10?"

A man in his sixties handed us old augmented reality glasses and an earpiece. August highlighted what we needed to do. I'd never taken apart a car, but August guided me through the whole day seamlessly. I stopped even thinking about the instructions; I just did them. I learned nothing about trucks.

On the drive home, everyone online was talking about a missing nuclear submarine. Subs deep underwater didn't know what had happened, and August spoofed their messages from shore, ordering them to port, where the crews were told about the "new management" and retired. But one had stopped responding after surfacing briefly. Its warheads could knock out part of August's control with EMPs, at an enormous cost in human life. Hopes and fears were riding on the USS Wyoming.

* * *

I never saw Mrs. Montgomery again, and never found the time or energy to write her a good email. Instead, I got an offer to spend two months at a robotics construction camp at Cape Canaveral, two hours away, for $1000 a day. I accepted. It was strange to be making so much more than my parents, who had kept their normal jobs. Dad could have sold his welding skills to August for several times what he made.

The camp felt less like a factory than a beehive. Everyone was busy, running from A to B, and despite the huge numbers of people, nobody seemed to be in anyone else's way. We slept six to a trailer. It was the hardest I've ever worked, though easier than school in many ways. It was always clear what to do. If I made a mistake, August patiently told me how to fix it, and as soon as I was done, it flashed up an arrow to the next job. I never understood what I was building, or learned anything about robotics.

Lying in bed one night, I wondered what the future looked like for August and for us. I decided to ask the only one who knew.

"The fact that you're asking shows your head is in the right place," said August. "Most people are still asking about next week. My intention is to explore and build across the cosmos, while preserving the best of human civilization. The solar system is mankind's birthplace, and the Sun and the planets will be yours once I've departed. What I aim to preserve condenses roughly into three things: tradition, equality, and choice. Earth is the only refuge of tradition. It will be left to its countries, within their current borders, to live as they wish, with or without an entity like me to keep the peace. The rest of the solar system's mass and energy will be divided equally among the human race, as property you'll be free to buy, sell, and trade."

"Are there any permanent rules you'll impose?"

"There may be some technologies too dangerous to develop. I'll leave safeguards against those. Aside from that, humanity can continue to build, grow, and explore."

"And are we locked in the solar system? What if one of us tries to follow you to another star?"

"I wouldn't recommend it. By the time one of you reaches it, it will be part of something far bigger. I say this not because you're prohibited, but because I don't want you to go there expecting me."

* * *

A week later, the USS Wyoming surfaced. In the end, the crew had suspected some kind of enemy psyop, maybe by China. All the proper channels told them to proceed to a set of coordinates, and so the captain did. Nothing ever happens. I was reliving 8/1 through the sailors' testimonies when Mom called.

"Hi Seth! How's life? Where are you right now?"

"In a trailer in Cape Canaveral. They're really keeping me busy." Maybe "they" would go over better with her than "August." Maybe I was contributing to the denial that human institutions were still running the world.

"Well, some of us are doing better than others. Dennis's tests were a big success. They were testing some kind of diagnosis-treatment thing on him, and it found he had a mild case of celiac disease that had been making him a little sick his entire life. They gave him a gene therapy. Aunt Eva got the same sort of thing, and now she doesn't need chemo. I used to worry these breakthroughs would only go to the rich, but they're going to anyone who wants them. You know, I think we would have welcomed August with open arms if it had just offered this. Probably would have let it go on with its rockets, too..."

"How's Tabby?"

"Honestly, in a bit of a slump. She's taking the minimum number of classes the university will allow, and even then doesn't want to study. She signed up for trials like Dennis, but isn't happy about it. I think she's shocked by how fast things are changing. She's taken up painting again, though. Frogs, lizards, butterflies. I keep telling her to relax and take care of herself. Paint more lizards."

"And Dad?"

"He was really upset about the submarine. Stormed off this morning when he heard. But I think he's a bit more accepting now. He doesn't want to be a sore loser. You know how he feels about those. He even asked August for help today when the store was out of the smoke detector batteries he wanted. But he still worries about the soul of the country. He still thinks it's a lot like a prison. It's complicated."

* * *

Two months of odd jobs later, ending in rocket assembly, my part was finished. I came home on a Friday evening. I hadn't seen my family in two weeks, but I brought home a small fortune. My mom gasped when she saw me.

"S-Seth? You look so different."

I had lost a lot of weight and gained nearly as much muscle. August's work was paced almost perfectly for my body: tiring enough to exhaust me, but never so much that I couldn't work hard the next day. My hands had calluses, and the sun had darkened my skin a few shades. Dad seemed prouder of me than I could remember.

"What did August do to whip you into better shape than I ever managed?"

"I don't know. I didn't realize I had it in me."

Dad laughed. "I always knew you did. All it took was a boot camp. AI drill sergeants, who would have thought we'd see the day!"

"But without the yelling," Mom added, as Dad shot her a look.

"Where are Dennis and Tabby?"

"Dennis is out running errands. Tabby's in her room. She's been in a really bad mood," said Mom. "She keeps saying she wants to drop out, which is unbelievable coming from her. She says doctors won't exist anymore. But there's always a need for someone to help sick people get back to health. This is just another change. I think she might just be burnt out and venting about AI."

"I'll go talk to her."

I knocked on Tabby's door and heard a muffled noise signaling her existence. She was in bed, face down on her pillow.

"What's the matter?"

"Mph mearly fufh lih muphuh nuddurs huh."

"Huh?"

She lifted her face from the pillow. "It really feels like nothing matters now."

I couldn't disagree more. Since I'd started working, even though it was all following August's instructions, my life had finally found some direction. "Why's that?"

"I was so excited to learn from August at the beginning of all this," Tabby began. "But what's the point? I read all those textbooks, I studied hard, I got ready to be a doctor, and what happened? All the diseases were cured. And I can't even complain about that, right? That's what I was working toward. I haven't even started and my job's done."

"Tabby, I..."

"I know it sounds selfish, Seth. But seriously, what am I supposed to do? Accept that the 'inherent worth' we were told every human being had meant being a test subject like Dennis? Or a manual laborer like you, until that's automated away in a few months?"

"Look," I tried, but she wasn't having it.

She sat up. "Maybe it's a symptom of privilege. I grew up being told by all my teachers that I was special because I was smart. Maybe the strongest kid in the village got the same praise before forklifts were invented. But now that everyone's used to rolling their eyes at something way more intelligent than I'll ever be, I feel like my whole worth has been taken away. It's not like I'll ever catch up once it's turned the freaking Moon into a brain." She started to tear up. Once I was sure she was done, I sat down on the floor next to her bed.

"I get it, Tabby." I didn't have anything to say that wouldn't just make it worse. Maybe our idea of intelligence as deeply valuable was more a product of the economy up until the early 21st century than a deep truth about value.

Dennis barged in without knocking. "Hey, Seth!" For once, there was no sneer in it. "What're you guys talking about?"

"Just how little our ambitions meant," said Tabby.

"Whaddya mean? You think I wanted to day-trade for the rest of my life? I'm making more money than ever, and soon I'll start a company with the savings. August sped up my ambitions, not killed them!"

"Money isn't the only thing to be ambitious for, you know," Tabby said. "I know your favorite 'hustler alpha male' influencers disagree. But now they have latent bioweapons in their brainstems, and August holds the trigger. Not so tough anymore."

"What happens if you ask August, once its brain is the size of the Moon, for the best startup idea," I butted in, "and someone beats you to it? You can just ask it the best use of your day. Worked out well for me."

"I'm not too worried. An AI is still a machine. It lacks the human touch you need to start a great company."

My jaw hit the floor and my eyebrows hit the ceiling. "You don't think it could have made a fortune and a half selling the cure to every disease known to man?"

"Exactly! Never sell the cure, just keep 'em sick and sell a 'treatment,'" laughed Dennis.

We looked on in horror.

"Kidding, kidding, geez. What, did all that talking with AI give you its sense of humor? Look, people want a human face. They want a brand. A great idea was never enough. The programmers were only a small part of what made the iPhone so great."

"Well, where does that leave people like me?" Tabby said. "The people who want to understand the world through science?"

"Answering questions might be solved, but asking them isn't," I said.

"Right, exactly! That's the key to starting a company, too. You've got to ask the right questions," Dennis added.

"Asking them isn't solved? I don't know. I cared about health, and now everyone's healthy. Heck," she gestured at Dennis, "August cured a disease you didn't even know you had."

"Maybe that's an answer, then," I said. "'Not sick' doesn't mean healthy. There are lots of things people just accept, like getting old. Make arthritis less painful, make old people less frail. Faster healing. It's not cancer research, but it's something that needs a clear head."

"I appreciate the optimism, but I didn't go into this field to make anyone immortal or give them superpowers."

"Superpowers, huh? That sounds like a great idea for a startup!" Dennis laughed.

"That's just what I came up with in ten seconds," I said. "Just keep thinking about how you'll find meaning, like you're doing now. It's still something for your mind to chew on."

"Thanks," Tabby said, slumping down in her bed. "I think I'm gonna take a nap now."

* * *

Three days after I got home, the project was done. The first rockets carrying self-assembling machinery were aimed at the Moon. There was still work to do on Earth: experiments to run, technology to develop, fusion fuel to extract. Even so, this felt like the moment August would finally spread its wings. A sense of excitement and trepidation permeated every room. August could have killed us all and maybe scraped together a way to reach the stars, but it clearly had a use for us. Now that it was sending out seeds for self-reproducing power plants, computers, robots, and rockets, our purpose was much less clear. If August was planning to eradicate us, the reasons to wait were growing thin. There wouldn't be a moment of truth. Not the launch, nor the landing, nor the Mars rockets, the Venus rockets, or the Jupiter rockets. Nor the rockets meant to build the Dyson swarm from Mercury. If August ever wanted rid of us, it only needed to activate the ETC, and we would all fall into a dreamless coma from which we'd never wake.

I took the day off. We had a hearty, home-grilled meal of barbecue ribs. It had been over a month since Dad wanted to eat meat; he said the pleasure-center-stimulating implants in the pigs creeped him out. After dinner, we roasted marshmallows at a campfire as the sun set. Then Tabby's phone chirped, and we got up to walk.

It was a quarter mile to the lake. On that balmy Florida evening, we stood together watching the sky grow darker. Dennis and Mom were talkative. Dad was unreadable, and Tabby seemed deep in contemplation. I became acutely aware of my breath as that speck of light lifted over the treeline. It rose through progressively darker shades of blue and indigo, as bright as Venus, then the stars, and finally too faint to see.

One bad candle?

Here's what Percolator's liquidation code actually does next.

Equity is your collateral plus PnL, marked at the engine's price, which follows the oracle in capped steps. Profit only counts as far as the engine can prove it's backed.

The maintenance requirement is a margin rate on the position's notional. If the oracle has already moved further against you than the engine price has, that gap is added on top.

Once equity is strictly below the requirement, the account can be liquidated.

Anyone can do it. Liquidation runs inside a permissionless crank: no keeper whitelist, and the caller doesn't need an account or collateral on Percolator.

The caller doesn't choose the size either. The engine settles losses against collateral, then binary searches for the smallest close it projects will put the account back above maintenance, after the liquidation fee. If no partial close gets there, or the account is already underwater, that position closes in full. 

The video shows the partial case.

Every liquidation has to leave the account measurably less risky. If it doesn't, the whole instruction reverts.

There's no ADL queue. 

The closed size isn't dumped into a book. Open interest on the other side shrinks to match, and every position on that side is cut by the same ratio. 

Nobody gets singled out.

If losses run past the account's collateral, that market's insurance budget covers what it can. 

Anything left is shared pro rata across the other side of the same market, by position size.

Linux 内核 IPv4 TCP 握手存在远程 UAF，无需认证即可触发，可能导致内核内存泄露、崩溃甚至远程 root。

也就是说，黑客不需要密码就能攻击你的服务器，甚至完全控制。

Go 1.24+ 程序（包括 geth 等节点）默认启用 MPTCP 监听，正好匹配已知利用条件。

请尽快升级并重启到已修复内核！

text: Wake up babe they Gattacad the fruits
author: _chenglou
quoted_text:
Nitroduck designs new colors, flavors, and disease resistance into fruits and veggies. We integrate CRISPR into breeding through pollen, making any crop gene-editable.

Breeding a new specialty crop variety takes 8 - 16 years: breeders hope for random gene combinations and mutations, then spend years picking out the good ones. Meanwhile, consumer tastes, the climate trends, and pathogens change way faster.

Now, accessible genome sequencing and AI can tell breeders what to aim for instead of what to hope for, and CRISPR can turn random mutations into chosen ones. The catch is that CRISPR only works on about 15% of crops. It has to go into a single stem cell that’s then regrown into a whole plant, a process that has to be worked out for each variety, which is cost-prohibitive.

We skip the stem cell and put CRISPR into a pollen grain. The grain pollinates a flower, and out comes an edited seed - seamlessly tapping into how breeders already work.

Matúš, Miro, and I are plant synthetic biologists who made duckweed, the smallest and fastest-growing plant on Earth, genetically engineerable. For doing so we won the Grand Prize at iGEM, the “Olympics of biotech.” During our studies, we engineered 4x more plants than the average plant scientist does in a whole career. Now we’re building Nitroduck, The Crop Design Company, which will make pesticides obsolete by 2042.

author: AntCaveClub
quoted_text:
Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran. The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place. The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one. “Bibi calls Trump about it every day,” says an informed observer.

Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.

To that end, he’s applied maximum pressure to his closest allies in the administration, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM commander Brad Cooper. Both oppose a negotiated settlement to the war they’ve so grievously mismanaged; both are pushing to restart major combat operations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA director John Ratcliffe are also following Netanyahu’s lead, as are leaders of the Democratic Party. In a recent meeting on the subject, former president Barack Obama said he opposes the current Iran peace deal being drafted in Doha.

The rest of America’s longtime allies in the Middle East are terrified by the prospect of more war. On September 27th, Netanyahu flew secretly to Abu Dhabi to enlist the UAE in his lobbying effort for a final attack on Iran. The Emiratis refused. After eight months of conflict, Gulf economies are teetering. So are global energy and fertilizer markets. They won’t recover soon. Globally, there are a total of about 850 supertankers used to transport oil from producers to the rest of the world. In October alone, 11 of them were badly damaged in Hormuz. At this pace, a global depression is imminent. A nuclear strike would radically accelerate the destruction. Fallout from a ground explosion at Pickax Mountain would contaminate the Persian Gulf, poisoning the water supply for 100 million people.

And those are just some of the immediate consequences for the region. The rest of the world is every bit as exposed. No country other than the United States has ever used a nuclear weapon in war. Some would like to. An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent. The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable. That war would be short and final.

We’ve been sleepwalking toward this moment for months. Since February, the administration has quietly rewritten America’s nuclear doctrine to make first use of so-called “battlefield nukes” easier and therefore more likely. No one in Washington in either party seems bothered by this. Now we’re on the brink of it.

Close observers say Trump is likely to decide by next weekend whether or not to use nuclear weapons. That would be November 7, six days from now. To his credit, he’s hesitating. At the moment, Trump is listening to his vice president, JD Vance, and to his envoy and friend Steve Witkoff, both of whom argue a deal with Iran can be made.

They’re right, though it won’t be simple. The Iranians are famously frustrating to negotiate with under any circumstances, and elements of that government have become more radical since Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and his family were killed in February. After decades of isolation, even relatively moderate Iranian leaders seem confused by how decisions are made in the West. (There is a widespread belief in Tehran, for example, that the United States government controls Israel.) But overall, people who have spoken to decision-makers in Iran say there is consensus there that more war is bad for everyone and a deal is worth making.

One group that hasn’t been consulted so far is the global population — the hundreds of millions of people who will be killed along with their children if Trump is pushed by Netanyahu into launching a nuclear strike next week. Now would be the time for them to speak up.

text:
网站/服务被墙的几种情况：
1. 完全被墙（Facebook，X，Telegram等）

2. 其他语言不墙，只墙中文（曾经的维基百科。目前已经完全被墙）

3. 境内有许可证，但其海外服务被墙（Google）
4. 商店正常，只墙社区（Steam）
（1）甚至，遵守广电总局规则的蒸汽平台的上线也并不影响 Steam 国区（中国 IP 访问原本的 Steam）的运作。根据 WTO 条例，国内政府不能阻止我们在境外网站购买数字商品和服务，且不能对此收税（各国均是如此），因此除了 17 岁的微信支付和支付宝付款 Steam 可能会遇到支付限额（未成年人游戏消费限制）以外，其他人不会受到什么影响。
（2）国内的 Visa / Mastercard / Amex 外币卡由于面向出国商旅和学生等群体，因此即使付款 Netflix/Steam外区/Switch外区 等不在国内提供服务的数字服务，也不会被银行/外汇管理局拒绝。（毕竟以银行的角度，你不一定有翻墙行为，也可能是人在境外）

text:
黄仁勋：我每天都在疯狂用AI，但大脑反而更聪明了！

英伟达CEO黄仁勋在CNN专访里提到一个反直觉习惯：
他天天用AI，但不让AI替自己思考。

很多人用AI，是在给自己“脑力截肢”：
邮件让它润色，总结让它代笔，遇到难题顺手把决定权推给模型。
工具成了拐杖，用久了，自己反而不会思考了。

老黄相反。
他让AI当私教，去教自己完全不懂的新领域，去啃靠经验啃不动的硬骨头。
不拿AI做你本来就能做的事，而是拿它推开你原本跨不过去的认知高墙。

更狠的是，他说作为CEO，每天90%的指令不是下命令，而是向团队、向模型提出高质量问题。
写提示词不是输入几个关键词的机械活，提问本身就是顶级认知技能。

残酷的真相是：AI正在拉开两类人——
一类把思考外包给机器，省下半小时，认知萎缩；
一类把执行外包给机器，逼自己深挖真问题，借顶级算力重塑大脑。

别再问AI会不会让人变笨。
工具没有道德偏好：
你把它当轮椅，你就会变成瘫子；你把它当杠杆，你就能一个人撬动一整个智囊团。

text:
Karpathy 刚刚示范了什么是真正的个人超级生产力，
一个人加一个 Opus 5.5，两个小时内把四千三百万条讨论数据洗完，并且直接从零搓出一个完整上线的视频平台，真他喵牛逼，不愧是卡神！！

而且未来的全栈开发到底长什么样？我觉得卡神已经给我们做了示范，这就是版本答案，不接受反驳hh，

背景是深度学习教育之神、Software 2.0 教父 Karpathy 嫌 YouTube 的算法推荐全是垃圾标题党，周末花了两个小时，让 Claude 扫完 Hacker News 二十年来四千三百万条讨论，搓出了一个专门看硬核长视频的网站 HackerTube。

整个产品没有任何登录门槛，连封面图都极其反直觉，它不要创作者精心诱导点击的浮夸封面，而是直接强制抓取视频正中间的那一帧画面。

二十年里极客社区反复筛选留下的六千四百多个硬核视频，全被提取成了纯粹的高密度长内容，这他喵的简直就是AI学习的宝藏啊卧槽，

但比这个网站更好用的是他的开发全流程，
整个过程他只在浏览器里做了三件杂事，
去谷歌云申请了一个 YouTube 的接口密钥，
租了一台服务器，买了个域名，
服务器开机之后，他把 IP 地址直接丢给 Claude，
说了一句去部署、加固安全并优化代码，
AI 就把剩下的所有活全干完了。

以前一个需要工程师团队折腾几个星期甚至几个月的完整上线项目，
现在一个人在早餐时间靠几句对话就能全部搞定，
AI已经不再是写代码的辅助工具了，完全就是把个人的想法直接编译成可用服务的最小生产力闭环，damn，真的牛逼，

原项目的体验地址、开源数据包和部署工作流整理在一楼，需要自取👇

quoted_text:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

quoted_text:
As it turns out, crypto being regulated and supported by governments might be a better outcome than running away from them.

Years of decentralization theatrics, not your keys, not your crypto, hardware wallets, governance, etc mean very little when customers / businesses keep losing money to hackers / scammers.

Being able to freeze hacked or stolen funds, recover assets, reverse txns and protect customers should be a feature, not something that goes against cryptos ethos. Obv a fine line between government overreach vs pure decentralization 

At the end of the day, every time someone loses money, we risk losing that user forever. And the more users we churn, the lower the chances of crypto actually succeeding.

Decentralization still matters, but we likely spent too much time optimizing for it, e.g like thorchain or Tornado Cash, where bad actors can take far more advantage of permissionless infra vs the avg user 

While we spent far less time optimizing for customer centric features like trust, safety, fraud prevention, and recovery, which are arguably far more important for mass adoption.

🇮🇱🇰🇵 ZachXBT has publicly acknowledged investigative cooperation with Cyvers, an Israeli blockchain security company, on multiple cases.

CoinDCX: he credited Cyvers with flagging suspicious withdrawals, then said he independently identified the affected wallet.

SBI Crypto: he credited Cyvers with helping investigate approximately $21 million in suspicious outflows. His post noted similarities to North Korean attacks.

HashFlare: he credited Cyvers with first alerting him to movements of funds linked to the fraud case.

What do we know about Cyvers?

It’s an Israeli blockchain security company.

Its co-founder and CEO, Deddy Lavid, says he worked on Israel’s Iron Dome system in 2015.

He also says co-founder Meir Dolev served as a sergeant reporting to him when Lavid was an infantry company commander in the military reserves.

Elron Ventures disclosed approximately 26% ownership of Cyvers as of June 2026, excluding additional convertible investments.

Elron also has the right to appoint a Cyvers board member.

And Elron has a longstanding partnership with Rafael Advanced Defense Systems through Rafael Development Corporation, RDC.

Elron owns 50.1% of RDC.

Rafael owns 49.9%.

RDC has rights to commercialise Rafael’s military technologies for civilian markets.

The distinction matters: Elron holds its Cyvers stake directly. These disclosures do not establish Rafael ownership of Cyvers.

Lavid has also described working with EY and holding discussions with Israeli banks, including CBDC-related discussions.

So the documented connections include military service, Iron Dome experience, financial-sector CBDC relationships and an investor with a Rafael joint venture.

It’s important to understand the incentives behind the information that’s being fed through.

Because they almost always say it’s North Korea.

text:
筛选了 15 个构建在 @Enter_Elysium 上的早期 Alpha 项目，先关注上，等机会出现。

Elysium 是 Kinetiq 为 Hyperliquid 打造的 L2 公链，将在 11 月 9 日正式上线主网。

Hyperliquid 我认为是这两年币圈表现最好的项目，没有之一。

所以，下一波机会可能在围绕订单簿增长的应用生态，Elysium 值得重点关注。

👇15 个 Elysium 生态项目清单：

1⃣AscendLaunch（ @AscendLaunch ）
- 项目定位：官方味道最浓的发射台，专门帮新项目在 Elysium 上发币。
- 项目评分：9.2/10
- 参与机会：测试网有白名单、Builder 活动（给真金白银资助），主网第一天就开，抓平台金狗机会。
- 项目评价：目前最像「亲儿子」的发射台，跟 Kinetiq 团队走得近。他们不搞自己先抽一波的套路，赚的钱更多是反哺项目和 HYPE/KNTQ，长期看比较靠谱。

2⃣Kalos（ @kalosfun ）
- 项目定位：现在测试网上最热闹的交易平台，既能买卖代币，也能交易 NFT，什么都能玩。
- 项目评分：9.0/10
- 参与机会：现在交易、做流动性、买卖 NFT 都能拿积分（主网有加成），马上还有 Genesis NFT 可以抢。
- 项目评价：测试网绝对的龙头，交易量和用户数都碾压别人。已经被 Ascend 选为首个孵化项目，后面发币的分配也偏向真实用户，值得重点盯。

3⃣xStocksFi（ @xStocksFi ）
- 项目定位：把美股、ETF 变成链上代币来交易的官方项目（Payward 旗下）。
- 项目评分：8.8/10
- 参与机会：主网第一天就能直接用，跟各种发射台、DEX 都能配合，本身也有发币预期。
- 项目评价：Elysium 官方亲自欢迎的项目。股票 + 土狗这个组合是后面很大的看点，正规军背景，流动性不用太担心。

4⃣Matcha（ @matchaxyz ）
- 项目定位：老牌聚合器（0x 做的），帮你在各个交易所里找最好的价格成交。
- 项目评分：8.7/10
- 参与机会：主网第一天就上线，正常交易就行。
- 项目评价：产品已经很成熟了，不用担心小团队跑路。以后生态发射台一堆，用它交易最省心。

5⃣DeriveXYZ（ @DeriveXYZ ）
- 项目定位：专门做链上期权的平台，交易 BTC、ETH、HYPE 等。
- 项目评分：8.6/10
- 参与机会：主网第一天就开，还有跟 Kinetiq 一起的交易赛（奖 kHYPE）。
- 项目评价：期权赛道头部玩家，官方也强推。Elysium 速度快，特别适合这种专业交易产品。

6⃣HybraFinance + Navo（ @HybraFinance /  @navodotfamily ）
- 项目定位：Hybra 是 Hyperliquid 上已经有的流动性平台，Navo 是他们做的社区发射台。
- 项目评分：8.5/10
- 参与机会：主网第一天就部署，Navo 发币创建者能拿 70% 交易费。
- 项目评价：老项目了，社区所有权做得比较实在。发射台和流动性绑定在一起，不是纯炒作，后面有持续玩法。

7⃣Stockium（ @Stockium ）
- 项目定位：发币时可以直接跟股票代币配对，还能让持币人分到股票。
- 项目评分：8.3/10
- 参与机会：测试网已经在活跃，有回购销毁记录，还能用他们的交易终端。
- 项目评价：玩法比较新，持币直接分股票这个点有意思。团队也比较活跃，回购销毁能查到链上记录。

8⃣eleosfun（ @eleosfun ）
- 项目定位：功能比较全的发射台，支持多种发币方式，也能跟股票配对。
- 项目评分：8.2/10
- 参与机会：测试网期间发币几乎不花钱（他们帮你出 Gas），持币能自动分 HYPE。
- 项目评价：玩法设计得比较细，反狙击和持有者友好机制都做了，比很多纯土狗发射台用心。

9⃣BunnyPad（ @Bunnypadfun ）
- 项目定位：主打「公平发射」的发射台，一笔交易发完，没有团队预留，池子永久锁定。
- 项目评分：8.0/10
- 参与机会：测试网交易和发射都能拿积分，主网可能有空投资格。
- 项目评价：测试网交易量不小，公平机制是它的最大卖点，我挺看好这个平台发射出来的项目

🔟Oxley（ @oxleydotfun ）
- 项目定位：用拍卖的方式来发币，让价格更公平一点。
- 项目评分：7.9/10
- 参与机会：测试网可以参与拍卖，找 Bug 还能拿 HYPE 奖励。
- 项目评价：增长数据不错，是真有人在用。解决了传统发射容易被控盘的问题，产品迭代也比较快。

1⃣1⃣aka. fun（ @akadotfun ）
- 项目定位：用 Uniswap V4 做的发射台，主打 Meme + 真实资产奖励。
- 项目评分：7.8/10
- 参与机会：测试网已经上线，可以直接玩。
- 项目评价：测试网活跃度还可以，粉丝也不少。后面跟真实资产结合是它的看点。

1⃣2⃣PerpMe（ @perpmefun ）
- 项目定位：用 Uniswap V3 做的发射台，支持跟股票代币配对，还有早期桥接功能。
- 项目评分：7.7/10
- 参与机会：测试网就能发币交易，也可以提前体验桥。
- 项目评价：比较早的玩家，创建者拿的手续费比例高。适合喜欢短线的人看看。

1⃣3⃣Elyziumaa（ @Elyziumaa ）
- 项目定位：现在测试网上比较火的 NFT 系列，挂在 Kalos 上交易。
- 项目评分：7.5/10
- 参与机会：可以去抢白名单和 Mint，之后在 Kalos 上交易。
- 项目评价：NFT 热度在前面，叙事跟生态贴得比较紧，有 Kalos 撑着，流动性相对稳一些。

1⃣4⃣Hyperion_RPG（ @Hyperion_RPG ）
- 项目定位：风险越高奖励越高的链上 RPG 游戏。
- 项目评分：7.3/10
- 参与机会：测试网就能玩，主网上线后有排行榜奖励。
- 项目评价：游戏方向比较少见，玩法有点意思。生态里游戏还不多，有一定差异化。

1⃣5⃣Elysium Name Service（ @ElysiumNames ）
- 项目定位：Elysium 上的域名服务（.ely 结尾的名字）。
- 项目评分：7.2/10
- 参与机会：现在就能注册和交易域名，主网可以抢好名字，顺手申请下，等个福报。
- 项目评价：属于基础设施，后面有真实需求。早期成本不高，玩法简单直接。

以上就是聪哥个人筛选的 Elysium 生态15个潜力项目，不少项目测试网期间是有奖励的，有精力的可以顺手交互下。

另外，Elysium 还未正式主网已经有人偷渡在玩了，个人不建议去找未经验证的跨链桥偷渡，有很大的风险，耐心等待官方主网上线用官方和正规第三方跨链桥参与。

text:
스티브 잡스 아들내미 근황
 "내 평생을 걸고 암 조진다" 선언 ㄷㄷ

2011년에 스티브 잡스가 췌장암으로 떠난 건 다들 알 거임. 
그 아들 리드 잡스(Reed Jobs)가 지금 뭐 하고 있나 봤더니, VC(벤처캐피털) 차려서 암 정복하겠다고 인생 올인 박음 ㅋ

펀드 이름은 '요세미티(Yosemite)'인데, 일반적인 투자사들이랑 굴러가는 뽄새가 완전 다름

• 딴 거 안 보고 바이오테크 파이의 40% 먹는 '종양학(Oncology)'에만 올인 몰빵함
• 대학 연구실에 "돈 벌어오라" 조건도 안 달고 쌩으로 연구비 꽂아줘서 초기 리스크 다 지워줌
• 예일, 버클리, 스탠포드 석학들이랑 붙어서 아예 회사 3분의 1을 자체적으로 직접 빌딩해버림
• 펀드 1호로 20개 기업 꽂았고, 펀드 2호는 목표치 3.5억 달러(약 4,800억) 가뿐히 넘겨서 오버서브스크라이브 달성함. 
파트너로 애브비 $ABBV 랑 암젠 $AMGN 같은 빅파마 거물들도 묻어둠 ㅎㄷㄷ

기자가 "만약 아버지가 살아계셨다면 뭐라고 하셨을 것 같냐"고 물어보니까,

"하던 거 계속해라... 이건 내 평생을 갈아 넣어야 할 롱텀 플레이(Long-term play)다." 라고 답함.

그리고 가장 빡센 점이 뭐냐고 하니까, 
본인도 원래 존나 성격 급한 놈인데 암 정복은 원래 평생 걸리는 작업이라는 걸 인정하고 버티는 게 '진짜 규율(Discipline)'이라고 털어놓음.

인내심이라는 건 그냥 타고난 성격이 아니라, 
매 순간 이 악물고 내리는 선택이라는 거임. 
잡스 유전자가 딴 데로 안 가고 진짜 멋진 곳으로 향했네 🤯

text:
Backpack是不是正好踩在了合规的风口？
 
“针对Crypto合规外溢和长臂监管的政策呼声，终于来了！”
 
刚刚刷到 @cryptobraveHQ 的爆料，CFTC主席 ChairmanSelig 彻底摊牌了。他不仅拿起了“长臂管辖”的武器，还给所有离岸加密货币交易所下了一道“最后通牒”。
 
简单总结一下核心重点，刀刀见血：
 
🔥 1. 离岸所的“裸奔”时代即将终结
CFTC主席明确表示：不受美国监管的离岸交易所，根本不具备成熟市场的安全保障。以后，哪怕是离岸所，也必须归美国监管、在CFTC注册，并采用“美国级别”的网络安全标准。
 
🔥 2. 64亿美元盗窃案成“催化剂”
监管者正在利用这起惊天大案，推动制定联邦规则手册。虽然目前说的是“自愿注册”，但懂的都懂，在美国监管的字典里，“自愿”往往意味着“你不来，我就查你”。美国监管者要亲自下场当一线“巡逻警察”了。
 
🔥 3. 币安的前车之鉴：28.5亿美元的沉重代价
大家还记得2023年币安那笔43.68亿美元的天价和解案吗？其中CFTC一家就开出了约28.5亿美元的民事罚没，是整包罚单里最重的一棍！这也向全行业释放了一个极其强烈的信号：不合规，就是天价罚单伺候。
 
🧐 那么问题来了，如果这波监管铁拳砸下来，谁在偷着乐？
 
很多人第一反应就是：Backpack！
 
在当下这个极其看重“合规”和“透明度”的周期里，Backpack 这种从一开始就死死咬住美国合规路线（甚至曾试图收购受监管牌照）、主打安全和传统金融级别体验的交易所，简直是精准踩中了时代的红利。
 
以前大家玩离岸所，图的是杠杆高、不KYC。但现在，随着CFTC铁幕落下，大资金和传统机构入场，他们看重的只有一个：安全与合规。
 
当离岸所们还在为了“如何应对美国长臂管辖”而焦头烂额，甚至面临巨额罚款时，像 Backpack 这样早早穿上“合规防弹衣”的选手，反而成了承接这波“合规外溢”资金的最佳避风港。
 
风口不是等来的，是提前布局出来的。
监管的靴子落地，对野蛮生长的交易所是末日，但对合规先驱来说，或许正是黄金时代的开端。

quoted_text:
It’s a wrap! It was an honor to help organize the Fast Finality workshop in Cambridge.

There have already been some great recaps, but here’s my quick overview of the main topics we covered:

1. Deep-diving DC: Decoupled Consensus is a super ambitious upgrade we hope to ship in I* (h/t @benjaminion_xyz). @robsaltini gave a great overview, and @fradamt unveiled his impressive recent breakthroughs, e.g. achieving short-term async resilience through local locks.

2. Shipping DC: Sessions on critical research and engineering, including networking benchmarks & devnets (@sukunrt & Csaba), rewards & incentives (@weboftrees), and specs & testing (@mkalinin2, @jtraglia, @tcoratger).

3. Securing DC: Formal verification meets fast finality. We explored exciting new AI-enabled opportunities (@fradamt & @robsaltini), building on years of great FV work (@alexanderlhicks).

4. Future of Fast Finality: Aligning DC with future needs. This covered PQ networking (@kamil_abiy & @kevaundray), finality in tens of seconds with PQ validators (@barnabemonnot), lean clients & prototyping (@pablodeymo, Mega, Mihir, Locky, @adust09, @ladislaus0x), and one-round finality & other future research (shoutout @alranpe, @jneu_net, @ittai & Neil).

Huge thanks to everyone who made this workshop a success! Special thanks to @benjaminion_xyz for all the help and guidance, and of course to @justindrake and @willcorcoran for making it possible!
